Accurately measuring uncertainty in machine learning models is crucial to evaluating the reliability of their predictions. However, the quality of these estimates can be compromised by several factors, particularly model misspecification, a pervasive issue due to models being simplifications or approximations of reality. It remains unclear whether estimated uncertainty holds up in the face of model misspecification, prompting the need to elevate this consideration. We advocate for a more nuanced approach by means of theoretical illustrations and informed references to existing literature.

Integer programming's branch-and-bound methods require determining the order of nodes to explore next, a problem known as node comparison. To address this, a novel siamese graph neural network model is proposed that represents nodes as bipartite graphs with attributes. By mimicking a diving oracle that converges to the optimal solution, the model is trained. Evaluation of this approach reveals that it outperforms SCIP's default ranking function and competing machine learning methods in terms of solving speed and branch-and-bound tree size on three NP-hard benchmarks. Furthermore, its results generalize to larger instances beyond the training set. The experiment code is publicly available on GitHub.

We investigate a specific type of Markov game where multiple agents collaborate or compete to achieve a goal, represented by nonlinear functions. We concentrate on low-dimensional Markov games with underlying structures that are difficult to identify. Our objective is to develop an efficient algorithm that can discover an approximate optimal policy without prior knowledge of the game environment or its representation. Furthermore, we want the algorithm to be compatible with deep learning. By utilizing representation learning, we devise both model-based and model-free approaches to build a data-driven representation. Our methods achieve an optimal solution within a sample complexity of poly(H, d, A, 1/ε), where H is the game duration, d is the feature vector dimension, A is the joint action space size, and ε is the optimality gap. However, when dealing with a large number of agents, this approach can lead to an exponential increase in computational requirements. To address this issue, we consider a specific type of Markov game where the transition structure can be factored. Our results provide a sample-efficient algorithm that overcomes the exponential scaling challenge, making it the first algorithm of its kind to efficiently incorporate nonlinear function approximation in multi-agent general-sum Markov games. We complement our theoretical findings with a neural network implementation of our algorithm, comparing its performance against a widely used baseline.

The Data Bricks Space Mission is a pilot program that uses interactive data
representation to engage students aged 10-12 in data literacy. The project's design
was informed by a review of existing research and discussions with elementary school
educators. By leveraging Lego bricks and a narrative space exploration theme, the
activity aims to enable kids to collect data, convey their insights, and deepen their
understanding of the connection between data and the world at large.

Accurate space situational awareness, especially in the low Earth orbit region, relies heavily on precise orbit predictions. However, the uncertainty in atmospheric density estimation poses a significant challenge. This paper explores the impact of density uncertainty on orbit error distribution. To achieve this, probabilistic machine learning techniques are utilized, incorporating models such as HASDM-ML, CHAMP-ML, and MSIS-UQ. The study involves multiple Monte Carlo methods to capture different spatiotemporal correlations of atmospheric density values, but due to their computational expense, an alternative Kalman filtering technique is investigated. A novel filter, the consider covariance sigma point (CCSP) filter, is applied to address density uncertainty in orbit propagation. To validate its effectiveness, a comparison is conducted between CCSP and Monte Carlo methods. Finally, an ensemble approach is proposed for quantifying orbit uncertainty under diverse space weather conditions using HASDM-ML, CHAMP-ML, and MSIS-UQ models.

Conventional cluster-robust standard errors are not as robust as they seem. They're particularly susceptible to data sets that feature a small number of large clusters, an issue that becomes evident when considering a sample that spans 51 US states - in this case, California comprises roughly 10% of the sample. This scenario, unfortunately, contravenes the assumptions required for widely used cluster-robust methods to be reliable. Our research demonstrates that these conventional methods will fail if cluster sizes adhere to a power law with an exponent below two. We reference actual research examples and propose an alternative, the weighted cluster-robust method, as a straightforward solution to overcome the limitations of existing cluster-robust methods. Simulation studies confirm that the weighted method outperforms the conventional approach under similar conditions.

The difficulty in utilizing dynamic graphs for predictive tasks arises from 
extracting detailed temporal patterns within an evolving graph, coupled with 
limited, costly, and imbalanced task labels for complex dynamic graphs.
Recent graph self-supervised learning developments have shown promise but are 
focusing on static graphs. Current state-of-the-art models for dynamic graphs not 
only conflict with the self-supervised learning paradigm but also struggle to 
forecast long-term interactions. To overcome these constraints, we introduce 
DyG2Vec, an efficient self-supervised learning model for representation learning 
on dynamic graphs. By employing a window-based approach, DyG2Vec generates 
task-agnostic node embeddings that enable forecasting of future interactions. 
Our results demonstrate that DyG2Vec outperforms state-of-the-art benchmarks on 
target datasets while achieving significantly reduced training and inference times. 
We extend two self-supervised learning evaluation methods to accommodate dynamic 
graphs, thereby illustrating the effectiveness of SSL pre-training in learning 
more resilient temporal node representations, particularly for scenarios with few 
labels.

In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson introduced a local and combinatorial formula for calculating the Pontrjagin classes of a differential manifold, building upon which, we present an in-depth exploration of their findings and delve into the inception of combinatorial differential manifolds in their research.

The revival of interest in fission fragment angular momentum research is driven by recent findings. The examination of neutrons and gamma rays in conjunction with fission fragments remains essential to understanding fission physics. In order to accomplish this goal, we developed an integrated system consisting of an advanced fission fragment detector and neutron-gamma radiation sensors. A novel, two-part Frisch-gridded ionization chamber has been engineered for the purpose of utilizing a spontaneous fission source in conjunction with a 40-trans-stilbene organic scintillator array at the Argonne National Laboratory. This new ionization chamber design aims at reducing particle obstruction within the chamber walls and creating a compact device suitable for placement within existing experimental frameworks. The chamber is capable of measuring fission fragment masses and kinetic energies, whereas the scintillator array captures neutron and gamma-ray frequencies and multiplicities. This document outlines the assembly details of both detectors, including the first experimental outcomes obtained using the proposed setup. Upcoming event-by-event analysis and future experiments are also briefly mentioned.

A hypothetical model for neutron star scalarization proposed by Damour and Esposito-Farese indicates that a general relativistic branch can become unstable, leading to rapid growth of a scalar field phi toward a scalarized branch. However, this instability doesn't align with inflation and matter dominance periods during cosmology, as well as constraints imposed by our solar system's current field value. A study involving a coupling between phi and an inflaton field suggests that an inflated phi value can be suppressed by an inflation-driven mass rate, while the scalar field phi can remain relatively small even when its value grows in later epochs. Researchers analyzed the phi dynamics throughout various cosmological periods, including the reheating epoch, with a focus on specified inflaton potentials. In certain scenarios, a parametric resonance enhances phi values through the oscillations of the inflaton. However, the effects of particle creation are found to significantly diminish the maximum phi values achieved during preheating, under a specific approximation. Moreover, it is discovered that a range of g values is acceptable to meet solar system phi bounds at the end of the reheating epoch, with the minimum required values being in the order of 10^-5. As a result, this cosmological model, based on the proposal by Anson et al., leads to viable and consistent evolution for phi without modifying neutron star scalarization properties.

Classifying objects in LiDAR 3D point cloud data is essential for modern applications such as self-driving vehicles. However, annotating these point cloud data sets is time-consuming due to the need for human analysts to view and inspect the data from multiple viewpoints. To address this challenge, we introduce a semi-supervised cross-domain learning approach that doesn't rely on human annotation of point clouds and produces results comparable to fully-supervised methods. By leveraging pre-existing 3D object models, our approach trains classifiers that can generalize to real-world point cloud data. We simulate the acquisition of real-world data by sampling object models from various viewpoints and with arbitrary partial occlusions, then augment the generated point clouds through random rotations and noise addition to better emulate real-world scenarios. We train models such as DGCNN and PointNet++ on these synthesized datasets and assess their performance on real-world datasets. Additionally, we introduce a new benchmark dataset called Point-Syn2Real, designed specifically for cross-domain learning on point clouds. Experimental results using this dataset show that our proposed cross-domain learning approach significantly outperforms related and state-of-the-art methods in both indoor and outdoor settings in terms of cross-domain adaptability. The associated code and data will be publicly available after publication.

This paper introduces novel attacks on federated learning when applied to text models, specifically targeting Google's GBoard app. Our research shows that the words entered on a user's mobile device, even during routine tasks like sending messages, can be accurately retrieved in various scenarios. Moreover, we found that countermeasures like mini-batches and noise addition are insufficient. Notably, we were able to reconstruct the word order and sentence structure with high accuracy, highlighting serious privacy implications given GBoard's use in production environments.

In 2019, researchers successfully constructed a pair of operators in Banach spaces that are equivalent after extension but not Schur coupled, answering a long-standing question posed by Bart and Tsekanovskii in the 1990s. The newly constructed operators are defined on Banach spaces with no specific incomparability conditions, which is an essential departure from the previous context. The paper investigates equivalence after extension and Schur coupling for Fredholm operators on arbitrary Banach spaces and reveals a crucial connection between these two concepts. The results show that for a fixed index k, the set of pairs of Schur coupled Fredholm operators on two Banach spaces X and Y is either empty or consists entirely of equivalent after extension pairs, thus establishing that the coincidence of these two concepts depends solely on the geometry of the Banach spaces. The authors then introduce two numerical indices to capture this coincidence and analyze its relationship with the geometry of Banach spaces. Additionally, they present various examples based on exotic Banach spaces and illustrate the possible values of these indices, showcasing their interplay with the geometric properties of the Banach spaces.

We have introduced new limitations on the principles that guide galaxy formation, 
specifically at very high redshifts ($z\gtrsim7$) and in ultra-faint dwarf galaxies 
like Eridanus II with masses of approximately  $10^5$ solar masses. Utilizing a 
hierarchical Bayesian framework and a one-zone chemical evolution model, we've 
determined that Eridanus II underwent a brief, rapidly declining period of star 
formation (lasting 0.39 Gyr with a significant uncertainty of $\pm_{0.13}^{0.18}$ 
Gyr), had a relatively low star-formation efficiency, and a high rate of mass loss 
due to outflows ($194.53\pm_{42.67}^{33.37}$). Our findings are consistent with 
Eri II's stars being primarily formed before the reionization era ended. The high 
rate of mass loss observed is in line with theoretical expectations for strong, 
momentum-driven outflows, leading to over 90% of the produced metals being ejected. 
Our predictions for the distribution of magnesium and iron abundance in Eri II and 
the presence of ultra-metal poor stars can be verified by future abundance 
measurements. Further spectroscopic studies of Eri II's highest metallicity stars 
would greatly enhance the precision of our model constraints. This novel 
framework can be applied to other Local Group ultra-faint dwarf galaxies to gain 
new insights into the physics governing the evolution of the most faint galaxies 
that existed during the reionization era.

The distribution of hydrogen content in galaxies across all stages of evolution is described by the neutral atomic hydrogen mass function (HIMF), which serves as a crucial testing ground for models of galaxy formation and evolution. Our study utilizes Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope HI 21cm spectroscopy to investigate blue star-forming galaxies at $z\approx0.20-0.42$ in the Extended Groth Strip. By combining the HI 21cm signals of galaxy subsamples with different absolute B-band magnitudes, we established a scaling relation between the average HI mass ($\rm{M_{HI}}$) and the absolute B-band magnitude ($\rm{M_B}$) of these galaxies at $z \approx 0.35$. This scaling relation, which is crucial to estimating the HIMF at $z\approx0.35$, was determined by stacking HI 21cm emission signals in various $\rm{M_B}$ ranges. We then combined this relation with the known B-band luminosity function of star-forming galaxies at the same redshift to calculate the HIMF at $z\approx0.35$. Our results reveal that the HIMF underwent a significant evolution from $z\approx0.35$ to $z\approx0$, specifically in the high-mass end, with a notable decrease in high-mass galaxies ($\rm{M_{HI} \gtrsim 10^{10}\ M_\odot}$) and an increase in low-mass galaxies ($\rm{M_{HI} \approx 10^9\ M_\odot}$). Despite potential cosmic variance, our findings indicate that massive star-forming galaxies have accumulated a considerable amount of hydrogen via merger events or accretion from the circumgalactic medium over the past four Gyr.

This article focuses on dispersive flows with cubic nonlinearity in one dimension. The authors previously proposed a conjecture for these flows in the defocusing case, stating that small initial data leads to global scattering solutions. The conjecture was proven for Schrödinger dispersion, with global solutions meeting $L^6$ Strichartz estimates and bilinear $L^2$ bounds without localization assumptions. This article addresses the focusing scenario where small solitons may form, precluding general global scattering solutions. Instead, we examine long-term solutions and the time-scale on which they exist and meet desired estimates. Our main result, also applicable to the Schrödinger dispersion relation, shows that solutions exist for $\epsilon^{-8}$ time with $\epsilon^{-6}$ time-scale $L^6$ Strichartz estimates and bilinear $L^2$ bounds, representing the first achievement of this threshold.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares have been observed using high-precision photometry from space missions such as Kepler and TESS, which are essential for determining biosignatures and ultraviolet radiation dosages for habitable exoplanets. However, current assessments lack near-ultraviolet data of stellar flares. To address this, a grid of radiative-hydrodynamic simulations was employed to forecast the near-ultraviolet flux during a superflare from AD Leo, utilizing a model consisting of high and low energy electron beams. These simulations accurately predict the broadening of hydrogen lines, continuum colors, and far-ultraviolet strength during the flare's rise and peak phases. By comparing the results with solar flare data, the model can be interpreted as the combination of intense, bright kernels and fainter, more widespread ribbons.

We investigate the dynamics of the coupled system, comprised of a physical pendulum with a cavity filled by a viscous and compressible fluid. The fluid's influence can significantly impact the pendulum's motion. Specifically, under certain conditions, the fluid behaves as a damper, driving the coupled system towards a stable equilibrium state characterized by a steady density distribution of the fluid and a centered position of the system's mass. This conclusion is established within a broad framework of weak solutions and holds regardless of the initial conditions, provided the system has a finite energy level. To supplement our findings, we also present numerical simulations that demonstrate the intriguing phenomenon where increased fluid compressibility accelerates the damping process, thereby shortening the time required for the system to reach equilibrium.

We characterise countable locally standard measure algebras via pairs of Steinitz numbers and a real number greater than or equal to one, drawing inspiration from J.Dixmier's and A.A.Baranov's theorems.

Recommender systems encounter challenges whenever a new user or item is introduced. To resolve item-related issues, we introduce a dynamic storage mechanism that replaces the traditional embedding layer, allowing for an indefinite number of representations without requiring learnable weights. Our proposed model, FELRec, is a comprehensive embedding network that iteratively refines existing user and item representations as new information emerges. This approach differs from comparable models by representing new entities without supplementary data or time-consuming fine-tuning. Notably, FELRec outperforms analogous models by a substantial margin of 29.50% to 47.45% in the case of item-related cold-start scenarios. Furthermore, our model exhibits strong generalizability to unseen datasets. The source code for FELRec is available on GitHub at kweimann/FELRec.

Modularizing a transducer model for end-to-end speech recognition poses a significant challenge due to its absence of distinct components for the acoustic model, language model, and blank model. To address this, a modular hybrid autoregressive transducer (MHAT) is introduced, which features separate decoders for labels and blanks and a shared acoustic encoder to predict respective distributions. The encoder and label decoder outputs are directly mapped onto the acoustic model and internal language model scores, then combined to produce label posteriors. MHAT is trained with both internal language model loss and HAT loss, allowing the internal language model to be adapted effectively for text-based applications. Additionally, MHAT's text adaptation enables a more efficient language model fusion than methods based on internal language model subtraction, leading to improved results on a large production dataset. A multi-domain MHAT model adapted with 100 billion sentences demonstrates relative word error rate reductions of up to 12.4% without language model fusion and 21.5% with fusion compared to a 400,000-hour trained HAT.

Complex models have been employed to find approximate solutions to NP-hard combinatorial problems, including graph vertex classification. This method, which determines an optimal boundary between vertices, has been effectively used for the maximum clique enumeration problem by applying a pruning process through a learning framework. We investigated various vertex representations, utilizing techniques such as Node2vec, DeepWalk, and higher-order graph features. Our findings suggest that Node2vec and DeepWalk are viable node embedding methods for classification purposes, while incorporating local graph features with feature elimination enhances accuracy. Furthermore, we demonstrated the effectiveness and scalability of our approach on random graphs.

This study investigates how high-frequency waves behave when traveling through complex, highly-scattering materials that also exhibit a nonlinear form of energy absorption. We employ advanced mathematical tools including the Wigner transform and multiscale analysis to develop semilinear models that describe how the intensity of these waves propagates through space and how they behave over various scales. Additionally, we examine the diffusion of these waves and the resulting transport models. Furthermore, we address a specific challenge: using information about the wave's solution to calculate the material's absorption coefficients, ultimately proving that this process has a unique outcome.

Melanoma arises from the uncontrolled multiplication of melanocytes within human skin, a condition that can be successfully treated through early detection. The ability of medical professionals to accurately diagnose this life-threatening skin cancer is greatly aided by the application of automated skin lesion segmentation. Several Fully Convolutional Network (FCN) models, notably the U-Net architecture, have been developed specifically for this task and have achieved impressive results. However, a significant drawback of the U-Net design lies in its convolutional operation limitations, which restrict its capacity to capture complex relationships between distant features. To overcome this limitation, researchers have developed Transformer-based alternatives, such as the Swin Transformer, to enable the network to identify both local and global patterns. Our research focuses on enhancing the performance of the Swin U-Net architecture through the incorporation of an attention mechanism into the skip connection path. By conducting an exhaustive comparison of our proposed design with existing models on various skin lesion segmentation datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the attention mechanism and its ability to improve the accuracy of skin cancer diagnosis.

Structural searches under high pressure on superhydrides CeBeH$_8$ and CeBH$_8$ have been conducted up to 300 GPa at ambient conditions. Our findings reveal that $Fm\overline{3}m$-CeBeH$_8$ is a superconductor with a critical transition temperature of 56 K at 10 GPa. The pressure increase also led to the discovery of two more phases with space groups $R\overline{3}m$ and $C2/m$. In a similar manner, CeBH$_8$ underwent a phase transition with higher transition pressures and critical temperatures. We found that $Fm\overline{3}m$-CeBH$_8$ is predicted to be superconducting above 120 GPa with a maximum critical transition temperature of 118 K at 150 GPa. The other two phases, $R\overline{3}m$-CeBH$_8$ and $C2/m$-CeBH$_8$, are dynamically stable above 120 GPa and 100 GPa respectively. Moreover, $R\overline{3}m$-CeBH$_8$ achieved its maximum critical transition temperature of 123 K at 195 GPa and $C2/m$-CeBH$_8$ reached a maximum critical transition temperature of 115 K at 350 GPa. This study contributes to the family of ternary hydrides and provides valuable insights for further searches of superconducting hydrides under low and moderate pressures.

The transport of biomolecules across cell membranes is a crucial process underlying the biological functions of cells. In this research, we examine the translocation of polymers through a conical pore by employing molecular dynamics simulations. Our investigation focuses on how variations in the pore geometry and polymer length influence translocation times, waiting times, and velocity profiles. To highlight the impact of asymmetric pore geometry, we compare translocation processes initiated from both ends of the conical pore. Our results reveal distinct translocation dynamics, consistent with experimental findings, and demonstrate the influence of polymer rigidity and chain length on both processes. These findings can inform our understanding of the transition from direction-dependent to direction-independent translocation through asymmetric channels.

The goal of precision agriculture is to leverage advanced technology in the agricultural industry to boost efficiency, lower operational expenses, and minimize the use of resources. This research is influenced by the way bees see and incorporates ultraviolet-reflectance into a flower detection system using remote sensing. We show how this approach yields high-quality images for deep learning-based strawberry flower identification and implement it within a cost-efficient and scalable robotic aerial monitoring system. Additionally, we compare the effectiveness of our UV, green, and blue image detector with a comparable work using traditional red, green, and blue images.

We have combined the EUHFORIA and iPATH models to simulate a major 2020 solar event and compared our findings with real-time data from various spacecraft, including PSP, STEREO-A, SOHO, and Solar Orbiter. Our focus was on how past shock acceleration influenced the SEP time intensity profiles, which revealed the importance of a realistic solar wind in shock expansion and characteristics. Our simulations accurately recreated the time intensity profiles at PSP and showed a similar two-phase enhancement at STEREO-A. These results emphasize the need for realistic solar wind models in SEP event characterization. The modelled decay phase at Earth matched observational data, highlighting the significance of perpendicular diffusion in widespread SEP events. When accounting for curved magnetic field lines at Solar Orbiter, our modelled time intensity profiles were in good agreement with observations. This suggests that distorted magnetic field lines due to a stream interaction region may have played a crucial role in the SEP event observed at Solar Orbiter.

This study examines personalized dosing strategies through Bayesian optimization, 
which determines the optimal medication dosage for each individual, ultimately 
enhancing treatment efficacy. Safe learning techniques, specifically the interior 
point method, are employed to guarantee patient safety with a high degree of 
certainty. The proposed method is applied to the task of determining the 
optimal bolus insulin dosage for individuals with type 1 diabetes to counteract 
post-meal fluctuations. Our algorithm, which starts with no prior knowledge of 
the patients, successfully improves treatment outcomes (measured in % time-in-
range) while ensuring patient safety is not compromised. The method's potential 
for other healthcare applications is also explored.

Point cloud data is extensively used in various scientific disciplines and is now being effectively analyzed using geometric deep learning (GDL) for prediction tasks. However, the complexity and lack of interpretability in GDL models make it challenging for scientists to use them in research and experiments. A novel approach called learnable randomness injection (LRI) is proposed to build inherently interpretable models based on established GDL frameworks. LRI enables trained models to pinpoint specific points in the data that are indicative of the predicted outcome. To evaluate the effectiveness of LRI, this work presents four datasets from real-world scientific applications spanning high-energy physics and biochemistry. The results show that LRI performs significantly better than previous methods for interpreting complex models, producing results that are more consistent with scientifically meaningful patterns. Furthermore, LRI-induced models exhibit improved robustness when dealing with variations in data distribution. All relevant code and datasets are freely available at a specified GitHub repository.

This paper presents a potential-based reward shaping mechanism known as Value Iteration Network for Reward Shaping (VIN-RS), which utilizes a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). The VIN-RS system incorporates a CNN trained on computed labels by employing the message passing mechanism of the Hidden Markov Model, allowing it to process environment images or graphs and predict shaping values. A key limitation of previous reward shaping methods is their inability to effectively train on Markov Decision Process (MDP) representations and estimate transition matrices. VIN-RS addresses this issue by constructing a potential function from an estimated MDP while automatically inferring the environment transition matrix, with the CNN learning the transition matrix through self-extracted convolutional filters. Leveraging previous successes in using message passing for reward shaping and the CNN's planning behavior, the VIN-RS system uses these messages to train its CNN. Experiments conducted on various environments, including tabular games, Atari 2600, and MuJoCo, with both discrete and continuous action spaces, demonstrate promising improvements in learning speed and maximum cumulative reward compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Segerman's 15+4 puzzle is a variation of the classic 15-puzzle, with the added feature of tiles that rotate when sliding. In 1974, Wilson established the classification of solution groups for standard sliding puzzles. Our study extends Wilson's work to include puzzles with rotational capabilities, such as the 15+4 puzzle, in which the solution sets are subgroups of generalized symmetric groups. Notably, with a couple of exceptions, the solution group of such a puzzle is either the entire generalized symmetric group or one of its specific subgroups of order two.
This paper disputes certain claims made by Marques and Lengyel regarding the p-adic valuations found in the Tribonacci sequence.

Flow visualization tools like particle tracking velocimetry are extensively employed in understanding complex three-dimensional turbulent flows that occur naturally and in industrial processes. Although advancements have been made in acquiring three-dimensional data, existing algorithms for particle tracking struggle with large particle movements, densely populated particle distributions, and high computational costs. To address these challenges, a novel deep learning network called GotFlow3D, which is based on a combination of recurrent Graph Optimal Transport, is introduced as a solution to learn 3D fluid flow dynamics directly from particle image pairs. The network constructs two graphs and combines particle representations with learned features from a graph neural network, enabling the extraction of optimal transport plans that establish correspondences between particle pairs. These correspondences are iteratively refined to inform the recurrent flow learning process. Experimental results, including simulations and real-world experiments, demonstrate that GotFlow3D outperforms other scene flow learners and particle tracking methods in terms of accuracy, robustness, and generalizability, providing valuable insights into intricate physical and biological systems.

At the core of numerous intriguing optical and acoustic phenomena in non-conservative systems lies an anomaly known as an exceptional point. Despite extensive research over the past two decades, there has been a lack of understanding of the collective behaviors exhibited by multiple exceptional points and their interactions. We've discovered a universal rule governing these behaviors in multiband non-Hermitian systems and revealed several counter-intuitive phenomena. Our research shows that two exceptional points, regardless of how they were created, may not annihilate each other if they approach each other in a certain way. Additionally, the rule imposes specific constraints on the configurations of exceptional lines, excluding certain structures while allowing for novel arrangements like staggered rings composed of non-commutative lines. These findings have been illustrated using concrete models that can be easily implemented in various platforms, paving the way for a deeper understanding of exceptional non-Abelian topology and its potential applications.

Electrical system malfunctions can trigger fires, result in electrocution, and impair the infrastructure itself. Detecting High Impedance Faults (HIF), despite being hazardous, is particularly difficult due to their lower fault currents, time-varying characteristics, and non-linear behavior. Given New Zealand's extensive and largely unmonitored distribution networks, finding effective HIF detection schemes is an ongoing research focus. 

We have established a physical testing facility for analyzing power system faults, which we've utilized to develop and assess a fault detection system. By simulating Low and High Impedance Faults with varied fault surface materials and load-switching scenarios, we have documented the distinct fault patterns for both types of faults in 400V systems and trained an AI-based classifier to identify fault types based on unique characteristics. We've designed and installed a pole-mountable sensing system within Wellington Electricity's network for ongoing evaluation.

This paper will describe our testing facility, our experience designing and deploying the sensing system, and the results of our research. Our experiments involving a tree branch uncovered the most diverse range of HIF phenomena. For the purpose of this report, we will focus on the tree-branch experiments, while outcomes from other fault surface materials will be presented elsewhere. Finally, we will detail the pole-mountable sensing system we installed in Wellington Electricity's network and the results we've observed so far.

In the mining supply chain, the transportation of ore from mines to ports is a critical issue, often plagued by escalating costs and resource scarcity. Consequently, large mining companies seek to optimize their resource allocation to minimize operational expenses. Historically, the problem has been studied under the umbrella of resource-constrained job scheduling (RCJS), where various optimization techniques have been proposed for its deterministic counterpart. However, the inherent uncertainty associated with resource availability in mining operations has received limited attention. Addressing this, RCJS with uncertainty is a complex optimization problem that resists efficient solution with current methods. This study introduces an adaptive population-based simulated annealing algorithm to overcome existing RCJS with uncertainty limitations, particularly premature convergence, the excessive number of hyperparameters, and inefficiency in handling diverse uncertainty levels. The new algorithm is engineered to harmonize exploration and exploitation by utilizing a population, adjusting the Metropolis-Hastings cooling schedule, and implementing an adaptive perturbation operator selection mechanism. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm surpasses existing approaches on a wide array of RCJS benchmark instances and uncertainty levels, while also uncovering novel optimal solutions for all but one problem instance across all uncertainty levels.

One of the most significant questions in contemporary physics is determining whether gravity operates according to classical or quantum principles in controlled laboratory environments. A recent proposal involves testing the quantum aspect of gravity by creating quantum superpositions of two close neutral masses, allowing their quantum properties to interact and become entangled while minimizing other Standard Model influences. However, preparing a superposition state in one mass (the lighter system) inherently involves the presence of a heavier laboratory apparatus (the heavier system), which can also be treated as a quantum system due to gravity's universality, thus creating a source of gravitational decoherence for the lighter system. This paper examines two pairs of quantum systems (probe-detector pairs), consisting of two light and two heavy oscillators, and explores the conditions under which entanglement between the light systems can evade decoherence induced by the heavier systems, ultimately estimating the decoherence's magnitude in the proposed experiment designed to investigate gravity's quantum nature.

Expanding language technology beyond a single language and modality, researchers 
have explored various NLP tasks in multiple areas. Although individual directions have 
gained significant momentum, the majority of multimodal research remains centered on 
English, and multilingual research focuses primarily on text contexts. In response, a new 
area of research has emerged, seeking to unify multilingual and multimodal approaches 
(MultiX) by categorizing tasks, datasets, and methods used to address these scenarios. 
This review provides an in-depth examination of the languages, datasets, and modeling 
strategies used in MultiX, highlighting their strengths and weaknesses, and outlining the 
current state of the field and future research directions.

A significant merger within the Milky Way galaxy is ongoing. The Sagittarius dwarf spheroidal galaxy is being torn apart while orbiting the Milky Way, with its close approaches causing disturbances in the Milky Way disc. Using hydrodynamic simulations, we have studied the effects of massive dwarf galaxies on a quasi-polar orbit like Sagittarius on the star formation activity in Milky Way-like discs. Our findings confirm that interactions with orbiting satellites increase the star formation rate in the host galaxy, particularly due to the close passages of massive gas-poor satellites. However, for gas-rich satellites, the impact on star formation is observed on a longer timescale without prominent peaks, attributed to the steady gas stripping and accretion onto the host galaxy. We discovered that the effects of satellite perturbations primarily occur in the outer disc of the host and are associated with the formation of low-metallicity stars following gas infall from the satellites. Our simulations suggest a connection between the recent passages of the Sagittarius galaxy and the star formation bursts in the solar neighbourhood, which could have occurred around 1 and 2 Gyr ago; however, to reproduce the initial star formation burst approximately 6 Gyr ago, a close pericentric passage and significant mass loss from the Sagittarius precursor were necessary.

Research on a honeycomb lattice system with antiferromagnetic properties has used the t-J model and slave boson mean field theory to study its behavior at half band filling. The investigation of order parameters and single particle dispersion relations at different band fillings reveals an unexpected increase in superconductivity when antiferromagnetism is present. This leads to the discovery of nodal single particle dispersion relations at specific band filling fractions, contrary to the typical nodeless chiral-d wave superconducting state. A comparison with other types of states has been conducted to identify key characteristics of chiral-d wave superconductivity. The findings may be relevant to materials with a honeycomb lattice structure, such as the In$_3$Cu$_2$VO$_9$ compound.

A non-destructive inspection technique known as neutron imaging is widely applicable but faces a key challenge: achieving micrometer-scale resolution. Creating a neutron detector with a high level of detail is a complex task. Certain neutron detectors made from fine-grained nuclear emulsion show potential for high-resolution imaging. High track density is essential to enhance neutron imaging quality, yet current analysis methods struggle to function at high track density. To address this issue, simulated images were utilized to determine the required track density for neutron imaging. It was determined that approximately 10,000 tracks per 100x100 micrometers squared are sufficient for using neutron detectors in imaging. Furthermore, the contrast resolution was evaluated across various image data sets featuring diverse track densities and neutron transmission rates. Experiments were conducted for imaging gadolinium-based gratings with predefined structures. The gratings' structures were successfully resolved. The calculated 1σ 10-90% edge response, using grayscale images of the grating slits, with a periodic structure of 9 micrometers, was 0.945 ± 0.004 micrometers.

In 6G cellular networks, Joint Communication and Sensing (JCAS) aims to balance wireless connectivity with environmental awareness, particularly regarding human presence. To prevent signal blockage, identifying and recognizing blockage types is the first step, which can be approximated by detecting human motion. This approach, known as a surrogate task, simplifies model testing and pre-training, reducing the need for extensive data collection in the JCAS environment. Our study employs a small dataset from a 26 GHz multi-user device with hybrid beamforming to validate this method, using DFS-converted data for hypothesis testing. The results indicate that domain shift between training and inference data necessitates adaptable DL models, and that diluting DFS data or relying on small input datasets compromises performance. Additionally, achieving higher sensing resolution requires compensating with increased activities, lowered sampling rates, and optimizing STFT processing for each specific learning task.

Assignment problems involving multiple items and owners are prevalent across various industries, such as marketing, loan management, and e-commerce. These problems can be formulated as constrained optimization tasks with objective functions and multiple restrictions, often falling under the NP-hard category. This makes it increasingly difficult to find exact solutions when dealing with massive numbers of items and owners, such as in the case of hundreds of millions of items and tens of owners. This issue is particularly pertinent in the digital sector, where companies make decisions for large groups of users. By relaxing the requirement for integer values, we can create a broader optimization problem that encompasses various assignment tasks, with a convex objective function and constraints that are either linear or convex and separable. Our study aims to solve this generalized assignment problem within the framework of the Bregman Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (BADMM), leveraging Bregman divergence to convert the Augmented Lagrangian into a form that allows for the parallel solution of sub-problems. The entire solution process can be executed using a MapReduce-style distributed computation framework. Experimental results on both artificial and real-world datasets are provided to validate its efficacy and scalability.

We introduce new deep joint source-channel coding methods for wireless image transmission over MIMO channels with Rayleigh fading, with CSI only available at the receiver. We develop two transmission strategies; one leverages spatial diversity via an OSTBC to enhance robustness against channel fluctuations, and the other exploits spatial multiplexing, allowing for more information to be sent about the source signal. Simulation results demonstrate that the diversity scheme performs better at lower SNR values and smaller numbers of receive antennas. However, when the number of transmit antennas exceeds two, the full-diversity scheme becomes less advantageous. Additionally, our diversity and multiplexing schemes can achieve comparable performance to the state-of-the-art BPG algorithm in terms of MIMO capacity.

A novel Monte Carlo method, the replica exchange preconditioned Langevin diffusion (repCNLD), has been developed to efficiently handle complex high-dimensional distributions with multiple modes. This challenge arises when standard Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) chains struggle to converge in high-dimensional spaces and fail to capture all modes when the energy function is non-convex. The repCNLD approach improves the convergence speed of the preconditioned Crank-Nicolson Langevin diffusion (pCNLD) and is capable of capturing all modes of multi-modal distributions. A key feature of repCNLD is its robust Crank-Nicolson discretization, which exhibits a linear growth of discretization error with respect to the time step size. To further accelerate convergence and reduce computational costs, the repCNLD method has been extended to a multi-variance setting. Additionally, an unbiased estimator of the swapping rate for the multi-variance repCNLD has been derived, facilitating the choice of a suitable low-fidelity model for the second chain. The performance of repCNLD has been evaluated using high-dimensional Gaussian mixture models and nonlinear partial differential equation (PDE) inverse problems. To address the computational complexity of nonlinear PDE inverse problems, the discrete adjoint method has been employed to efficiently compute gradients.

A commonly used framework, Multiple Instance Learning, has been applied to process gigapixel images with annotations at the image level. To streamline analysis, large images are typically broken down into smaller sections called patches, with extracted features for these patches reducing computational demands and addressing memory constraints of modern graphics processing units. To further alleviate these limitations, we've developed a new system called EmbAugmenter, which leverages a generative adversarial network to produce data augmentations in an abstract feature space, greatly minimizing processing requirements. Our approach demonstrated superior results when applied to the SICAPv2 dataset, outperforming un-augmented analysis and matching the effectiveness of traditional patch-level augmentations at a significantly faster pace.

This overview details recent advancements in understanding CP violation and mixing within $B$ meson decays. We analyze $B^0_d \to J/\psi K^0_S$ and $B^0_s \to J/\psi \phi$ decays, focusing on the measurement of the mixing phases $\phi_d$ and $\phi_s$ and accounting for hadronic uncertainties with the aid of existing data. However, patterns of CP violation observed in non-leptonic $B$ meson decays $B \to \pi K$ and $B^0_s \to D_s^{\mp} K^{\pm}$ present intriguing discrepancies that might signal the presence of new physics.

We focus on developing efficient methods to derive the k-th derangement or ménage permutation from a lexicographically ordered list. Specifically, given such a list, we will outline an algorithm to rapidly extract and produce the k-th permutation. This will be achieved by first transforming the problem into computing the count of restricted permutations sharing a specified prefix, then applying concepts from rook theory to solve the counting problem. These efforts will have practical implications in fields like combinatorics, probability, statistics, and modeling.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) leverage the structural relationships of data to enhance basic Neural Networks (NNs), departing from the iid assumption. Although GNNs often outperform NNs in real-world applications, there are instances where their benefits are minimal or even non-existent compared to NNs without graph structure awareness. To pinpoint these scenarios, two metrics, rooted in graph signal processing and statistical hypothesis testing, are proposed to evaluate instances where edge relationships in data and labels fail to confer advantages. These metrics enable the determination of a threshold value that can predict the potential superiority of GNNs over graph-agnostic NNs in specific cases.

Our novel white-box adversarial attack approach for transformer models is grounded in the observation that transformers segment words into subtokens, and replacing adjacent subtokens has a similar effect to modifying characters at the character level. This method consists of three key steps. Firstly, a gradient-based technique identifies the most susceptible words in a sentence, which are then split into subtokens to replace the original tokenization. In the final step, an adversarial loss is used to guide the substitution of replaceable subtokens, facilitated by the Gumbel-softmax trick to enable gradient backpropagation, while also incorporating visual and length constraints to minimize character modifications. Experimental results on both sentence-level and token-level tasks demonstrate our method's superiority in success rate and edit distance compared to previous attack methods, and human evaluation confirms that our adversarial examples retain their original labels.

The remnants of supernovae have a significant impact on the interstellar medium through the transfer of energy, which is dispersed in multiple phases of gas. Warm molecular hydrogen is often responsible for the cooling of shocked gas, and it has been studied through near-infrared observations that reveal H$_2$ emission lines. While past studies have been limited by poor resolution or limited observations, new data collected using the KMOS instrument on the VLT offers a more detailed understanding of the A, B, C, and G regions within the supernova remnant IC 443. The collected data reveal the presence of 20 H$_2$ transitions, along with lines from hydrogen and iron, which dominate near-infrared images of the region. Analysis shows that H$_2$ is distributed in a clumpy manner across various scales, suggesting a complex structure. This complexity is further supported by the presence of multiple shock types and temperatures between 1500 and 2500 K. In addition, the data confirm that certain previously identified young stellar objects in the region are not actually associated with young stars, which raises questions about the possibility of triggered star formation by supernova shocks.

Accelerating neural network training while minimizing power consumption is achievable through data quantization. Nonetheless, implementing low-bit quantized training poses significant challenges. It can either compromise accuracy or fail to reduce the bit width effectively. In contrast, current mixed-precision methods are capable of substantial compression but struggle to assign optimal bit widths efficiently. To address this issue, we propose DYNASTY, a novel neural network training framework that utilizes block-wise dynamic-precision techniques. This framework offers real-time data sensitivity insights through analytics and ensures stable training convergence via an adaptive bit-width mapping mechanism. Experimental results on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet datasets demonstrate that DYNASTY can achieve up to $5.1\times$ speed improvement and $4.7\times$ energy consumption reduction compared to 8-bit quantization baseline, without any loss in accuracy and with minimal hardware overhead.

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) holds significant promise for showcasing quantum computing's superiority with current technology. However, high device error rates hinder its effectiveness when applied to problems involving multiple qubits. QAOA translates problem graphs into quantum circuits where each edge corresponds to CNOT operations, which in turn limits the algorithm's fidelity due to their inherent error susceptibility. 

Observing that real-world problem graphs predominantly conform to the power-law distribution, where a few highly connected nodes dominate the network, we propose an innovative approach called FrozenQubits. This method freezes the critical nodes and divides the problem into smaller sub-spaces that can be independently solved, resulting in significantly more robust QAOA sub-circuits with reduced CNOT operations. Unlike previous methods, FrozenQubits does not require complex post-processing, as evidenced by our evaluation on 5,300 QAOA circuits across eight IBM quantum computers, yielding an average improvement of 8.73x in solution quality at a 2x resource cost, and up to 57x in some cases.

To understand matter's dynamic behavior, we could turn to natural laws, space-time geometry, or the topological structure of space-time. However, some argue that these explanations rely on overly complex metaphysics. An alternative approach involves reversing the explanation's direction and placing dynamics first. This approach, which can be seen in Lewis's Best Systems Analysis and Huggett's Regularity Relationism, views natural laws and geometric structures as merely reflecting patterns in matter's dynamic behavior. Building on this idea, this dissertation takes a novel step by viewing the space-time manifold as a representation of certain dynamic patterns in matter. It provides mathematical tools to evaluate space-time codifications based on their fit to the theory's dynamics and kinematics, much like the competition between different law-like codifications in the BSA framework.

BLI with limited bilingual guidance is a critical yet difficult task in multilingual NLP. Recent state-of-the-art methods in BLI rely heavily on the development of cross-lingual word embeddings to identify word similarities across languages; such cross-lingual embeddings are typically generated either 1) using static models (like VecMap), 2) extracting word-level embeddings from pre-trained multilingual language models, or 3) by combining these options. This work proposes a novel semi-supervised post-processing technique, BLICEr, which can be applied to any pre-computed cross-lingual word embedding space, to enhance their BLI performance. The core concept is to incorporate cross-lingual linguistic information from pre-trained models and combine it with the original cross-lingual embeddings, accomplished by 1) creating a word similarity dataset with true translations and negative word pairs derived from the original embedding space, 2) fine-tuning a multilingual pre-trained model using cross-encoder architecture to predict word similarity scores, and 3) combining the scores from the original embedding space with the BLI-tuned model at inference. BLICEr outperforms several strong baseline models on two benchmark datasets and also demonstrates robust performance across different cross-lingual embeddings.

Images with annotated diagnoses and ground truth for diagnosing rare diseases are extremely rare, mainly because the small patient population and limited clinical expertise make image annotation a challenging task. The skewed class distributions in many disease classification datasets also limit the effectiveness of traditional training methods. Consequently, researchers have turned to few-shot learning and meta-learning to improve classification performance in low-data environments. This study aims to enhance meta-learning for diagnosing skin diseases from dermoscopic images by introducing a baseline method that enables a network to learn generalizable feature embeddings. Our method is based on the idea that feature-rich representations are more valuable than sophisticated meta-learning algorithms. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach in learning transferable feature embeddings and show that even simple classifiers can outperform conventional meta-learning methods when trained on these representations.

Niobium is a superconductor that has been extensively studied in both theoretical and experimental contexts due to its significance in various applications and its exceptionally high superconducting transition temperature of $T_{c}=9.33$ K among pure metals. Beyond its uses in alloys for power applications, niobium is utilized in precise magneto-sensing, radio-frequency cavities, and as a circuit material in superconducting qubits, necessitating an in-depth comprehension of its electronic and superconducting properties. Specifically, understanding its anisotropies in both normal and superconducting states is crucial for preventing loss of quantum coherence in these devices. A novel theory addressing the disorder-induced anisotropic characteristics of niobium was recently proposed, prompting our investigation of its predictions by subjecting thin niobium films, similar to those employed in transmon qubits, to 3.5 MeV proton irradiation. By analyzing the effect of disorder-induced scattering on the superconducting transition temperature and upper critical fields, we observed a notable suppression of $T_{c}$ directly linked to the anisotropic order parameter, and found an almost exact agreement between the theoretical model and our experimental results.

The presence of public art can profoundly affect a sense of community in urban areas, conveying whose values and heritage are being promoted. In this research, a graph matching strategy with localized constraints is suggested to create a tool for selecting public art that fosters inclusive environments. By building on Schelling's theory of segregation, a cost matrix is generated and used as input for a projected gradient descent method to produce a soft assignment matrix. To establish curatorial constraints, regularization terms are explored and integrated into the optimization program. The program aims to reduce "in-group" biases by satisfying requirements for diversity and exposure. A fairness metric is developed based on existing studies to evaluate the output of our algorithm. Utilizing Tufts University as a test site, the effectiveness of this approach is assessed, and its potential drawbacks are discussed from the perspectives of curators and equity advocates.

The interplay between quantum mechanics and gravity, essential for predicting various phenomena like Hawking radiation, is still poorly understood due to a lack of experiments that can reliably test it in a real-world setting. We suggest a novel approach to create a photon with a superposition state across two rotating Sagnac interferometers of varying diameters, which would mimic a superposition of two distinct spacetimes. Notably, our predictions indicate that this experiment could yield entanglement at even low rotation frequencies and could be detectable due to Earth's rotation, thus offering a feasible platform to investigate how spacetime affects the generation of entanglement.

We explore the non-perturbative implications of a $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetry compliant modification to the Mathieu differential equation. Initially, we establish a connection between the non-Hermitian and Hermitian scenarios via a complex plane reparameterization, coupled with a constraint on the $\mathcal{PT}$-deformation parameter, which ensures the preservation of $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetry information in the Hermitian scenario. We notice that this factor is inherent in non-perturbative outcomes and the transseries representation of the deformed Mathieu partition function, which we have obtained. Our analysis in quantum mechanics reveals that the $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetry deformation parameter influences the real instanton solution for the Mathieu deformed potential in the Hermitian scenario, where its increasing value smooths the instanton's passage between minima by adjusting its width due to the decreasing potential barrier height. This effect extends to multi-instanton configurations and the bounce limit of an instanton-anti-instanton pair, the motion of which is analogous to the resistively shunted junction (RSJ) model.

Over the past few years, the world has seen an escalating concern over air pollution, prompting countries in the global north to introduce large-scale monitoring systems to inform decision-making. However, existing efforts are hindered by significant shortcomings, including exorbitant costs, difficulties in swift implementation, an overemphasis on urban areas at the expense of equal distribution, and a lack of transparency in estimating air pollution levels. This paper outlines an innovative approach that leverages open-source information on road infrastructure to estimate air pollution levels, with a focus on England and Wales in the United Kingdom. Our methodology allows for the creation of a cost-effective, transparent, and accurate model that can be applied globally, providing policymakers with the tools needed to make informed decisions about clean-air initiatives, particularly in low-income countries where comprehensive monitoring networks are often unaffordable.

Currently, end-users are unable to access substantial amounts of Adaptive-Optics (AO) control loop data and telemetry. Opening up access to these data has the potential to transform the AO landscape, enabling various applications such as determining a system's PSF, characterising turbulence, and optimizing control systems. A major barrier to sharing this data is the lack of standardisation, which obstructs access. To address this issue, we introduce an object-oriented Python package for AO telemetry, which features a data model that conceals the underlying standard for data exchange based on the Flexible Image Transport System (FITS). The package is designed to accommodate data from various AO systems, both in their raw format and abstracted from instrument specifics. The usage of the package is demonstrated with active AO systems from 10m-class observatories, with support initially available for the AOF and Keck systems, with plans for expansion to additional systems.

This is the third installment of a series focusing on creating virtual structure sheaves and related $K$-theoretic invariants within the context of moduli theory. The key objects of interest are almost perfect obstruction theories, a concept first proposed by Y.-H. Kiem and the author as a suitable framework for defining $K$-theoretic invariants for several moduli stacks, including generalized $K$-theoretic Donaldson-Thomas invariants.

In this paper, we demonstrate the existence of virtual Riemann-Roch theorems in almost perfect obstruction theory, covering both non-equivariant and equivariant scenarios, as well as cosection localized versions. This work generalizes and simplifies the technical assumptions inherent in the virtual Riemann-Roch theorems established by Fantechi-G\"{o}ttsche and Ravi-Sreedhar. Our primary contributions are comprised of a detailed analysis of the equivariant $K$-theory and Gysin map of sheaf stacks, along with a derivation of the virtual Todd class formula.

In neuroscience, researchers typically verify hypotheses using behavioral and neurological data to identify connections between various factors and specific outcomes. Recently, deep learning has emerged as a possible method for analyzing this data, enabling predictions based on numerous variables and pinpointing those most relevant to the results. Despite its potential, this approach has had a limited impact because its findings are not directly tied to statistical evidence supporting the hypotheses in question. In this article, we introduce a novel and adaptable method combining hypothesis testing with data-driven deep learning, incorporating permutation testing to strengthen the analysis. Using a dataset from the NCANDA study involving over 600 adolescent participants, we applied this approach to predict the presence of a major depressive disorder symptom and successfully isolated key risk factors that contribute to its manifestation.

This article explores the $L^{p}$-boundedness of pseudo-differential operators on a homogeneous tree, with a focus on establishing links and proving analogues in this specific context. Specifically, for a certain range of $p$ values between 1 and 2, it examines the relationship between operator boundedness on the tree and the group of integers. Additionally, a tree-based analogue of a key theorem in operator theory is developed for all $p$ except 2.

A fairness measure is proposed which modifies the equal odds fairness framework by removing equality constraints. An iterative and grid-based algorithm, independent of the specific model used, is designed to adjust the outcomes based on each sensitive attribute value to align with the new measure. The algorithm can efficiently handle attributes with high numbers of possible values and sanitizes the outcomes separately for different protected attribute values. To accommodate scenarios involving multiple attributes, the algorithm is extended to handle such cases. Our proposed algorithm is demonstrated to achieve fairness in a real-world context, such as fraud detection, for a single protected attribute, multiple protected attributes. When compared with existing fairness methods that primarily consider two groups, the proposed algorithm achieves comparable performance across several publicly available datasets.

This paper presents ThielSort, an efficient implementation of the Diverting Fast Radix (DFR) algorithm. Key advantages over traditional radix sorts are theoretically established, and implementation specifics are provided to illustrate ThielSort's competitiveness with contemporary sorting methods. The performance of ThielSort is evaluated by examining various standard datasets and input configurations.

To verify the hypothesis that entropy is conserved between Big Bang nucleosynthesis and recombination, we investigate a heavy particle that decomposes into a mix of photons and other fast-moving particles. We utilize the Planck temperature and polarization fluctuations, COBE/FIRAS spectral distortion limits, and the observed initial deuterium abundance to constrain the decay processes. If a massive particle decays into photons, transferring between 56 and 71 percent of its energy, it will only minimally affect the N_eff value at recombination, and the Planck data alone allows significant entropy injection. If the decay injects photons, Planck data and spectral distortion constraints set the minimum decay rate at 1.91 x 10^-6 seconds^-1 at 95 percent confidence level. We find that bounds on the energy density of the massive particle improve significantly when combined with limits on initial deuterium abundance, indicating the particle can contribute a maximum of 2.35 percent (95 percent CL) of the universe's energy density before it decays.

Our research focuses on Edgeworth expansions within limit theorems for self-normalized sums, where we obtain non-uniform bounds under minimal moment conditions, including cases with non-integer moments and reduced remainder terms. These bounds also enable non-uniform expansions in local limit theorems and are sufficient for deriving Edgeworth-type expansions and central limit theorems in total variation distance for self-normalized sums with enhanced tail accuracy.

Researchers studying quantum thermodynamics are seeking to understand how fundamental laws of thermodynamics apply to quantum-based machines operating at extremely low temperatures where quantum effects play a significant role. Despite advancements, developing machines where quantum effects have a substantial impact has proven challenging. In our study, we've conducted an experiment to measure the actual impact of quantum mechanics on the work-energy relationship. We used a trapped ion and laser pulses to simulate a process that allowed us to test the boundaries of classical and quantum mechanics. The results from our experiment confirmed predictions that the work-energy relationship behaves differently under quantum conditions, diverging significantly from the classical expectation and also dismissing alternative theories. Furthermore, our results validate that the quantum correction to the work-energy relationship disappears when temperatures are high.

This research explores AdS$_3$ solutions in minimal supersymmetric settings on G$_2$-oriented backgrounds within IIA and IIB supergravity theories, utilizing the bispinor formalism to derive these solutions. A direct argument reveals the absence of AdS$_3$ solutions in massless type IIA string theory on such backgrounds. Additionally, it is demonstrated that AdS$_3$ solutions in massive type IIA do exhibit scale separation, whereas this phenomenon is not observed in type IIB configurations. Moreover, a universal formula for the 3-dimensional superpotential in the bispinor framework is provided, applicable to both IIA and IIB configurations, showing that the supersymmetry conditions of this superpotential ultimately lead back to the bispinor equations.

Throughout a series of lectures, the laws governing the behavior of random points, curves, and surfaces will be explored. Starting with a review of martingales, one-dimensional Brownian motion and Bessel processes, the discussion will progress to Dyson's Brownian motion model before examining the Gaussian analytic functions and determinantal point processes that arise as zeros of these functions. The lectures will also cover Schramm-Loewner evolution and its complexification of Bessel processes. The final topic is the construction of multiple SLE models driven by N-particle processes and the establishment of a multiple SLE/GFF coupling, specifically the identification of the driving process with Dyson's Brownian motion.

A general model of quadratic gravity linked to a single scalar is examined to understand how the gravitational degrees of freedom influence inflationary parameters. We determine that quantum corrections generated by the massive spin-2 ghost make considerable contributions to the effective inflationary potential, enabling spontaneous breaking of global scale invariance without needing extra scalar fields. Inflationary parameters are calculated, and these predictions align well with expectations from known inflationary models, conforming to constraints outlined by the Planck and BICEP/Keck collaborations on inflation.

This paper aims to introduce a system capable of producing synthetic sequential data within the Synthetic Data Vault. To accomplish this, we detail the Sequential model available in SDV, an end-to-end framework designed to build generative models for complex, real-world data. The system utilizes a cutting-edge neural network-based machine learning model, the conditional probabilistic auto-regressive model. The complete system and model can be accessed through the open-source Synthetic Data Vault library on GitHub, along with other models tailored to different synthetic data requirements. 

Following the development of the Sequential SDV, we employed it to generate synthetic data and compared its quality to a non-sequential generative adversarial network-based model known as CTGAN. To evaluate the similarity between the sequential synthetic data and its real counterpart, we developed the Multi-Sequence Aggregate Similarity metric, which allowed us to conclude that our Sequential SDV model effectively identifies higher-level patterns without compromising synthetic data quality.

Maximum likelihood estimation, which involves using observed data to constrain theoretical models, is a critical aspect of many physics experiments. To address common obstacles in determining reliable confidence intervals - namely limited datasets, restricted parameters, and effective management of nuisance parameters - the Profiled Feldman-Cousins technique offers a viable solution. This approach has been shown to provide more precise frequentist coverage than competing methods and can be applied broadly to parameter estimation in fields such as neutrino oscillations and related measurements. In the context of the NOvA experiment, we outline an implementation of this technique.

This study focuses on finding the minimum energy solutions under external influences within a broad space defined by function $\kappa$, satisfying specified principles. For an external field with considerable generality, the conditions under which the minimum solution exists have been established for a wide range of domains $A$ and fields $f$, thus answering a long-standing question. These findings particularly apply to Riesz kernels, offering a detailed analysis and examples. Furthermore, the study provides alternative characterizations and an examination of the continuity of the minimum solution when the domain expands through compact subsets. The results apply to a range of significant kernels within classical and modern potential theory.

Over the years, convolutional neural networks have been the benchmark for computer vision tasks, particularly excelling in feature extraction and classification. Their opaque nature, however, restricts understanding of their decision-making process, necessitating the use of eXplainable AI techniques. In medical research, most work has centered around binary and multiclass classification. Nevertheless, real-world applications, like chest X-ray analysis, involve identifying multiple diseases simultaneously, giving rise to the need for multilabel classification. A common obstacle in these tasks is class imbalance. This paper presents a novel Deep Learning approach for tackling multilabel chest X-ray datasets with class imbalance. It sets a benchmark for the underutilized PadChest dataset and proposes an eXplainable AI technique that utilizes heatmaps to provide visual insights. This method also incorporates label probabilities and model matching. Our results are encouraging, especially considering the complexity of multilabel classification. The heatmaps accurately pinpoint the critical areas that an expert would consider when making a diagnosis.

This study explores the dynamical instability of a fluid sphere in a framework of ideal monatomic fluids, extending Chandrasekhar's criterion to various dimensions. Once the instability sets in, it may potentially collapse into a black hole unless an external influence intervenes. The research reveals a distinct advantage of the three-dimensional spacetime, as it represents the margin at which the ideal fluid is stable yet not excessively so, allowing for hydrostatic equilibrium even with a positive cosmological constant. Higher-dimensional spacetimes beyond three are intrinsically unstable, in contrast to lower dimensions like (2+1)-dimensional spacetime, where the fluid is overly stable according to both Newton's theory of gravity and general relativity. The research also sheds light on the significance of the negative cosmological constant in the Bañados-Teitelboim-Zanelli black hole solution, which prevents a homogeneous fluid disk from collapsing into a naked singularity. Nevertheless, black holes with a positive mass could still emerge from the collapse of fluid disks. The research discusses the implications of spacetime dimensionality, highlighting its crucial role in the formation of various astrophysical phenomena.

A well-established phase imaging method called ptychography enables non-invasive imaging at the nanoscale, and its applications have grown to span various fields including materials science and defense. However, this technique is limited by a lengthy data acquisition time, resulting from the requirement of substantial overlap between adjacent illumination areas for accurate reconstruction. Conventional approaches attempting reduced overlap lead to reconstructions plagued by artifacts. This paper introduces an innovative method of compensating for undersampled data by incorporating it with data generated from a deep learning network, thus meeting the sampling requirements in ptychography. Since the network is pre-trained, the experimental data and data collection time can be significantly reduced. The proposed approach is validated by comparing the reconstruction quality with previous methods and highlighting its advantages and disadvantages.

The Gini index fails to provide a consistently reliable evaluation metric. As a result, prioritizing it could result in suboptimal choices. This discrepancy stems from the Gini index being a ranking-based score insensitive to calibration issues. Nonetheless, our findings demonstrate that the Gini index can be used as a consistent scoring rule if we limit it to auto-calibrated regression models.

For countably infinite tensegrities and related structures, specific equilibrium stress thresholds are established, and key characterizations of rigidity are extended. General conditions for stability and rigidity in infinite frameworks are derived and demonstrated to guarantee rigidity in response to specific types of continuous motion. These results build upon a concise proof that stability is sufficient for rigidity in finite frameworks.

This paper introduces Language Models as Data (LAD), a method for creating synthetic data that can accurately simulate real conversations. By utilizing GPT-3, LAD increases the diversity of language used, which leads to significant performance improvements in zero-shot scenarios. Specifically, LAD achieves substantial gains in intent prediction (+15%), slot filling (+31.4 F-1 score), and next action prediction (+11 F-1 score). Additionally, an interactive human evaluation reveals that training with LAD is comparable to training on actual human conversations. Furthermore, the code and data used in LAD are available in an open-source format on GitHub, located at https://github.com/Shikib/lad.

Consider a primitive character $\chi$ modulo a prime $q$, and let $\delta > 0$. We revisit a previously observed phenomenon that large-order primitive characters with $d \geq d_0(\delta)$ yield non-trivial values $\chi(n)$ for some $n \leq q^\delta$. Our new proof for this fact is simple and straightforward. Furthermore, when the order $d$ is squarefree, we establish that the number of $n \leq x$ such that $\chi(n)$ equals any $d$th root of unity $\alpha$ is negligible with respect to $x$ whenever $x > q^\delta$. Consequently, when primitive characters have sufficiently large orders, their values $\{\chi(n)\}_{n \leq q^\delta}$ cannot form clusters near 1 for any positive $\delta$. Our proof hinges on a non-trivial second moment estimate for short sums of the characters $\chi^\ell$, averaged over $1 \leq \ell \leq d-1$, provided $d$ has no small prime factors, and may have independent interest. Specifically, for any $\delta > 0$, we demonstrate that for all but negligible powers $1 \leq \ell \leq d-1$, the partial sums of $\chi^\ell$ exhibit cancellation in intervals $n \leq q^\delta$ as long as $d \geq d_0(\delta)$, building on Burgess' theorem. This argument integrates results from pretentious number theory and additive combinatorics. Lastly, we show that the P\'{o}lya-Vinogradov inequality may be uniformly improved over prime $3 \leq d \leq q-1$ for $\chi^\ell$, averaged over $1 \leq \ell \leq d-1$, which extends the work of Granville and Soundararajan.

Developing AI systems that can learn throughout their lifespan presents a significant challenge, and researchers have proposed various approaches and metrics to assess the capabilities of lifelong learning algorithms. However, existing metrics are limited in their ability to isolate algorithmic contributions due to the complexities of task and scenario design.
