configurations until about a billion years after the initial collision. 
Subsequent direct minor mergers greatly reduced the number of cold fronts, 
while indirect mergers had a more moderate effect, with outer cold fronts 
remaining largely intact.  The results suggest that minor mergers are 
common occurrences that can easily form and long-lasting cold fronts, but 
identifying a cluster's history from the presence of these fronts may be 
more complicated than initially thought.

To develop more reliable reduced-order models for the compressible Euler equations using proper orthogonal decomposition and Galerkin or least-squares minimization, a choice must be made regarding the spaces in which projections and norms are computed. Typically, the L2 inner product space is selected, but this yields inconsistent reduced-order models that often lack robustness. This work investigates a different set of inner products with the aim of improving consistency in the compressible Euler equations model reduction. We examine non-dimensional inner products as a means of enhancing both POD and Galerkin/least-squares reduced-order models, and demonstrate that physics-based inner products grounded in entropy principles produce more accurate and robust results. The proposed approach is validated using well-known test cases including the Sod shock tube, the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, and homogeneous isotropic turbulence.

Reduced order models derived from projection methods can still be computationally intensive due to terms scaling with the full dimension. To further alleviate this issue, hyper-reduction techniques like sampling methods are employed to approximate high-dimensional terms using smaller dimensions. The current work involves utilizing an optimization-based points selection algorithm, initially developed by Shin and Xiu, as a means of hyper-reduction. This algorithm, referred to as S-OPT, was originally designed for uncertainty quantification through stochastic collocation. S-OPT aims to maximize a metric that combines orthogonality and determinant measures. To demonstrate its efficiency, numerical examples comparing S-OPT with an over-sampled DEIM algorithm are presented, revealing that S-OPT achieves higher accuracy for the full order solutions given a specific number of indices.

Rotating boson stars are a theoretical type of dense stellar object that can be identified through unique gravitational signals in GW observations. We demonstrate that rotating boson stars adhere to a general, universal relationship involving their angular momentum, quadrupole moment, and moment of inertia. This relationship differs significantly from that of neutron stars, allowing for the clear distinction of boson stars from other celestial objects in gravitational wave observations. This universal relationship not only serves as a tool to distinguish boson stars but also aids in testing general relativity and constraining the matter equation within compact stars in the strong gravity regime.

State-of-the-art coreference resolution models rely on individual mention-by-mention decisions, whereas our approach learns coreference at a document-wide level and makes global choices. To achieve this, we employ a graph-based model that views text as nodes with connections representing relationships, and predict this graph in a non-autoregressive manner. The model then iteratively refines its predictions based on past choices to account for global dependencies. Our experiments demonstrate enhanced performance relative to established baselines, supporting the idea that document-level context enhances coreference resolution capabilities.

The second public data release from the DECam Local Volume Exploration survey, known as DELVE DR2, combines both newly acquired and previously recorded observations from various programs. DELVE DR2 comprises a substantial collection of ~160,000 exposures covering an extensive area of >21,000 square degrees in the high-latitude sky, utilizing four distinct broadband optical/near-infrared filters. This data release encompasses ~2.5 billion astronomical sources, offering detailed photometric measurements with a high sensitivity. Furthermore, it significantly expands upon the previous DELVE data release, covering more than four times the area and containing nearly five times the number of objects, making DELVE DR2 available to the public via the NOIRLab Astro Data Lab.

Current galaxy simulations have advanced to a point where they can model individual giant molecular clouds that eventually give birth to dense star clusters. The evolution of these young massive clusters into the old globular clusters seen in many galaxies is influenced by a complex combination of internal and external factors. We have developed a novel approach, based on a star-by-star simulation of large star clusters formed within a simulated Milky Way-sized galaxy. This method involves selecting a representative sample of young massive clusters and simulating their evolution over time. Our study predicts that a galaxy like the Milky Way would have around 148 globular clusters, most of which would have formed during an early, rapid period of star formation. Notably, our simulated globular clusters are younger, less massive, and more centrally condensed than their real counterparts in the Milky Way or Andromeda. This difference is attributed to the clusters' history within their host galaxy, including the strength of the galaxy's gravitational pull and the presence of massive black holes. The results highlight the importance of taking into account the galaxy's evolution when studying the properties of its globular clusters.

The rise of the digital age has led to a renewed interest in "dark mode" design in everyday applications and professional tools, such as text editors and developer environments. We argue for incorporating a dark mode theme into astronomy journals, along with a sample modified class file, showcasing a potential implementation. Dark mode themes possess several advantages for users, including conserving battery life, reducing screen wear on OLED devices, streamlining navigation, and complementing colorblind-friendly color schemes, while minimizing eye strain during extended observations. Analyzing design trends from recent AAS conferences, we estimate that approximately 35-42% of the astronomy community would welcome this feature in journals. However, we acknowledge that dark mode themes may have drawbacks, such as increased ink consumption in print formats and reduced readability in low-light conditions, which can be mitigated by offering both dark and traditional modes. By incorporating dark mode themes into journals, astronomers may become more proficient in their field.

A longstanding challenge in solid mechanics involves calibrating constitutive models with detailed experimental data, especially for materials undergoing significant deformation. To address this issue, this research develops a deep-learning framework that uses physical laws to find optimal model parameters using full-field displacement measurements and overall force-displacement data. In contrast to other recent approaches, this method incorporates physical constraints by utilizing the weak form of the governing equations, rather than the strong form. This approach is computationally efficient, can handle complex geometric domains, and directly incorporates displacement data without the need for grid interpolation. The proposed framework is applied to a range of hyperelastic material models, including the Neo-Hookean, Gent, and Blatz-Ko models, which are representative of general hyperelastic behavior, polymer behavior with locking, and compressible foam behavior, respectively. This work demonstrates the potential of physics-informed machine learning to revolutionize the calibration of constitutive models under finite deformation using full-field experimental data.

We present dGSLM, the pioneering "textless" model that can create authentic spoken dialogue audio samples, drawing upon unsupervised spoken unit discovery and a dual-tower transformer architecture with cross-attention, trained on extensive two-channel conversational audio data from the Fisher dataset.

Our research centers on solving Partial Differential Equation (PDE) based Data Assimilation challenges through variational techniques and the Kalman filter method. We recently introduced a novel Domain Decomposition framework called DD-DA, which divides the entire physical domain into subregions across both space and time, merging concepts from Schwarz' methods and parallel time processing. To efficiently parallelize DD-DA algorithms, the computational workload must be evenly distributed among subdomains. This typically involves assigning computational tasks to partitions proportionally to the amount of data entities and minimizing inter-subdomain communication. However, when dealing with nonuniform and general sparse observation distributions, a new parallel load balancing approach is required. Our proposed method, DyDD, dynamically and adaptively determines subdomain boundaries based on data locations, aiming to balance the workload accordingly. For validation, we utilize the constrained least square model (CLS), a fundamental model underlying the so-called discretize-then-optimize approach to data assimilation, and test DyDD on diverse scenarios.

Floquet time crystals with discrete properties break their intrinsic periodic symmetry,
similar to equilibrium critical points. Time-crystalline phases exhibit distinct behaviour
manifested in oscillations with periods multiple than 2 times the driving period.
To detect crystalline phases without limitations, and also diagnose chaos, we introduce a novel order parameter.
This allows us to thoroughly investigate the phase diagram of the long-range kicked Ising model, revealing a complex landscape with self-similar boundaries.
Our comprehensive theoretical framework describes how DFTCs emerge as a function of the drive's strength and period, capturing the underlying Zp symmetry in the Floquet-Bloch waves.

For calculating the Cabbibo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix element $|V_{cb}|$ using inclusive data, it is essential to know the semileptonic $b \to c$ decay rate accurately. Due to the poor convergence properties of this observable when using heavy quark masses from on-shell or $\overline{\text{MS}}$ schemes, recent determinations have employed the kinetic mass scheme. To utilize these schemes to a high degree of precision, we need a well-established relationship between them. Our latest calculations provide both elements at the level of $\mathcal{O}(\alpha_s^3)$, allowing for an enhanced inclusive determination of $|V_{cb}|$.

Astronomers use photon counting to analyze low-signal targets observed by EMCCDs by amplifying the signal and applying a threshold to isolate the signal's photo-electrons while minimizing noise. To achieve greater accuracy, specific photometric corrections have been developed, allowing the Nancy Grace Roman Telescope to plan optimal coronagraph observations using a noise-based SNR expression. We provide mathematical expressions for the SNR in photon counting, both with and without these photometric corrections in place.

This study examines a discrete-time Stackelberg mean field game, involving a finite number of leaders and a large population of followers, who are further divided into a limited number of major and infinite minor followers. Each individual, including leaders, holds private information about their types, which evolve independently based on controlled Markov processes. The leaders adhere to the Stackelberg strategy, committing to a dynamic policy. In this setting, both major and minor followers respond optimally to the policies of the Stackelberg leaders and one another, with the major followers interacting in a mean field game. Given that followers would engage in a mean field game, each Stackelberg leader selects a policy that maximizes their own reward, yielding a Stackelberg mean field equilibrium with multiple leaders. This paper provides a master equation that facilitates the computation of all possible Stackelberg mean field equilibria, and further extends this concept to the case of infinite leaders.

Automated vulnerability management in open-source software has become increasingly important due to the escalating number of identified vulnerabilities over time. To prevent these vulnerabilities from being exploited, part of the standard process involves monitoring commits that fix vulnerabilities, however manually detecting these commits is a time-consuming task due to the sheer volume of commits to review. In recent years, researchers have developed machine learning-based solutions for automatically detecting vulnerability-fixing commits, but most of these approaches either fail to incorporate deep learning or only use deep learning on limited sources of information. This research presents VulCurator, a novel tool that utilises deep learning to classify vulnerability-fixing commits by leveraging richer information sources, such as commit messages, code modifications and issue reports. Our experiments show that VulCurator significantly outperforms existing benchmarks, achieving an improvement of up to 16.1% in F1-score. The VulCurator tool is available on GitHub and Zenodo, along with a demo video on YouTube.

The flavoured anti-$k_{\text{T}}$ jet algorithm is applied to the $Wb\bar{b}$ process at the 8 TeV Large Hadron Collider. Next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) QCD predictions are provided for the total cross section and differential distributions. This work investigates the remaining freedom within the flavoured anti-$k_{\text{T}}$ approach and compares it with the standard flavour-$k_{\text{T}}$ method. Results for the total cross section are matched with the CMS dataset, showing a satisfactory agreement. Including NNLO QCD corrections significantly enhances the match with experimental data.

Astrophysical systems often experience magnetic reconnection, accompanied by significant cooling of the plasma due to synchrotron radiation. Our study focuses on relativistic magnetic reconnection in a particular environment, where intense synchrotron cooling occurs and the system's magnetic properties have high levels of compactness and magnetization. As a result of this process, the creation of electron-positron pairs from synchrotron photons is inevitable, regulating the system's magnetic field in the vicinity of the current sheet. Through analytical investigation, we identify a self-regulating equilibrium for systems with a specific magnetic compactness and initial magnetization. This outcome can help determine the system's magnetization levels, especially in situations where plasma density is unknown, and it can be applied to study a variety of astrophysical phenomena. We demonstrate this approach through the analysis of current sheets near M87's supermassive black hole and the equatorial current sheet of the Crab pulsar's outer light cylinder.

Investigating the internal dynamics of NGC 346, a young star-forming region in the Small Magellanic Cloud, involved analyzing deep space observations from two distinct time periods separated by 11 years. Utilizing data from the Hubble Space Telescope, we derived the movements of various populations within this region based on their color and spatial distributions. Results showed a complex pattern of star movement, with those in the upper-main sequence and pre-main sequence stages displaying consistent patterns. Outer cluster parts exhibited both outward and inward motion, while inner areas exhibited a mix of rotation and inflow, with rotation reaching up to 3 km/s and inflow reaching up to 1 km/s. The presence of sub-clusters and massive stars in NGC 346, positioned where changes in star movement patterns occur, suggests turbulence as the driving force behind star formation. Notably, similar patterns of star movement observed in NGC 346, a metal-poor region, and Milky Way star-forming regions indicate that metallicity and dust density differences between the SMC and our galaxy have minimal impact on star cluster assembly. Our findings align with existing star cluster formation models, suggesting that fundamental characteristics of star formation are relatively universal.

Programmers use names to identify functions, variables, and data structures within code, yet these names often exhibit high variability, reflecting individual preferences and conventions. This diversity creates challenges when comparing code elements due to differing naming conventions, synonyms, and potential spelling or typing errors. To address this issue, we've developed a specialized library featuring a range of comparison functions designed to capture the nuances of human perception in code naming, balancing precision with a more flexible approach to lexical matching.

This paper offers a formula for the nth term of a generalized Fibonacci sequence, 
which generalizes the traditional Fibonacci sequence by incorporating k initial terms, 
and subsequent terms are the sum of the previous k terms. The derivation of the formula 
was achieved by identifying patterns in the derived formulas of specific sequences, 
namely, Fibonacci-like, Tribonacci-like, and Tetrabonacci-like sequences. Additionally, 
we have obtained and employed the formula for the k-generalized sequence in proving 
the main outcome of this paper.

Graph artificial intelligence has shown impressive capabilities in modeling intricate systems across various domains, such as biological networks and physical particle interactions. The escalating diversity of graph datasets necessitates the development of multimodal methods capable of integrating different predictive assumptions, which algorithms use for novel input predictions. The process of learning on multimodal graph datasets poses inherent difficulties due to differing assumptions across data modalities and the potential lack of explicit graph input. To address these challenges, researchers combine multiple modalities while exploiting cross-modal relationships. We conduct an analysis of 145 graph AI studies and observe a trend of combining diverse datasets via graphs, which are then fed into sophisticated multimodal methods, classified as image-centric, knowledge-driven, and language-focused models. Building on this categorization, we propose a framework for multimodal graph AI to facilitate a comprehensive review of existing approaches and inform the design of future methods.

In the context of adjoint optimization, nonlinear conservation laws create significant challenges regarding the existence and uniqueness of direct and adjoint solutions, as well as the well-posedness of the problem for sensitivity analysis and gradient-based optimization. This paper will investigate the convergence of adjoint equations to known solutions of the inviscid Burgers' equation for diverse numerical methods, examining the influence of the non-differentiability of approximate Riemann solvers, differentiation methods, and time advancement inconsistencies.

An active particle settling in still fluid is influenced by an inertial force that causes it to align its motion so that its largest side faces down, similar to a passive object. In the case of a spherical swimmer, it is observed to experience a stabilizing or destabilizing torque based on its swimming direction, determined by the swimming velocity and the settling velocity due to gravity.

This research delves into the current stability of cosmic strings with bosonic superconductivity, focusing on how non-zero string curvature can lead to quantum instability in current-carrying particles. The decay rates of these particles are investigated across various model parameters, curved string geometries, and decay processes. Additionally, the study applies these findings to cosmological contexts, examining the stability of superconducting strings within the string network and cosmic vortons through their cosmological evolution. The research reveals that the zero mode and vorton are generally unstable in scenarios where there's a mass hierarchy between the current-carrying particle and string tension, or when the particle has significant interactions with lighter species, such as the Standard Model particles.

In a study using circularly polarized light and longitudinal light, the properties of the magnetic field-induced Hofstadter butterfly in single-twist trilayer graphene were examined. We found two distinct chiral equilibrium states, resulting in a more defined Hofstadter butterfly. Circularly polarized light was found to cause a significant energy gap at the central band and between Landau levels. However, this effect had a distinct asymmetry at zero energy, where right-handed CPL caused a downward shift in the central band and left-handed CPL resulted in an upward shift. Additionally, an investigation into the impact of longitudinally polarized light from a waveguide revealed broken chiral symmetries at low driving strengths, which then recovered at higher driving strengths, an effect differing from that observed in twisted bilayer graphene.

Recently, there has been significant interest in compounds with non-centrosymmetric crystal structures due to their potential to exhibit unconventional superconductivity properties. A new compound, NbIr2B2, has been discovered to have superconducting capabilities below 7.3 Kelvin and a very high upper critical field, exceeding the Pauli limit. This study presents the results of muon spin rotation experiments to investigate the magnetic penetration depth in NbIr2B2 as it relates to temperature and magnetic field. The results suggest a fully gapped s-wave superconductivity, supported by high field transport measurements. Notably, the compound's superconducting ratio is comparable to that of unconventional superconductors. Furthermore, muon spin relaxation data indicates that time-reversal symmetry is preserved in the superconducting state, with no significant change in spin relaxation rate above and below the critical temperature. These findings are expected to prompt theoretical research to uncover the microscopic origins of superconductivity with preserved time reversal symmetry in this unique, non-centrosymmetric system.

In this research, we explore efficient communication protocols for distributed data storage and processing applications, specifically focused on calculating weighted sums of encoded symbols from a code. Given a codeword in a Reed-Solomon code and access to a subset of its components, we design low-bandwidth methods to evaluate the sum of a select number of these symbols by retrieving specific sub-symbols from a limited set of nodes, when certain conditions are met. Our approach outperforms existing methods in many scenarios and also leads to a general characterization of evaluation schemes for various types of linear codes, with a specific lower bound for Reed-Solomon codes.

High-entropy alloys have garnered significant attention due to their unique mechanical properties and extensive compositional possibilities. Nevertheless, their complex chemical makeup hinders the comprehension of novel physical mechanisms, which in turn obstructs the design of new HEAs. A primary issue lies in the immense complexity that hampers both theoretical modeling and the development of macro-scale models for high-throughput screening of potential alloys. Machine learning provides an innovative solution by effectively handling complex relationships. This review aims to demonstrate the efficacy and potential of employing machine learning to overcome these challenges. It begins by introducing the fundamentals of machine learning algorithms and their practical applications. Subsequently, it discusses the state-of-the-art machine learning models for describing atomic interactions, atomistic simulations, thermodynamic, and mechanical properties. The review gives particular emphasis to phase predictions, defect calculations, and simulations of plastic deformation. Additionally, it delves into machine learning models for macro-scale properties, such as lattice structures, phase formations, and mechanical characteristics. To illustrate the workflow, machine-learned phase-formation rules and order parameters are employed as examples. Lastly, the review discusses the remaining challenges and presents a vision for future research directions, including uncertainty quantification and the use of machine learning to guide the inverse design of materials.

The root-mean-square velocity of non-relativistic warm dark matter particles is directly proportional to the inverse of the universe's expansion parameter. This velocity dispersion results in the power spectrum of density fluctuations having a cut-off due to dark matter's free-streaming effect. Studies of galaxy stellar masses and UV luminosities indicate a velocity of 0.41 km/s with a 68% confidence interval of 0.29 to 0.53 km/s, and a free-streaming cut-off wavenumber of 2.0 Mpc^-1 with a 68% confidence interval of 1.2 to 2.8 Mpc^-1, consistent with reionization. This is in line with earlier measurements from spiral galaxy rotation curves and the formation of the first galaxies. The results are used to determine the temperature-to-mass ratio of warm dark matter, which aligns with the scenario of spin-0 dark matter decoupling early from the standard model. However, spin 1/2 and spin 1 dark matter particles are less favored under this scenario. A theoretical model of scalar dark matter, which fits current measurements, is reviewed.

We develop a fluctuation algebra framework for fermions in a nearly free state, and also investigate its temporal evolution under quasifree dynamics. Furthermore, we identify and examine a Bose-Einstein condensate to assess its stability under the influence of interaction.

In numerous scientific computations, linear algebra expressions are computed through sequences of library calls from building blocks, like BLAS and LAPACK. These sequences define computational strategies, which can be referred to as algorithms, with multiple alternatives existing for a single linear algebra expression. Although these algorithms have the same mathematical basis, they often exhibit significant variations in terms of performance due to their differing computational approaches. High-level languages and tools for matrix computations, such as Julia and Linnea, make algorithmic choices based on minimizing the number of Floating Point Operations. However, there are instances where multiple algorithms share nearly identical FLOP counts yet exhibit disparate execution times. Furthermore, it's possible that the algorithm with the fewest FLOPs is not the one that achieves the fastest execution times. This work proposes a method to evaluate the reliability of FLOPs as a discriminant for linear algebra algorithms. By inputting a set of algorithms for a specific linear algebra expression, this methodology ranks them into performance classes, with multiple algorithms allowed to share the same rank. Through iterative measurements until the changes in ranks approach zero, the methodology determines whether FLOPs are a valid discriminant for a given instance by verifying if the algorithms with the minimum FLOPs are assigned the best rank. If not, the instance is classified as an anomaly, facilitating further investigation into the root causes of performance disparities.

This study examines the backscattering rate in HgTe and (Hg,Mn)Te quantum wells under the quantum spin Hall regime, with a focus on the impact of specific interactions and effects, such as exchange interactions and Kondo coupling. Our findings demonstrate that the theoretical model aligns with existing experimental data for the conductance of HgTe and (Hg,Mn)Te quantum wells.

The contextual bandit framework is a theoretically sound approach with numerous applications across various fields. Past research typically assumes independence between noise and context, whereas our work introduces a more realistic scenario where noise influences both context and reward. This confounded setting is more representative of real-world applications and has the potential for a broader scope of uses. However, unresolved confounding in reward estimation can result in significant bias, leading to substantial regret. To mitigate these issues, we utilize dual instrumental variable regression to accurately identify the true reward function. We demonstrate that this method's convergence rate is nearly optimal in two types of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. Consequently, we can design computationally efficient and regret-minimizing algorithms that are guaranteed by the theoretical properties for confounded bandit problems. Numerical experiments verify the effectiveness of our proposed algorithms in the context of confounded bandits.

In a previous study, it was established that each minimal symplectic filling of an oriented lens space can be produced by applying a series of symplectic rational blowdowns to the minimal resolution of its corresponding cyclic quotient singularity. Here, a simplified visual approach is presented using the triangulations of a convex polygon to illustrate our rational blowdown algorithm. As a result, we can categorize the symplectic deformation equivalence classes of all minimal symplectic fillings of a given lens space into a structured graph, with the minimal resolution as the starting point and each step being a symplectic rational blowdown along a specific linear plumbing graph. Additionally, we determine the maximum number of symplectic rational blowdowns required for each minimal symplectic filling.

A long-standing issue in unmanned surface vehicle technology is generating efficient trajectories within complex dynamic environments. This paper presents a cooperative trajectory planning algorithm for USV-UAV systems that ensures safe, smooth navigation through multiple obstacles. The UAV acts as a sensor, providing real-time maps and obstacle information using advanced image processing. The initial trajectory is then generated using a graph-based search method, and optimized for USV motion control using dynamic constraints and numerical methods. A motion control method is also proposed, minimizing energy consumption during execution. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of the system, with the generated trajectory being locally optimal and highly trackable.

Autonomous marine vessels are increasingly employed in oceanic research and conservation efforts. To ensure successful mission completion, trajectory planning and navigation systems are essential components. This study introduces an innovative method for generating and tracking autonomous marine vessel trajectories utilizing optimization techniques. We model the vessel's dynamic behavior using differential flatness, allowing the trajectory to be optimized within a linear framework to minimize boundary conditions. To enhance efficiency, the trajectory is refined locally using optimization. Additionally, dynamic constraints are incorporated into the optimization process to ensure the generated path adheres to the vessel's kinematic properties, simplifying tracking. Furthermore, we integrate model predictive control into motion tracking, employing sequential quadratic programming to achieve optimal results. Experimental findings demonstrate the optimized trajectory aligns better with the vessel's characteristics, maintaining superior tracking precision.

The use of currency is universal in facilitating business, but its use in developing countries like those in Africa often relies on physical cash. In Ethiopia, one of the countries with the world's highest rates of blindness and low vision, over 4 million people are visually impaired, including 1.7 million with complete vision loss. Daily activities such as exchanging money in bus stations or shopping centers pose significant challenges for the visually impaired. This research addresses these challenges through the application of AI and ML technology. A mobile app developed for Android and IOS devices achieved a high classification accuracy of 98.9% on its dataset, incorporating voice functionality that identifies currencies in the local Amharic language. The user-friendly app aims to alleviate the difficulties faced by visually impaired Ethiopians.

Researchers have long been intrigued by the role vortices play in planetary formation. These whirlpools can collect dust particles within their cores in protoplanetary discs, but their stability is uncertain. We conducted 2D simulations of vortices to address this question, using a local shearing box model to efficiently run high-resolution simulations of interacting gas and dust. Our findings indicate that vortex stability depends on their size and how they interact with dust. Small vortices remain stable for thousands of orbits, while larger ones may initially contract, becoming increasingly dusty, before eventually breaking apart due to drag instability, which is influenced by dust grain size. Although the presence of dust reduces the lifespan of larger vortices, it still allows them to accumulate significant amounts of dust, potentially affecting the stability of other vortices formed through different processes.

In recent years, machine learning potentials for simulations of atomic structures have gained significant interest in chemistry and materials science. Researchers have developed numerous new approaches aimed at applying the precision of electronic structure calculations to large systems comprising thousands of atoms. Despite this progress, assessing the reliability of modern machine learning potentials in accurately modeling the intricate characteristics of multi-dimensional potential energy landscapes for such complex systems remains a challenging task. In contrast, moderately sized systems that allow for thorough validation of simulation results are now relatively uncommon. This study employs high-quality benchmark harmonic and anharmonic vibrational frequencies as a sensitive evaluation tool for validating high-dimensional neural network potentials. Using the formic acid dimer as a well-studied model system for which recent high-resolution spectroscopic data is available, we demonstrate that state-of-the-art calculations can produce highly accurate vibrational frequencies in excellent agreement with coupled cluster theory and experimental data.

Studying human anatomy, shape, and related health issues can be accomplished through the analysis of medical imaging data. However, limitations in accessing such data are primarily due to governance and privacy restrictions, ownership issues, and the expense associated with obtaining these images, thereby hindering our comprehension of the human body. One potential solution lies in developing a model that can learn and subsequently generate artificial images of the human body based on particular attributes of relevance, such as age, gender, and the presence of a disease. Although deep generative models have been utilized to create synthetic 2D images of natural scenes, the production of high-resolution 3D volumetric imaging data with accurate anatomical structure has been constrained by the scarcity of available data and limitations in algorithms and computing capacity. This research presents a generative model capable of generating anatomically correct, high-resolution, and realistic images of the brain with sufficient quality to facilitate further analyses. The ability to create a theoretically limitless amount of data not only enables extensive studies of human anatomy and pathology without compromising patient confidentiality but also significantly advances research in areas such as anomaly detection, data synthesis, and learning with limited information. The code and trained models can be accessed at the following link: https://github.com/AmigoLab/SynthAnatomy.

Remote attacks on laptop computers have increased, using malware to access
webcams and microphones, compromising user privacy. While webcam protection has
become more accessible, there is still a need for a solution to safeguard laptop
mics from such attacks. Our initial defense mechanism, TickTock, aims to combat
these attacks by detecting the on/off status of laptop mics. We utilize a unique
approach, which involves measuring the electromagnetic signals emitted from
mic-related laptop circuitry when a mic is in use, thereby determining its
recording state. Our experiment demonstrates the feasibility of TickTock by
successfully detecting mic status on 30 different laptop models with high
accuracy rates, proving its effectiveness in identifying mic usage in various
situations.

We expand upon existing fixed point theorems, adapting them for functions that do not necessarily map back to themselves. Our method yields a more straightforward proof for an earlier result, Hillam's, without requiring assumptions about the compactness or boundedness of the mapping's image. By doing so, we generalize Hillam's findings to include self-mappings on the real number line. Additionally, we provide an innovative proof for the global convergence of the Newton-Raphson method.

Recent studies have demonstrated that iron chalcogenides exhibit intrinsic topological superconducting properties, making them suitable for quantum computing due to their distinct electronic structures. The existence of topologically non-trivial surface states in FeTe$_{0.5}$Se$_{0.5}$ was previously predicted by calculations and later confirmed through precise photoemission and scanning tunneling experiments. Despite this, conclusive electrical transport evidence for these surface states remained absent until now. Our research team has performed electrical transport experiments and observed a non-linear Hall conductivity and linear magnetoresistance near the superconducting transition temperature, indicating a topological transition. Additionally, we noticed a sign change in the Hall coefficient accompanied by a concurrent softening of the ${A}_{1g}$ phonon mode at approximately 40 K, pointing to a nematic transition. The synchronization of phonon softening with nematicity suggests the presence of an enhanced fluctuation state, driven by the spin-phonon interaction. Our findings unambiguously confirm the existence of topological surface states in FeTe$_{0.5}$Se$_{0.5}$ and provide valuable insights into the superconducting mechanism in iron chalcogenides.

We investigate how two-dimensional arrays of subwavelength quantum emitters can be utilized to create efficient optical components in the linear regime. Under normally incident light, the cooperative interaction between emitters enables the manipulation of the array's transmission properties, resonance frequency, and spectral bandwidth. By employing analytical techniques and numerical simulations, we uncover optimal conditions for specific operations, including the filtering of fully polarized light using devices like linear and circular polarizers, as well as phase retarders, which can be characterized using Jones matrices. Furthermore, our study highlights the significance of tailoring the array's geometry and carefully adjusting the amplitude and direction of external magnetic fields to achieve the desired optical effects.

One of the most significant scientific challenges currently is understanding how the mechanisms of SARS-CoV-2 evolve and spread. By combining advanced technologies such as artificial intelligence with detailed information from patient isolates, tens of thousands of genetic mutations, biophysical and bioinformatic principles, and topological algebra, researchers have found that the evolution of SARS-CoV-2 is primarily driven by a selection process based on its ability to infect. In summer 2020, AI analysis predicted the emergence of specific mutations at the L452 and N501 sites on the spike protein of the virus before they occurred in widely circulating variants. Subsequent studies identified another mechanism of natural selection, which involves the development of resistance to antibodies. AI-based forecasts of the spread of Omicron, the effectiveness of vaccines, and antibody resistance were later confirmed by experiments. AI models accurately predicted the replacement of the dominant BA.1 variant by BA.2 in late March, and also forecast the emergence of Omicron variants BA.4 and BA.5 as the new dominant COVID-19 strains in late June. Furthermore, AI models have been found to accurately predict the impact of mutations on the efficacy of monoclonal antibodies used to combat the virus.

Quantum mechanics relies on the promotion of position and momentum variables to operators in special coordinate systems, chosen to ensure a valid representation. To prevent ambiguity, we should select unique classical variables, and we will explain the specific variables and their corresponding operators that guarantee a valid quantization. Failure to follow this procedure may lead to mistaken interpretations of quantization, resulting in incorrect physical theories. This principle applies not only to particles but also to fields and gravity.

Rapidly spinning neutron stars' non-symmetrical crust deformations are a key focus in detecting persistent gravitational waves. The maximum distortion, or the fractional difference in moments of inertia, caused by crust deformities (termed'mountains'), sets an upper limit on the intensity of these persistent gravitational wave emitters. Our use of Gittins et al's 2021 formalism and a mainly lateral force of deformation resulted in a maximum ellipticity of 7.4$\times$10$^{-6}$. This is larger than Gittins et al's initial finding, yet in line with Ushomirsky et al's earlier work from 2000. This indicates that rotating neutron stars may serve as powerful sources of continuous gravitational waves.

In current deep learning model development, data privacy is a significant concern due to the often anonymous and sensitive nature of crowd-sourced training data. Differential privacy has become a widely accepted method for ensuring model confidentiality but may compromise model performance. Our study compares the DP-SGD algorithm to standard regularization techniques to evaluate the trade-off between privacy protection and model efficiency. We assess the models' overall utility and vulnerability to attacks such as membership inference and model inversion. Furthermore, we examine differential privacy's limitations and provide empirical evidence that alternative techniques like dropout and l2-regularization may offer enhanced privacy-preserving capabilities.

A cutting-edge optomechanical inertial sensor for detecting low-frequency movements has been designed, featuring a resonance rate of 4.7 Hz and capable of precision acceleration measurements. With a minimal mass of 2.6 grams, low power consumption, and high resistance to external factors such as magnetic interference, this sensor stands out as a top contender for geodesy missions due to its compact size, lightweight design, and low noise sensitivity, reaching approximately 5E-11 m s^-2 per root-Hz at 1Hz. We have successfully put this technology to the test by demonstrating its effectiveness in ground seismic noise detection and developing sophisticated data analysis methods to identify, categorize, and eliminate noise sources through direct comparison with a commercial seismometer.

Given two sequences of positive real numbers $\{ a_{n}\}$ and $\{ b_{n}\}$, where $\{ a_{n}\}$ tends to positive infinity and $\{ b_{n}\}$ follows the asymptotic relationship $b_{n} \sim k \cdot a_{n}$ with $k > 0$, it is shown that the limit of $\left(1+\frac{1}{a_{n}}\right)^{b_{n}}$ as $n$ approaches infinity is $e^{k}$.

In high-stakes environments like autonomous driving or robotics, it is crucial that object detection neural networks operate flawlessly even under unforeseen hardware failures like memory soft errors that can compromise the system's perception. Current metrics for evaluating these networks, such as average precision, provide vulnerability estimates at an object level rather than an image level, which can lead to inaccurate assessments of the safety risks posed by memory faults. To address this issue, we introduce a novel metric called IVMOD that assesses object detection vulnerability at an image level by considering incorrect image-level object detection caused by false positives or false negatives, combined with a severity analysis. Our evaluation of various object detection models reveals that even a single memory bit flip can lead to severe data corruption, resulting in hundreds of false positive detections or the loss of up to 90% of true positives in an image. Moreover, a single stuck-at-1 fault can affect an entire sequence of images, causing persistent ghost detections that can mask up to 83% of an image and result in the continuous missing of actual objects in the scene, with up to 64% of true positives lost. Our work provides a comprehensive understanding of the safety-related vulnerability of critical object detection workloads to hardware faults.

Deep Learning has tremendous potential to significantly enhance classification accuracy in Hyperspectral Imaging, yet the training process for hyperspectral datasets poses substantial difficulties due to their relatively small size and large channel dimension. Furthermore, the incompatibility of cameras from various manufacturers compounds these challenges. To address these obstacles, we present a novel 2D convolutional approach tailored for Hyperspectral Imaging, introducing a strategic model bias and dynamically adjusting the channel dimension. This model demonstrates superiority in two distinct hyperspectral applications – inline inspection and remote sensing – and provides additional interpretative insights. Moreover, it acquires necessary camera filters through data-driven learning, allowing for the design of an optimal camera based on these filters.

Recent findings demonstrate that any observable force can theoretically be
produced using quantum mechanics with a suitable wave function. In this research, we
further investigate the phenomenon by focusing on the gravitational pull experienced
by an object at various scales ranging from planetary to cosmic, and we identify
the wave function that would yield it as its quantum force. Essentially, our results
suggest that the gravitational interaction observed at all scales can be attributed
to an underlying quantum wave function. We also examine the implications of this
discovery.

Hadronic vacuum polarization-induced energy level shifts in hydrogen-like ions and muonic hydrogen are estimated using a semiempirical approach, where an experimentally derived parametric function for hadronic polarization is applied to determine an effective relativistic Uehling potential. Using analytical wave functions for low-lying states, energy corrections due to hadronic vacuum polarization are calculated, taking into account both Dirac-Coulomb and bound wave functions with finite nuclear size. Formulas for the hadronic Uehling potential of an extended nucleus and relativistic energy shifts in a point-like nucleus are derived and compared with non-relativistic analytic expressions.

The researchers have used 5.7 fb^-1 worth of proton-proton collision data taken at a 13 TeV center-of-mass energy by the LHCb detector to measure the time-integrated CP asymmetry in the Cabibbo-suppressed D^0 to K^-K^+ decay. The analysis required D^0 mesons to originate from prompt D*+ to D^0 pi^+ decays, using the companion pion's charge to identify the charm meson flavor. The time-integrated CP asymmetry in D^0 to K^-K^+ decay was found to be (6.8 pm 5.4 (stat) pm 1.6 (syst)) * 10^-4. From this value, the direct CP asymmetries in D^0 to K^- K^+ and D^0 to pi^- pi^+ decays were derived as (7.7 pm 5.7) * 10^-4 and (23.2 pm 6.1) * 10^-4 respectively, with a correlation coefficient of 0.88. These results show 1.4 and 3.8 standard deviations of deviation from CP symmetry in D^0 to K^- K^+ and D^0 to pi^- pi^+ decays respectively, which is the first evidence for direct CP violation in a specific D^0 decay.

We demonstrate that first-order logic can determine the decidability of binary overlap-free words, and more broadly, ${\alpha}$-free words for rational ${\alpha}$ within a specific range, with a corresponding decision-making process that enables the automation of previously laborious, case-specific proofs.

A partially populated Swapped Dragonfly topology, denoted as D3(K;M), with K global ports and M routers per group, has n=K*M*M routers. This paper investigates a restricted version of the Swapped Dragonfly and identifies four key cases for network operations. For a matrix product, if K is a perfect square, it can be completed in sqrt(n) rounds. In the event that K and M share a common factor, an all-to-all data exchange can be accomplished in n/s rounds. When equipped with a synchronized header, the network can facilitate x broadcasts in 3x/M rounds. Furthermore, if both K and M are powers of 2, the network can implement an ascend-descend algorithm at twice the cost of the Boolean hypercube of size n. Each algorithm is conflict-free and is compared to those on hypercubes and fully populated Dragonflies, yielding more applicable results due to the universal emulations of Swapped Dragonflies with reduced parameters (J <= K, L <= M).

On finite networks, we examine Activated Random Walks where particles are randomly inserted and absorbed at the boundary. Despite the process's non-reversibility and the unknown stationary distribution, we calculate the relaxation time of the process. Additionally, we establish that the separation cutoff is equivalent to the product condition. We also provide precise bounds for the cutoff window's center and width. To validate our results, we provide explicit separation cutoffs for networks of various structures, including: large subgraphs of infinite non-amenable graphs, and large vertex-transitive graphs. Our approach relies on the refined analysis of a strong stationary time by Levine and Liang, and involves the IDLA process.

The supersymmetry breaking mechanism predicts the presence of sgoldstinos, which could behave like wave-like dark matter, and these scalar particles' interaction with electromagnetic fields might cause fluctuations in the fine-structure constant. Using data from atomic clocks, researchers can potentially measure the SUSY breaking scale up to the GUT scale within a specific mass range for sgoldstinos, which falls between $10^{-22}$ eV and $4\times10^{-7}$ eV.

A recent innovation in calculating the action associated with tunneling in vacuum decay is the development of a new formulation for the tunneling potential. This new approach builds upon the original derivation, which relied on the principle that the variation of the action should yield the correct equations of motion and align with the Euclidean bounce action value. We propose an alternate method for deriving the tunneling potential action through canonical transformations. Our discussion encompasses both single-field and multi-field scenarios, as well as the gravitational case, and we also consider the potential of this new method to simplify calculations of the prefactor in the tunneling rate functional determinant.

The AWAKE CERN experiment has seen the development and implementation of advanced automation techniques leveraging unsupervised Machine Learning to enhance the performance and stability of electron bunches at injection, specifically in relation to proton-driven plasma wakefields. By combining numerical optimizers with various reinforcement learning agents, the experiment aimed to minimize bias and ensure accurate decision-making. To streamline the process further, a synthetic model of the beamline was created using a variational auto-encoder, which facilitated hyper-parameter selection. This study presents novel deep learning and reinforcement learning approaches for automating the setup of a low-energy beamline, such as the one used to deliver beam to the AWAKE facility. The results highlight the efficacy of unsupervised feature extraction from images through computer vision, while also exploring potential operational applications and broader applicability.

In freemium games, player revenue stems from in-app purchases and ad exposure, with longer playing sessions increasing revenue potential. Identifying imminent player abandonment (churn) is crucial to prevent loss, allowing for targeted retention efforts to prolong gameplay duration. This study examines how integrating sequential and aggregated data through diverse neural network configurations enhances churn prediction accuracy, ultimately demonstrating that combining both data types yields better outcomes than using either in isolation.

The knowledge of the instrument's Point Spread Function (PSF) significantly enhances astronomical applications. We detail a PSF reconstruction method for the LBT LUCI instrument facilitated by the SOUL adaptive optics system. The method focuses on real-time wavefront sensor data and a limited set of calibration readings, bypassing calculations for the Optical Transfer Function. It generates a series of wavefront maps, each linked to its corresponding PSF. We validated the algorithm under laboratory and nighttime conditions, accommodating various SOUL configurations and adjusting for guide star brightness and atmospheric conditions. This algorithm, dubbed "BRUTE," employs a direct one-to-one approach, mapping each wavefront slope to an instantaneous PSF.

One of the biggest mysteries in fundamental physics is why the cosmological constant is significantly non-zero, whereas quantum field theory predictions would suggest an enormous disparity with observations - as much as 10$^{120}$ times larger than the actual value. A theory of quantum gravity would likely resolve this discrepancy. We explore in this work how certain models, such as the generalized uncertainty principle, which attempt to describe quantum gravity, might rectify this anomaly by altering the phase space of quantum field theory, and subsequently affecting the integration of zero-point energies in momentum space. However, we also identify several challenges that would likely prevent generalized uncertainty principle models in their current form from effectively resolving the cosmological constant problem.

The dark $U(1)_d$ sector communicates with the visible Standard Model sector via kinetic mixing between the dark photon $Z_d^\mu$ and the SM $U(1)_Y$ gauge field $B_\mu$. After electroweak symmetry breaking, the dark photon $Z_d^\mu$ acquires a mass and combines with the SM neutral vector boson $Z_\mu$. This mixing results in a parity-violating interaction between $Z_d^\mu$ and the Standard Model, enabling exploration of their coupling through low-energy phenomena and high-energy particle collisions. In proposed future colliders, especially the Large Hadron-electron collider, the interaction structure of dark photons with SM fermions will be analyzed using polarized lepton decays and polarization observables, providing a clean and efficient environment for research. A $\chi^2$-analysis of these interactions has yielded 90% confidence level contours for the $\epsilon$-$m_{Z_d}$ and $\epsilon$-$g_V$ planes, offering constraints on the mass of the dark photon $Z_d^\mu$, its coupling strength $\epsilon$, and the Lorentz structure of dark photon couplings with SM fermions ($g_V$) at a center-of-mass energy of 1.3 TeV.

A new multimodal approach, called MBURST, has been developed to enhance audio-visual speech by incorporating insights from neurological studies on the prefrontal cortex. This method, known as burst propagation, uses a more realistic approach to the credit assignment problem by leveraging feedback, multiplexing information, approximating connections, and linearizing signals. As a result, MBURST can identify meaningful connections between audio signals and visual cues, thereby amplifying relevant information and suppressing noise. Experiments with large datasets revealed that MBURST can achieve comparable performance to its baseline counterpart while significantly reducing energy consumption by lowering neuron firing rates by up to $70\%$. This improvement makes it more suitable and energy-efficient for use in hearing aids and other embedded systems.

In the field of autonomous driving, vehicles will inevitably encounter severe weather conditions, necessitating a heightened emphasis on public safety. With climate change, heavy snowstorms are becoming more prevalent, posing a significant threat to safe navigation. Despite existing research focused on enhancing navigation resilience in winter conditions, there is a shortage of standardized metrics to measure the reduction in visibility experienced by lidar sensors during precipitation. This chapter proposes an innovative metric to assess lidar visibility loss in real-time, drawing inspiration from meteorological research on visibility. Evaluating this metric on the Canadian Adverse Driving Conditions dataset, we correlate its performance with a cutting-edge lidar-based localization algorithm, and examine the benefits of filtering point clouds before localization. Surprisingly, our results show the Iterative Closest Point algorithm exhibits robustness in snowy conditions, yet abrupt events like snow gusts significantly compromise its accuracy. These findings underscore the need for more extensive datasets focused on extreme events to accurately quantify their impact.

We propose that the area of a black hole's event horizon is quantized, defined as $A = l_P^2 \, (4 \ln 2) \, N$, with a finite number of associated degrees of freedom exhibiting fermionic characteristics. To explore this further, we delve into the general properties of black hole entropy, $S_{BH}$, particularly focusing on black-hole self-similarity. By establishing a one-to-two mapping between the black hole's configurations and ordered integer partitions, we develop a composition law for its constituent sub-parts within the entire configuration space. This approach provides a single framework to understand black hole self-similarity, derived from the inherent self-similarity of ordered integer partitions. Our findings are compared with established quantum corrections that necessitate unique statistical weights for each configuration.

MICADO is a fundamental instrument for the European Southern Observatory's Extremely Large Telescope, enabling first light capability in terms of diffraction-limited imaging and long-slit spectroscopy in the near-infrared range. The MICADO's PSF Reconstruction team has developed an innovative software solution for the blind reconstruction of the Point Spread Function, marking the first instance of its kind in all ESO telescopes. This service will function autonomously using adaptive optics telemetry data from the MORFEO module, supporting Single Conjugate Adaptive Optics and Multi-Conjugate Adaptive Optics. This software will facilitate cutting-edge post-processing scientific analysis for MICADO's imaging and spectroscopic data. This update describes the PSF-R service tool's progress, having completed the final design review phase, along with recent results from simulated and actual data collected from similar instruments to MICADO.

To decompose $3\times 3$ matrices and bounded operators, we will utilize commutators that express these terms as sums of elements adhering to polynomial relationships, and subsequently apply them to free modules and endomorphisms with infinite rank. Specifically, we demonstrate that any operator of a complex Hilbert space of infinite dimensionality is expressible as the sum of four third-order automorphisms, and it's shown that every simple ring resulting from a quotient of an infinitely dimensional vector space's endomorphism ring and its maximal ideal can be represented as the sum of three nilpotent subrings.

For massless particles, the stabiliser group, known as Wigner's little group, is the largest solvable subgroup of the Lorentz group of four dimensions, specifically the Borel subgroup. Without mass, particle states can be broken down into left- and right-handed components governed by the maximal solvable subgroups sol2 ± of order two. We derive the induced Lorentz transformations and apply them to generalised particle state representations. Additionally, we discuss how spin-flip effects are associated with non-physical spin operator appearances.

Creating a precise static call graph requires striking a balance between accuracy and reliability. However, typical program analysis methods used for constructing call graphs are generally imprecise, leading researchers to develop alternative solutions. A new method for improving call graph precision involves using machine learning to refine call graphs generated through static analysis by removing predicted false positives. While this approach has shown some promise, it still has limitations due to its lack of consideration for source code semantics. This paper proposes a novel technique, AutoPruner, which utilizes both statistical semantic and structural analysis to remove false positives in call graphs. By taking a Transformer-based approach, AutoPruner analyzes the semantic relationships between caller and callee functions in a call graph and uses this information to classify each edge as true or false. The model used by AutoPruner is pre-trained on a large corpus of code to understand the source code semantics. Empirical evaluation on a dataset of real-world programs demonstrates that AutoPruner significantly outperforms existing techniques, with improvements in F-measure of up to 13% in identifying false-positive edges in a static call graph.

This study aims to examine the structural characteristics of the sandpile group for a distinct subset of self-replicative graphs, specifically focusing on Abelian sandpiles on Sierpinski gasket graphs. A detailed characterization of the identity element and a recursive framework for the sandpile group is developed under normal boundary conditions. Moreover, the research explores Abelian sandpile Markov chains on these graphs and presents enhanced bounds for the rate of convergence to stationarity.

This research employs local projections to derive impulse responses in high-dimensional contexts, leveraging the desparsified lasso to accurately estimate the high-dimensional local projections, thereby isolating the impulse response parameter of interest. Theoretical backing for our proposed estimator is provided through a proof of its uniform asymptotic normality under broad assumptions. Moreover, our approach is validated through both simulation experiments and in-depth examinations of macroeconomic models in the realms of monetary policy and government spending.

The challenge of real-time object detection on Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) arises due to the constrained processing power of edge GPUs in IoT devices. This paper introduces a new, resource-efficient deep learning architecture called FasterX, built upon the YOLOX model, for real-time object detection on edge GPUs. Initially, an enhanced and lightweight PixSF head is designed to improve detection of small objects, which can then be optimized further through the application of depthwise separable convolution. To reduce network parameters while preserving accuracy, a SlimFPN layer with a slimmer structure is developed in the Neck. Additionally, an attention module is embedded in the Head to enhance feature extraction. Furthermore, the label assignment strategy and loss function are improved to address category imbalance and box optimization issues in UAV datasets. To enhance the PixSF head's ability to learn spatial features and extract relevant features, auxiliary heads are introduced for online knowledge distillation. Experimentation on NVIDIA Jetson NX and Jetson Nano platforms demonstrates that FasterX models achieve superior accuracy-latency trade-offs compared to state-of-the-art models on the VisDrone2021 dataset.

High-quality, diffraction-limited observations on the ground have been made possible by the advancements in adaptive optics (AO). However, unlocking the full scientific potential of this data requires a thorough understanding of the point spread function (PSF). As next-generation telescopes approach completion, precise PSF characterization becomes even more crucial to meet scientific goals. Consequently, there is a growing need for tools that can accurately reconstruct AO systems' observed PSFs. To meet this need, our group is developing a PSF reconstruction service for the MICADO@ELT instrument. Our approach involves blind PSF reconstruction to maximize applicability across various science cases, relying solely on telemetry and calibrations without extracting information from science data. Although our PSF-R algorithm is still under development, it has reached a level of maturity to test its performance using actual observations. This presentation will evaluate the reliability of our reconstructed PSFs from bright, on-axis observations taken with the SOUL+LUCI instrument and assess the associated measurement uncertainties. This is the first application of our algorithm to real data and demonstrates its readiness for further testing. Our PSF-R algorithm successfully reconstructs the PSFs' Strehl ratio and full-width at half maximum with errors of less than 2% and 4.5%, respectively. A thorough evaluation of the reconstructed PSFs was conducted using simulated observations of an ideal science case.

In numerous applications, such as plasma and astrophysics simulations, as well as chemical combustion analysis, multiple isolated linear system solutions arise. By combining these systems into a unified linear equation, general-purpose solvers can be utilized, but this approach fails to take advantage of the independent characteristics within these systems. Theoretically optimal performance from Krylov solvers is consequently lost. Modern GPU accelerators are equipped with numerous independent processing units, ideal for solving each of these systems individually. This approach maintains optimal Krylov performance while minimizing kernel launches and eliminating unnecessary global communication. This research focuses on creating portable solvers that can execute an entire linear system solution within a single operation on a GPU's processing unit, integrated within the PETSc numerical library framework.

The degree of anisotropy in redshift space bispectrum is usually determined using multipole moments. The feasibility of detecting these multipoles in any given survey is heavily dependent on statistical variability. A formalism is developed to compute the statistical variability associated with measuring bispectrum multipoles in galaxy surveys. Based on specifications of a survey like Euclid, two key metrics are presented: the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), which assesses the detectability of a multipole, and the rank correlation, which measures the correlation between measurement errors in pairs of multipoles. Our analysis reveals that the Euclid survey may potentially measure the bispectrum multipoles up to a certain value (ell=4) across different triangle shapes formed by vectors in Fourier space. Furthermore, it is found that SNR values depend on both observation scales and redshifts. Multipoles with an ell value of 2 or less can be detected with high SNR (>5) even at relatively small scales (k ≤ 0.1 Mpc^-1), but higher ell value multipoles require smaller scales or larger bin sizes for detection. While errors between different multipole pairs are generally weakly correlated, there are exceptions for specific triangle shapes, such as squeezed and stretched triangles, where errors are more strongly correlated. This phenomenon allows for the combination of multipole measurements to increase the effective SNR.

This paper explores online Reinforcement Learning in complex, partially observable systems. It centers around the Predictive State Representations model, an advanced framework encompassing models like Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes. PSR captures system states by predicting future observations and is defined solely by observable factors. A novel model-based algorithm for PSR is developed, capable of learning near-optimal policies with sample complexity scaling polynomially with system parameters. The algorithm accommodates function approximation, allowing its application to systems with extensive state and observation spaces. The work demonstrates that, given a realizable model class, the algorithm's sample complexity is influenced primarily by the model's complexity, rather than the system's dimensionality. This research is notable for being the first to show that polynomial sample complexities can rival the global optimality in PSR. Furthermore, the general theorem is utilized to derive specific sample complexity bounds for various special models.

Improving fast matrix multiplication approximations could significantly lower the cost of neural network predictions. By replacing complex multiplications with lookups from a precomputed table using a learned hash function from training data, previous studies have achieved significant gains. Our study expands on these ideas and adapts them to deep learning inference, where pre-trained weights and training data are available. We propose an additional method for optimizing entire neural networks while preserving accuracy, which we test on a basic image classification task. Although our results show a notable improvement over existing work, they still fall short of the precision offered by exact matrix multiplication. Despite this setback, our research lays the groundwork for future research into speeding up inner product calculations using nonlinear hashing techniques.

We perform explicit calculations of Vafa-Witten invariants on three-dimensional manifolds, mirroring the approach of Floer groups in Donaldson theory. This is demonstrated through the computation of Vafa-Witten invariants for specific, relevant 3-manifolds resulting from various surgical modifications, including the Gluck twist, knot surgeries, and log-transformation. Additionally, we outline the anticipated structural properties for general 3-manifolds, encompassing the modular group action, connection to Floer homology, infinite dimensionality for any given 3-manifold, and the non-existence of instantons.

Heavy, doublet-dominant Higgs bosons predicted in some Standard Model extensions are prime targets for high-energy collider searches, with ongoing efforts at the Large Hadron Collider to analyze their signatures. When these states are sufficiently heavy, they exhibit suppressed decay patterns due to the strong $SU(2)_{\mathrm{L}}$ symmetry. In models consisting of extra Higgs doublets alone, fermionic decays are generally favored over bosonic modes, except in cases where bosonic channels yield clearer signals. However, introducing singlet states and making them kinematically accessible fundamentally alters the picture, allowing for the possibility of Higgs-to-Higgs decays becoming dominant. Nevertheless, accurately interpreting experimental data within a specific model framework also depends on controlling radiative corrections. In this study, we investigate the bosonic decays of heavy doublet-dominant Higgs states in the MSSM and NMSSM, focusing on the impact of $SU(2)_{\mathrm{L}}$ symmetry and the emergence of substantial infrared-type effects, particularly in non-resonant three-boson final states.

Our findings show that discontinuous shear thickening can occur even in relatively thin or moderately packed suspensions made of smooth particles, which do not experience friction. Discontinuous shear thickening can be seen as a transition that switches from an active to an inactive state in suspensions under inertial forces. The kinetic theory approximations we've developed closely match the results obtained through the simulation of the Langevin model, across a wide range of particle concentrations, without needing any parameter adjustments.

Small dam reservoirs are crucial for meeting global climate targets and sustainable development objectives. Despite their importance, however, there is a significant data gap regarding their geographical locations. To address this deficiency, researchers propose utilizing remote sensing imagery and automated techniques for extracting dam reservoirs from satellite images. This task can be seen as a precise extraction of water bodies, distinguishing between artificial and natural water reservoirs. A novel approach using deep neural networks involves breaking down the task into two stages: water body segmentation, where images are separated into water and land, and dam reservoir classification, where each water body is identified as either artificial or natural. In the first stage, a metric learning approach helps address ambiguity between water and land boundaries. In the second stage, a prior-guided approach optimizes image embeddings for fine-grained recognition based on reservoir clusters. To facilitate future research, a new benchmark dataset is created with satellite images and manually labelled reservoirs from river basins in West Africa and India. Comprehensive experiments conducted on this dataset demonstrate superior performance of the proposed method over existing approaches in all three tasks.

In microelectronic devices, localized stress and strain concentrations at extremely small scales significantly impact performance, durability against mechanical stress, and radiation resistance. However, these tiny stress concentrations are difficult to detect using conventional methods. Our research shows that synchrotron X-ray differential aperture microscopy is an effective and non-destructive technique for identifying these stress and strain concentrations at different depths. By using this technique, we have successfully mapped strain patterns between the source and drain in a gallium nitride layer within transistors at a microscopic level. Our analysis reveals the effects of gamma radiation on strain patterns in both new and irradiated transistors, indicating radiation damage caused by the components attached to the gallium nitride during the irradiation process.

Evaluating the performance of medical software AI-based devices in real-world scenarios, where data may not follow the same patterns as in training, is essential before they are used in clinical settings. Given the constraints and challenges associated with collecting and labeling large amounts of medical data, as well as the regulatory requirements for medical devices, we have developed an approach to estimate the accuracy of an unknown black-box model without modifying its training process or making assumptions about the original data distribution. This black-box estimation technique, based on conformal prediction, is tested on medical imaging datasets and compared with other methods in various scenarios of data shift, which are relevant to clinical practices. Our goal is to promote more practical and reliable estimation techniques for black-box models, ultimately contributing to more standardized and trustworthy clinical AI tool evaluations.

We have developed a forward modeling framework for estimating galaxy redshift distributions using photometric data, without relying on spectroscopic calibration. Our framework consists of a detailed galaxy population model, a model linking galaxy properties to photometry, a model characterizing the observation process, and explicit consideration of selection cuts and redshift binning. This approach provides a bridge between photo-z inference and galaxy evolution physics, allowing for explicit control over modeling assumptions. In addition to estimating redshift distributions, our framework enables the derivation of robust statistical properties of the galaxy population. We have successfully applied this framework to the GAMA and VVDS surveys, accurately predicting their tomographic redshift distributions with a bias of less than 0.003 and 0.01, respectively, without any hyper-parameter tuning. We anticipate that future improvements to the model will enable accurate redshift distribution inference for Stage IV surveys.

We propose a bipedal walking model grounded in an inverted pendulum with two lightweight articulated legs, capable of navigating uneven terrain and inclined planes. The robot's stride arises from the swinging motion of a stationary leg and the articulated movement of the trailing leg, allowing for gait by alternating between these two roles and conserving the energy of pendular motion. Bipedal movement on uneven surfaces and inclined planes is feasible by maintaining a consistent maximal leg angle during stride transitions and adapting the duration of each stride. This model can be solved analytically and is time-reversible, capturing various bipedal locomotion patterns. Furthermore, we have derived several optimization results for the gait speed in relation to the robot's parameters.

The influence of insoluble surfactants on the turbulent behavior of jets is being investigated through three-dimensional numerical simulations that incorporate interface dynamics and Marangoni stresses resulting from surfactant concentration gradients. This research builds on previous work that examined the interaction between vortices and the surface in the absence of surfactants, and extends that study to a range of scenarios in which vorticity production is driven by both surface deformation and surfactant-induced Marangoni stresses. The current investigation reveals that surfactant concentration gradients play a key role in forming complex vortex structures, significantly impacting the interfacial dynamics in three-dimensional jets. Theoretical models for circulation rate in the presence of surfactants are also presented, highlighting the dominant contribution of Marangoni stresses in such flows.

We investigate the role of radiation in the formation of globular clusters through computer simulations of a head-on collision between two large gas clouds. Our simulations with and without radiation from stars or supernovae show that a dense cluster of stars forms within about 3 million years, but not through a single collapse event. Instead, it results from the merging of dense gas clumps and the accumulation of new gas. Radiation from stars has a significant impact on the cluster's growth, suppressing the collapse of gas and delaying the onset of photoionization until a sufficient number of stars have formed. Our simulations indicate that radiation feedback reduces the cluster's mass by about half and that the inclusion of extreme Lyman-alpha feedback reduces it even further. When radiation is present, supernovae explosions occur after the gas is dispersed and their metal content is not immediately incorporated into new star formation.

Considérons une variété projective lisse définie sur un corps de nombres. On suppose que $H^2(X,\mathcal O_X)=0.$ Dans ce cas, Colliot-Thélène et Raskind ont prouvé que le sous-groupe de torsion du groupe de Chow en codimension 2 est fini. Ensuite, nous établissons des bornes uniformes pour ce sous-groupe fini lorsque la variété varie dans une famille. Now consider a smooth projective variety defined over a number field.
