Specifically, when $K=\mathbb{Q}$, we establish that there are no non-trivial primitive integer solutions $(x,y,z)$ with $2|z$ for the signatures $(r,r,p)$ when $r$ is one of $\{5,7,11,13,19,23,37,47,53,59,61,67,71,79,83,101,103,107,131,139,149\}$ and $p$ is sufficiently large. Furthermore, similar findings hold for quadratic fields, such as $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$, where we show that there are no non-trivial primitive solutions $(x,y,z) \in \mathcal{O}_K^3$ with $\sqrt{2}|z$ for the signatures $(5,5,p),(7,7,p),(11,11,p),(13,13,p)$, given a sufficiently large $p$.

Advances in deep neural networks have significantly improved representation learning across different fields such as text, graph structures, and relation triplets. This has led to the development of relation extraction methods beyond traditional text-based approaches. However, the potential of integrating diverse domain information remains largely unexplored. In particular, leveraging heterogeneous information has the potential to provide substantial contributions to a wide range of problems. This dissertation focuses on the extraction of drug-drug interactions from literature as a case study, utilizing heterogeneous domain information. Initially, a deep neural network for relation extraction was established and its attention mechanism analyzed. Next, a method for combining molecular structure information and drug descriptions with text-based input was proposed and its effectiveness for relation extraction demonstrated. Subsequently, a dataset of heterogeneous information including protein entries, medical terms, and pathways was compiled from multiple existing databases and transformed into a knowledge graph. A link prediction task was conducted to generate embedding representations that captured the diverse domain information. Finally, a method that integrated the input sentence information with the knowledge graph was developed and evaluated on a well-established dataset, resulting in improved relation extraction performance.

A collaborative approach between humans and AI in creative projects is referred to as human-AI co-creativity, where they work together as equal partners. Current co-creative systems often rely on users interacting with AI through simple controls like buttons or sliders. However, these systems typically don't allow the AI to provide feedback to humans, limiting the perception of a collaborative partnership. To better understand this limitation, a study involving 38 participants was conducted to assess the impact of AI communication on user experience and engagement in co-creative systems. The findings revealed enhanced collaboration and user engagement when AI communicates with users, and users viewed the AI as more trustworthy, personal, and intelligent. These results highlight the need to examine potential ethics concerns related to engaging, communicative AI in co-creative settings. To address this, a research methodology is proposed to explore the ethics of co-creative AI, utilizing participatory design fiction as a tool for investigation.

Soft robots have shown great potential for complex tasks due to their flexibility,
reliability, and versatility. Despite this, the typical soft manipulator design
limits its functionality to a circular area. To overcome this limitation, a
research team designed and constructed a novel soft arm that includes a new
prismatic actuator at its base. This actuator utilizes pneumatic muscles and a
piston for enhanced back-driving capabilities. The addition of this prismatic joint
substantially expands the arm's task space, allowing for tasks that were previously
unachievable by soft robots, such as multi-point object placement and container
access. By combining a soft robotic arm with a prismatic joint, the usability of
soft robots in object manipulation is significantly enhanced. This development
paves the way for practical soft robotic applications in everyday environments.

To utilize bosonic quanta in high-speed quantum information processing, efficiently cooling motional modes is crucial. Our research focuses on pushing the cooling time limit below what's achievable with traditional sideband cooling methods. We present a new approach using deep reinforcement learning to achieve this. This technique has been effectively demonstrated in accelerating the cooling of macroscopic systems, such as a magnonic sphere, and can be uniformly applied to more complex setups, such as an opto-magno-mechanical tripartite system. In contrast to conventional cooling methods, which are restricted to specific regimes, our DRL scheme can be applied across a broad range of conditions, offering a comprehensive toolkit for rapidly controlling and generating macroscopic quantum states in various quantum technology applications.

Recently, a weighted numerical radius for Hilbert space operators was introduced.
This study examines additional properties and utilizes this recently defined
numerical radius to derive several novel inequalities for both the weighted and
ordinary numerical radius. Notably, new formulas for the numerical radius are
established, along with comparisons between the numerical radius and its real and
imaginary components, as well as sectorial operators.

We utilize specific characteristics of the transform $\mathscr{C}_{M,m}(A)$ to derive novel inequalities for the bounded linear operator $A$ acting on a complex Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$. Notably, we establish new relationships among $|A|$, $|A^*|$, $|\mathfrak{R}A|$, and $|\mathfrak{I}A|$, and also provide further inequalities of the numerical radius that build upon existing ones.

We propose EDS, a cutting-edge, direct monocular visual odometry system that utilizes both events and frames. Our innovative algorithm harnesses the event generation model to track camera movement during the intervals between captured frames. By adopting a probabilistic framework, we directly compute camera motion from observed brightness increments. This method leverages a sparse network of 3D points to predict brightness changes and compare them with events to estimate motion, minimizing the brightness increment error. EDS constructs a semi-dense 3D environment map using photometric bundle adjustment. Notably, our method is the first to achieve 6-DOF VO using events and frames with a direct approach, thereby circumventing issues related to changing visual appearances. Furthermore, EDS can operate at lower frame rates than existing frame-based VO solutions while maintaining target error performance, which has significant implications for low-power motion-tracking applications where frames are selectively captured on demand, allowing our method to fill in the gaps and continuously track motion. We make the code and datasets publicly available.

The ground state phase diagram for the spin-1/2 XX honeycomb model with dimerization under a transverse magnetic field is already understood. Without the magnetic field, the N\'eel and dimerized phases have been observed. However, when the field is applied, the canted N\'eel and paramagnetic phases also emerge. This paper employs the Lanczos exact diagonalization and Density matrix renormalization group methods to analyze the XX honeycomb model. The focus is on the nearest-neighbor spin quantum correlations, including concurrence and quantum discord. These correlations are shown to accurately identify quantum critical points across the phase diagram in line with previous findings. Although concurrence and quantum discord exhibit short-ranged properties, they can still provide information on long-ranged critical correlations. Furthermore, the phenomenon of "magnetic-entanglement" is observed, beginning from a highly entangled state near the saturation field.

Most deep learning models in computational imaging typically output a single reconstructed image. However, problems such as ill-posedness and nonlinearity often lead to misleading or insufficient results. Bayesian models jointly distribute images and measurements as random vectors to approximate the posterior distribution of unknowns. A new method, based on conditional normalizing flows, aims to replace traditional Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods but has drawbacks such as high memory and computation demands. We introduce C-Trumpets, injective flows specifically designed for imaging, which significantly alleviate these challenges. C-Trumpets reduce memory and training time while utilizing low-dimensional latent spaces and innovative architectural features. These improvements enable C-Trumpets to outperform other conditional flow models in various imaging tasks with lower computational and memory costs. C-Trumpets also facilitate fast approximation of point estimates and physically meaningful uncertainty quantification.

The ideal neural architecture for a particular machine learning task is influenced by multiple factors including data complexity, resource availability, and constraints such as processing time, power usage, and latency. Despite its significance, neural architecture search for table-based datasets has been under-explored. Conventional NAS algorithms, developed for image datasets, often embed resource constraints into reinforcement learning rewards, but this approach frequently leads to suboptimal results in tabular NAS. To address this, a novel technique called TabNAS has been proposed, which employs a rejection-based reinforcement learning strategy that rejects architectures violating resource constraints before training, rather than learning from them. This method incorporates a Monte Carlo correction to the policy update, resulting in more efficient and effective model discovery. Experiments conducted on various table-based datasets confirm the superiority of TabNAS over existing methods, demonstrating its ability to find better models that adhere to the specified constraints.

This article refines the triangle inequality for complex numbers by leveraging the Hermite-Hadamard inequality for convex functions, which in turn enables applications to operator inequalities, such as numerical radius and operator mean inequalities.

We develop a simplified, analytically solvable model to investigate non-equilibrium behavior in open quantum systems, particularly under time-varying conditions within the system or its surroundings. By linking specific bath configurations to a Kitaev chain and applying Third Quantization, we obtain a self-consistent Lindblad master equation, which can result in thermalization, especially when time dependencies are absent. We derive time-evolution equations for the correlation matrix, relating it to quasiparticle mode occupation, and use these findings to create efficient analytical and numerical models describing the non-equilibrium dynamics of open Kitaev chains under diverse driving protocols. This allows us to study the interplay between dissipative forces and coherent excitation generation, driven by rapid parameter changes, and to examine temperature-driven variations, such as Kibble-Zurek ramps, Floquet physics, and other non-equilibrium quantum many-body system behaviors.

In a novel approach, we offer a comprehensive, non-disruptive analysis of the chaotic quantum state within the realm of two-dimensional gravity, focusing on its ergodic phase. To achieve this, we develop a complete description of semi-classical 2D gravity through the lens of its associated universe field theory. Guided by the principles of a flavor-matrix theory, our work reveals the breaking and restoration of causal symmetry in the ergodic phase of holographic gravity, a concept that cannot be derived from JT gravity or its two-dimensional analogues on their own. Instead, their corresponding universe field theory, the Kodaira-Spencer theory of gravity, provides the necessary causal symmetry. By directly connecting the flavor-matrix theory to the Kodaira-Spencer theory via brane-antibrane correlations, we demonstrate that the symmetry breaking and restoration can be visualized through different topological D-brane vacua. Furthermore, we interpret our findings in light of an open-closed string duality between holomorphic Chern-Simons theory and its equivalent closed-string counterpart, the Kodaira-Spencer theory of gravity, highlighting the geometric principles underlying the chaotic quantum state and its characteristic spectral correlations.

When water droplets in clouds collide, they often fail to merge into larger droplets due to the air cushion between them, reducing their coalescence rate. This effect, known as collision efficiency, is not well understood and is often small. Researchers have used new tracking techniques to measure the positions of droplet pairs falling through calm air with high precision. This enabled them to calculate the droplets' relative positions, speeds, and accelerations as close as one-tenth of a droplet diameter apart. Their findings show that the accelerations of coalescing droplets differ from those that don't merge, with coalescing droplets having accelerations above a certain threshold. The researchers explain how these accelerations relate to the interactions between droplets and present theories to predict the threshold acceleration. They also propose that analyzing the distribution of accelerations in turbulent clouds could be used to estimate collision efficiency and predict coalescence rates of cloud droplets.

Recent research demonstrates that autoregressive language models can efficiently handle a wide array of NLP tasks via novel zero- and few-shot learning strategies, thus expanding the potential applications of pre-trained language models. This study presents two advanced autoregressive GPT-like models, one with 1.3 billion parameters and the other with 13 billion parameters, which were trained on a vast dataset comprising 60 languages from 25 language families using Wikipedia and the Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus. By leveraging GPT-2 architecture, sparse attention mechanism, and frameworks like Deepspeed and Megatron, the models achieved impressive results and showcased comparable performance to Facebook's XGLM models, while supporting more languages and enhancing the capabilities for low-resource languages in CIS countries and Russian-speaking nations. The paper provides a detailed account of the design rationale behind the chosen architecture, outlines the data preparation pipeline, and presents the results of training five smaller versions of the model to select the most effective multilingual tokenization approach. Furthermore, it evaluates the models' performance across a diverse range of multilingual tasks, including classification, generation, sequence labeling, and knowledge probing, utilizing both zero-shot and few-shot methods. Notably, the study also compares the models' classification results with those of the state-of-the-art multilingual model, XGLM, and makes the source code and the mGPT XL model publicly available.

We investigate the accelerated performance of the recently proposed Local Polynomial Interpolation-based Gradient Descent method (LPI-GD) for solving approximate empirical risk minimization problems (ERM) efficiently. LPI-GD targets strongly convex and smooth loss functions with a condition number of $\sigma$ and assumes an $\eta$-Hölder continuity in the data. The method's oracle complexity for achieving a specified accuracy $\varepsilon$ is found to be $\tilde{O}(\sigma m^d \log(1/\varepsilon))$, with $d$ representing the dimension of the parameter space and $m$ representing the size of an approximation grid. Furthermore, we observe that the factor $m^d$ can be expressed as $O((1/\varepsilon)^{d/2\eta})$. We note that LPI-GD outperforms both gradient descent (GD) and stochastic gradient descent (SGD) in certain parameter regimes. Our work proposes two new accelerated LPI-GD methods for solving ERM problems, which yield an oracle complexity of $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{\sigma} m^d \log(1/\varepsilon))$. Additionally, we conduct an empirical study on local polynomial interpolation-based gradient methods and confirm that LPI-GD outperforms GD and SGD in specific scenarios, while our proposed methods achieve accelerated results.

We have developed an innovative approach to particle filtering in dynamic systems governed by stochastic differential equations (SDEs). The new methodology involves converting the SDE into a discrete-time model and designing efficient particle filters to handle this transformed system. Our discretisation technique converges at a weak order of 1 and generates a unique structure in the sequential dependence of the state vector. We have introduced a category of space-sequential particle filters that leverage this property to enhance performance in high-dimensional systems. Numerical simulations on the stochastic Lorenz 96 system demonstrate that our approach results in constant estimation errors despite increasing system dimensions, with a computational cost that grows polynomially, not exponentially. Furthermore, this paper provides a comprehensive framework for discrete-time filtering of SDE-driven systems. We prove that the marginal posterior laws of the resulting discrete-time model converge to those of the original continuous-time model under a specific metric, a result applicable to various discretisation schemes and particle filters.

Large interstellar dust particles are thought to be created by supernovae and stellar winds, but smaller grains can be produced when larger ones are broken apart by stochastic acceleration. To better understand this acceleration, researchers have developed new methods for simulating it using complex astrophysical models. In a recent study, scientists treated dust particles as massive objects and simulated various physical scenarios to test the accuracy of their method. They also ran simulations of decaying turbulent systems, which suggested that dust grains can be accelerated to high speeds, even when they are electrically neutral. However, the researchers found that charged grains are more likely to experience a wide range of velocities, which may help protect them from breaking apart. These findings could have implications for the formation of relatively pristine dust grains, which have been preserved for long periods of time.
The document offers technical information on the Hybrid-AIM simulator employed in Sharon and Stone (2017) and Parks-Young and Sharon (2022).

We establish the non-existence of odd-dimensional stable, compact, and minimal immersions within the product of two complex projective spaces. Furthermore, we prove that the only stable, compact, and minimal immersions in the product of a quaternionic projective space and any other Riemannian manifold are those formed by products of quaternionic projective subspaces and immersions in the second manifold. This extends previous results by the second-named author from lower-dimensional or codimension immersions to arbitrary dimensions. Additionally, we demonstrate that the stable, compact, and minimal immersions in the product of an octonionic projective plane and any other Riemannian manifold can only consist of products of octonionic projective subspaces and immersions in the second manifold.

We consider the imaginary quadratic field $K$ and a prime $p$ that splits within it. This work establishes an anticyclotomic Euler system for the adjoint representation connected to elliptic modular forms that have been base changed to $K$. Our Euler system is linked to a $p$-adic $L$-function, which is constructed from a $p$-adic $L$-function for unitary groups developed by Eischen-Wan and Eischen-Harris-Li-Skinner. This relationship enables us to prove the Bloch-Kato conjecture in rank zero for new cases, as well as make progress on the Iwasawa main conjecture with respect to a certain divisibility.

The goal of active mapping involves selecting an optimal sequence of sensing views within a limited budget, such as a constrained distance traveled. This study explores the application of active occupancy grid mapping with range sensors, such as LiDAR or depth cameras, and addresses the challenge of optimizing information gain in the mapping process. Current methods rely on optimizing information-theoretic measures related to sensor data, but these methods face difficulties due to the non-differentiable nature of ray-tracing within a grid representation. This work proposes a novel approach that approximates the mutual information between a grid map and sensor data using a differentiable method, allowing for gradient-based optimization in the continuous space of sensor positions. As a result, the proposed method yields more informative sensing trajectories while minimizing the risk of occlusions and collisions, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations and real-world experiments in both 2-D and 3-D environments.

The goal of motion magnification techniques in video analysis is to enhance and reveal subtle movements. Two primary methods exist, with Eulerian and Lagrangian approaches differing in their approach. Eulerian magnifies motion indirectly through pixel-level manipulation, whereas Lagrangian employs optical flow analysis to amplify trajectory patterns. Facial microexpressions are fast and spatially confined, rendering detection challenging. A novel, local Lagrangian motion magnification method is proposed for analyzing facial micromovements, comprising three key components. Firstly, the recurrent all-pairs field transforms (RAFT) approach for facial optical flow is refined through the incorporation of ground truth data derived from the CASME II dataset using the variational dense inverse search algorithm. This enables efficient and accurate optical flow estimation for facial videos. Secondly, due to the spatial and temporal locality of facial micromovements, a sparse double decomposition is proposed, combining spatial and temporal component analysis. Thirdly, this decomposition is used to amplify micro-motions in specific facial regions through a novel forward warping strategy involving triangular splitting of the image grid and barycentric interpolation of RGB values. The efficacy of the approach is demonstrated through multiple examples.

Recent advancements in high-pressure synthesis have enabled the creation of (Pb,In)Te compounds with an increased indium concentration, resulting in higher superconducting transition temperatures compared to lead-rich compounds. This research investigates the temperature-dependent London penetration depth of the In$_{0.8}$Pb$_{0.2}$Te compound, which exhibits a bulk superconducting transition temperature of approximately 4.75 K. The obtained results show conventional superconducting behavior, excluding the possibility of odd-parity, topologically nontrivial pairing, but still allowing for odd-parity pairing. Additionally, critical field values and other key superconducting parameters measured below 1 K are presented in this study.

In human-AI collaborative creativity, both humans and AI work together as equal partners to produce a shared creative product. The success of these collaborations heavily relies on the interaction dynamics, including turn-taking, contribution type, and communication. Consequently, an interaction model plays a pivotal role in co-creative systems, yet there is limited research on interaction design in this area. Most existing co-creative systems lack a focus on interaction design, and previous research primarily concentrated on AI abilities rather than human-AI collaboration. This study highlights the importance of interaction design in co-creative systems by introducing the Co-Creative Framework for Interaction design (COFI). Researchers can utilize COFI to develop interaction models, model existing systems, and identify potential for improved human-AI collaboration through enhanced interaction models. By categorizing existing systems using COFI and analyzing the results, we have identified opportunities to shift the focus towards more effective interaction models that facilitate open communication and stronger human-AI partnerships.

We develop a comprehensive framework that combines quantum representations in both Condensed Matter Physics and Quantum Field Theory. This unified approach utilizes a fundamental operator called Y(u,v), defined in terms of mixed Hilbert spaces, to represent quantum systems involving bosons, fermions, and spin systems. This basis operator is built upon the momentum and position operators, which in turn are related to the creation and annihilation operators used in Quantum Field Theory. The coefficients for expanding this operator are derived from the Fourier transform of the Wigner distribution function. Consequently, this framework enables the conversion of spin systems into fermions via the Jordan-Wigner transformation and the mapping of bosons to spin operators through the Holstein-Primakoff transformation. Additionally, unitary transformations such as the Bogoliubov transformation are applicable to this formalism. Furthermore, the Jordan-Schwinger transformation provides an efficient method for computing representations when the operator Y(u,v) is expressed in matrix form. Notably, our unification encompasses the coherent states formulation of quantum physics as a special case. Moreover, a novel formulation of Quantum Field Theory based on the Q-distribution of functional-field variables is proposed. Finally, we discuss the application of this framework to nonequilibrium quantum transport physics, which involves non-Hermitian operators and time-reversal symmetry breaking, in an appendix.

This study focuses on the weighted $L_p$ affine surface areas, which are integral components of the newly formulated $L_p$ Steiner formula within the framework of the $L_p$ Brunn Minkowski theory. We demonstrate that these surface areas qualify as valuations for the set of convex bodies and establish isoperimetric inequalities. Furthermore, we establish a connection between these surface areas and $f$ divergences of cone measures from convex bodies and their polar counterparts, specifically the Kullback-Leibler and R\'enyi divergences.

In manganese-based nitride antiperovskites, such as Mn$_3$NiN, the triangular magnetic ordering over the kagome lattice is influenced by frustration, leading to a non-trivial balance between symmetric and asymmetric magnetic interactions that can only be achieved in a noncollinear magnetic configuration. The resulting electronic interactions and their susceptibility to external constraints, such as epitaxial strain, are critical in determining the microscopic and macroscopic properties of these topological systems. To investigate the impact of epitaxial strain on the magnetic and crystallographic symmetry, we studied the strain imposed within the (111)-plane, while keeping the magnetic and crystallographic symmetries fixed. Our results show a linear shift in the energy of the band structure and a linear increase/decrease in the available states near the Fermi level with the applied strain. Specifically, compression strain reduces the Mn-Mn distances within the (111) kagome plane while increasing the separation between stacked kagome lattices and the available states near the Fermi level. However, the anomalous Hall conductivity exhibits non-linear behavior, where the $\sigma_{111}$ conductivity nearly vanishes under tensile strain, but increases by up to 26% for compression strain close to $-$1.5%. This behavior can be attributed to the non-divergent Berry curvature within the kagome plane, which increases with constraining strain but decreases with expansion strain values.

To fully harness the vast data from forthcoming large-scale surveys, it is essential to extract the complex information about structure formation from the non-linear regime of the universe's evolution. However, due to the intricacies of theoretical and computational models, analyzing observational data in this area remains a significant challenge. We introduce a novel set of statistical tools, based on three-dimensional wavelets, to overcome this obstacle. These statistics involve taking the power $q$ of the complex modulus of the 3D wavelet transform, averaged over space, and are referred to as invariant wavelet moments. Our 3D wavelets are designed to be radially restricted and separable on a spherical coordinate system, and they come in three distinct types: isotropic, directional, and harmonic. We demonstrate the effectiveness of these statistical measures in the Fisher forecast framework using simulated matter fields from the Quijote suite, which show they achieve the best parameter estimates for both standard $\Lambda$CDM parameters and the total mass of neutrinos. Furthermore, we find that we can enhance constraints on all parameters by a factor of 5 to 10 when compared to the standard power spectrum baseline.

We establish limit theorems for the frequency of specific patterns on the edge of randomly chosen ranked tree-child networks. Building on a previous study by Bienvenu et al. (2022) on cherry patterns, our work examines fringe patterns of heights one and two, finding that they either become ubiquitous (possessing a mean that grows linearly and a normal distribution limit) or occur rarely (with a mean that remains constant and a Poisson limit distribution), or they never appear (with a mean tending towards zero and a degenerate limit distribution). We hypothesize that these scenarios are the sole possibilities for any fringe pattern.

Recent laws have sparked interest in machine unlearning, a process that involves removing specific training data points from a model as if they never existed. This may be necessary due to corrupted data, adversarial attacks, or a user's updated data privacy needs. While deleting samples can be effective for simple models, this approach is not applicable to more complex models that learn rich representations. Existing ideas that leverage optimization-based updates are often impractical for large models due to their computational demands. Our method, built upon a conditional independence coefficient, allows for identifying the most critical model parameters related to a specific data point. This approach avoids the need for matrix inversion and is suitable for various applications, including deep learning and vision tasks, by utilizing Markov blanket selection. Compared to other alternatives, our method makes approximate unlearning feasible in settings previously thought to be infeasible, including face recognition, person re-identification, and certain NLP models.

The field of requirements engineering for machine learning lacks comprehensive research and established guidelines, which leads to numerous challenges in designing and developing reliable ML systems. A more focused approach to RE for ML is crucial for enhancing system reliability. Building on past experiences and insights, we developed a comprehensive catalogue of 45 key concerns that should be considered during ML system specification, categorized under five essential aspects: objectives, user experience, infrastructure, models, and data. Examples of these concerns include the infrastructure perspective's execution engine and telemetry, as well as the model perspective's explainability and reproducibility. To validate the importance and practicality of our catalogue, we conducted a focus group with industry experts and received feedback that improved the catalogue and confirmed its relevance. This study's main contribution lies in offering a validated and structured set of concerns that can guide requirements engineers in effectively specifying ML systems.

This study examines the role of sandwiched Renyi relative entropy in the context of AdS/CFT and holographic quantum error correction models. Specifically, we propose a suitable generalization of sandwiched Renyi relative entropy over finite-dimensional von Neumann algebras in operator algebra quantum error correction. Our results demonstrate that the equivalence of bulk and boundary sandwiched relative Renyi entropies is equivalent to several fundamental principles, including the algebraic encoding of states, the Ryu-Takayanagi formula, the equality of relative entropy, and subregion duality. This adds to an existing equivalence theorem between these principles. We also discuss a modular operator definition of sandwiched Renyi relative entropy and its application in finite-dimensional models of holographic quantum error correction. Furthermore, we explore the numerical computation of sandwiched Renyi relative entropies in a simple holographic random tensor network to better understand the corrections to the exact equality of bulk and boundary sandwiched relative Renyi entropy.

The influence of low-excitation radio galaxies on the lifecycle of massive galaxies in the current universe is significant; however, the process by which these active galactic nuclei impact early galaxy development and their evolution remains unclear. A study of 10,481 low-excitation radio galaxies, spanning about 25 square degrees, reveals the radio luminosity function of these galaxies evolves relatively slowly up to redshift 2.5. When the low-excitation radio galaxies are divided into those hosted by inactive and star-forming galaxies, a previously unseen population of low-excitation radio galaxies hosted by star-forming galaxies at high redshift is discovered. The rate of low-excitation radio galaxies in inactive galaxies increases sharply with stellar mass up to redshift 1.5, consistent with data from the current universe, where gas cooling within hot halo regions triggers accretion. Inactive low-excitation radio galaxies dominate the luminosity functions at redshift less than 1, while showing a decline in density with increasing redshift, mirroring that of their host galaxies, and an increase in characteristic luminosity. Conversely, low-excitation radio galaxies hosted by star-forming galaxies increase in density with redshift, becoming the dominant population in most radio-luminosity ranges at redshift 1. The rate of low-excitation radio galaxies in star-forming galaxies shows a weak dependence on stellar mass, and an increase with redshift, implying a distinct fueling mechanism compared to their inactive counterparts, possibly linked to the cold gas supply within star-forming galaxies.

This paper introduces novel concepts, namely annular settling and output annular settling, for a broad class of nonlinear systems. Additionally, we develop and present necessary conditions for generalized Persidskii systems with essentially bounded inputs, encompassing short-time stability, boundedness, annular settling, and output annular settling. These conditions are validated through the satisfaction of linear matrix inequalities. A practical demonstration with recurrent neural networks highlights the relevance of these newly proposed notions and conditions.

Accurate measurement of the displacement of a mechanical oscillator or a microwave field can be achieved using trapped ions or superconducting circuits in combination with ancilla qubits, where the oscillator's information is transferred to and then read from the qubits. But so far, determining the displacement in an unknown direction in the phase space hasn't been successfully done in these oscillator-qubit systems. Here, a novel setup is proposed, which uses a combination of a mechanical oscillator and qubits in an interferometric way to determine displacements in any direction, leveraging feasible interactions that go beyond certain approximation methods. By applying this method, the performance surpasses that of individual estimation methods and a conventional interferometer. What's more, this approach shows that the level of sensitivity is unaffected by the thermal energy in the oscillator, eliminating the need to cool it to the lowest energy state before measuring. A detailed analysis is also conducted on how the qubits and the oscillator affect each other, showing that the proposed setup remains robust even when there's significant noise or thermal energy present.

Designers face challenges when tasked with optimizing designs by combining parameters to meet multiple objectives, which can be extremely complex and require expensive testing. Computational design algorithms can aid designers, but often rely on predefined models of the design space. In contrast, black-box methods can work with any design problem, yet existing research mostly involves either experts or end-users. It remains unclear whether these methods can help designers with real-world projects. This study investigates the potential of Bayesian optimization in guiding the design process. By suggesting the next design candidate to a designer based on previous results, the optimizer was found to help designers explore more design options and reach better solutions, albeit at the cost of reduced agency, creativity, and sense of control. The results suggest that human-in-the-loop optimization can still support novice designers, but may compromise on aspects like creativity and control, especially when agency is not crucial.

To analyze graded Frobenius algebras through a ring theory lens, we first introduce and examine graded quasi-Frobenius rings, their graded Frobenius counterparts, and their shifted variants, delving into the properties and representation theories of these entities. Additionally, we revisit and reevaluate graded left Artinian rings, graded semisimple rings, and establish graded adaptations of key results tied to the Jacobson and singular radicals, their links to injectivity and finiteness conditions. Furthermore, we derive a structural theorem for both graded and shift-graded Frobenius rings.

In this thesis, various optimization tools are developed to tackle diverse challenges in quantum information theory. Initially, a novel algorithm for quantum state estimation is introduced, employing orthogonal projections on intersecting hyperplanes that are determined by probability distributions and measurement operators. An evaluation of its performance is conducted, taking into account realistic error margins, in terms of both runtime and fidelity. Additionally, a technique for verifying quantum non-locality is presented, which identifies a Bell inequality that maximizes the gap between the local hidden variable and the quantum value for a given set of bipartite measurement frequencies. Lastly, an operator is developed to study the quantum marginal problem, along with an algorithm that takes in quantum marginals and eigenvalues and outputs a compatible density matrix, if one exists.

We examine a flat model in a modified theory of gravity, incorporating curvature and stress-energy tensor variations. Our analysis reveals this model emulates the late universe, characterized by accelerated expansion culminating in a cosmic rip. We use a parametric scale factor to devise a model, starting with a singularity marked by zero volume, infinite energy, and infinite temperature, which undergoes accelerated expansion currently, resembling Lambda-CDM in its later stages. Ultimately, our model behaves like a quintessence model for dark energy in the present era and aligns with Lambda-CDM cosmology at late times.

Using the holographic description, we investigate the correlators of fields linked to a quark-antiquark EPR pair within a super Yang-Mills theory through a string in AdS space. The string's endpoints either remain stationary or move uniformly in opposite directions, and we derive exact solutions for its profiles in both scenarios. We then calculate the two-point correlators for the boundary field, described by linearized perturbations, and find their all-time evolution. In the accelerating string case, the string worldsheet exhibits a two-sided AdS black hole with a wormhole, embodying the ER=EPR conjecture. Our analysis reveals that causality influences the nature of the dispersion relation and induced mutual interaction between particles. When the boundaries are causally disconnected, the induced effect results in dissipative dynamics for each particle, with no distance dependence, and the mutual coupling vanishes in late times following a power law. However, if the boundaries are connected, the dispersion relation becomes non-dissipative in the long term. Our research also explores implications for entangled particle dynamics and the ER=EPR conjecture.

We have investigated a cosmological model based on $f(R)$-gravity, where a cubic equation for scalar curvature $R$ yields terms that can be attributed to curvature-driven geometry, inducing an energy component. The outcome is an accelerating universe expansion accompanied by negative anti-gravitating pressure. Numerical methods have been employed to solve several key parameters. Our model's evolution has been compared against observational Hubble data (46 data points) and the Pantheon dataset, a compilation of SNIa observations (40 points in the $0.014 \leqslant z \leqslant1.62$ redshift range). By analyzing plots of various dynamic parameters, certain model characteristics have been elucidated. The deceleration parameter $q$ and the Hubble parameter $H$ graphs demonstrate the accelerating expansion during the present epoch. The transition from deceleration to acceleration for this model occurred at a redshift $z_{tr} \simeq 0.694069$, which is consistent with $\Lambda$CDM. Furthermore, a state finder analysis of our model has been conducted, and its late-time properties confirm that our model is consistent with $\Lambda$CDM.

A major challenge in machine learning-based machinery fault diagnosis lies in its lack of interpretability due to operating as a black box. To address this issue, we introduce a new neural network architecture called the Temporal Logic Neural Network (TLNN). TLNN combines the strengths of traditional neural networks with the added benefit of a formal, interpretable framework. This structure empowers the network to provide a detailed, weighted signal temporal logic explanation of its decision-making process, thereby enhancing the overall diagnosis accuracy and efficiency. Furthermore, TLNN enables users to understand the reasoning behind the diagnosis results.

We examine the degradation of a system's adiabaticity when cooling down a complex quantum system from an initial thermal state to a critical point. It is found that the density of excited particles, a measure of the adiabaticity of the system's evolution, adheres to common scaling laws as the cooling rate, initial, and final temperatures are varied. These laws are general and depend on the specific critical exponents of the underlying quantum phase transition. We verify these findings theoretically for a Kitaev quantum wire connected to dissipative baths, and extend the reasoning to more general conditions. Our study demonstrates that the unique characteristics of quantum critical points can be investigated using dynamic methods at finite temperatures without adjusting the control parameter governing the transition.

We show that basic communication methods and signal processing techniques can replicate the capabilities of edge servers in federated learning, allowing massive networks of user devices to perform large-scale collaborative learning without central servers. We've developed a training method that enables devices to process data continuously without being interrupted by periodic data uploads, thereby maximizing their computational potential. Analytical results confirm that our approach achieves comparable training efficiency to traditional server-based methods when there's minimal interference, but performance degradation occurs when interference is heavy-tailed. However, significant time savings can be achieved by processing data in parallel with communication, particularly in scenarios with high communication latency, as extensive simulations have demonstrated.

This paper focuses on generalized moment functions of higher order and their connections to established binomial-type functions across different structures. Our previous work on this topic explored these functions within the context of commutative groups. Specifically, we developed a characterization of generalized moment functions on such groups as a product of an exponential, a sequence of multivariate Bell polynomials, and additive functions. In this paper, we extend our research by analyzing generalized moment function sequences in an even more abstract setting: hypergroups. We establish a characterization of these functions within the polynomial hypergroup, linking them to partial derivatives of polynomial compositions and analytic functions. Our study includes a detailed example of moment generating functions for the Tchebyshev hypergroup with a rank of at most two.

We introduce GraphMoE, a novel neural network architecture that learns generative models for random graphs. By leveraging moment estimators, the network trains on graphlet features to replicate a specific distribution of random graphs. Taking random noise as input, the network produces vector representations for each graph node, enabling the realization of synthetic graphs via a kernel function. Demonstrations show that GraphMoE-generated graphs can convincingly mimic real-world data from chemistry, medicine, and social networks, successfully deceiving discriminator networks trained to distinguish between different graph classes.

Previous single-task models, although effective for specific tasks, have shown shortcomings in real-world applications, which involve multitasking and adapting to changing domains. In contrast, recent advancements in instructional prompts have demonstrated improved performance in handling multiple tasks; however, there has been a lack of comprehensive studies on the intersection of instructional prompts and multi-task learning within the biomedical field. Consequently, this research delves into the implications of instructional prompts on multi-task learning within the biomedical field, introducing a dataset of 32 instructional tasks for biomedical natural language processing across various categories, known as the BoX. By utilizing this meta-dataset, the proposed In-BoXBART model is able to simultaneously learn all tasks in the BoX without requiring task-specific modules. To date, this research represents the first attempt at developing a unified model in the biomedical field that leverages instructional prompts to achieve task generalization. Experimental outcomes reveal that the proposed In-BoXBART model outperforms single-task and multi-task (without instructional prompts) baselines, showcasing a ~23% improvement in few-shot learning and a ~18% average increase in overall performance. Additionally, the analysis indicates considerable room for improvement across tasks within the BoX, signifying opportunities for future research directions.

We investigate the distribution of the values $\frac{L'}{L}(1/2+\epsilon,\chi_D)$ for varying fundamental discriminants $D$, where $0<\epsilon<\frac{1}{2}$, as they relate to the real character associated with $D$. Furthermore, we obtain an upper limit on how quickly this family converges to its limiting distribution, ultimately yielding an asymptotic approximation for small absolute values of $\frac{L'}{L}(1/2+\epsilon,\chi_D)$.

Recent hyperspectral unmixing literature has seen increased deep learning application, notably using autoencoder architecture. We introduce a novel split architecture utilizing pseudo-ground truth abundances for unmixing network optimization, accompanied by an approximation network enhancing spatial correlation. The proposed Guided Encoder-Decoder Architecture for Hyperspectral Unmixing with Spatial Smoothness (GAUSS) leverages one-hot encoded abundances and eliminates prior hyperspectral unmixing method usage through k-means algorithm application. Additionally, we relax the single-layer mixing network constraint by incorporating unmixing network generated abundances. Furthermore, we experiment with GAUSS method modifications: GAUSS_blind and GAUSS_prime, which combine unmixing and mixing networks and utilize signal processing method results as pseudo-ground truth, respectively. Our architectures demonstrate comparable or superior performance to existing hyperspectral unmixing algorithms from both deep learning and signal processing domains, based on quantitative and graphical results for four experimental datasets.

We're examining 2-2 scattering in four-dimensional spacetime using Celestial variables and the crossing symmetric dispersion relation (CSDR) to reframe Celestial amplitudes in terms of symmetrical partial waves, which are affected by singularities in the complex Celestial variable. Local theories must remove these spurious singularities. By applying null constraints, we find that they can be expressed in a closed form, resulting in novel constraints on partial wave moments, and thereby enabling the assessment of low spin dominance for scalar theories. Our analysis reveals a previously unidentified kind of positivity present in a wide range of theories, which we prove is characteristic of theories that are dominated by spin-0 particles. By removing spurious singularities from crossing symmetric partial waves, we identify Feynman blocks, which exhibit unique properties in the Celestial variable. These properties include typically real values, and by leveraging Geometric Function Theory (GFT) techniques, we establish non-projective bounds on Wilson coefficients in relation to partial wave moments.

A novel approach to compress large pre-trained language models has been developed, using a technique called Knowledge Distillation (KD). This method has gained significant attention in recent years, and various methods have been proposed to improve its efficiency. Our research introduces CILDA, a data augmentation technique tailored for KD that utilizes contrastive learning and intermediate layer representations to generate more accurate augmented samples. Notably, CILDA leverages the main task's intermediate layer representations in contrastive learning for improved masked adversarial data augmentation. As a result, CILDA achieves superior performance compared to the current KD state-of-the-art methods on both the GLUE benchmark and an out-of-domain evaluation.

The Cuesta-Conway numbers, a subset of the surreal numbers, can be defined in a straightforward manner by considering their normal forms, which are composed of exponentials indexed by ordinals. Building upon the real numbers and ordinals, surreal numbers provide a foundation for addition, multiplication, and ordering in a total sequence. The construction of surreal numbers also generates a series of real-closed fields, serving as a precursor to a more comprehensive understanding. Ultimately, the surreal numbers can be proven to constitute a totally ordered, commutative, real-closed field.

Reinforcement learning has become increasingly prevalent in controlled text generation tasks like unsupervised text style transfer. A significant challenge in applying RL to these tasks lies in dealing with sparse rewards, which are only available after the full text is generated, and a large action space, resulting in inefficient and non-convergent training. Proposed solutions, such as reward-shaping strategies, have shown limited improvements. Conversely, this study presents a novel method that provides dense rewards for each token generated, significantly enhancing the efficiency and effectiveness of RL training. Our approach demonstrates substantial improvements over current state-of-the-art systems in unsupervised text style transfer, yielding 21% better human evaluation and 12% better automatic evaluation results. By adopting dense rewards, our method outperforms existing reward-shaping approaches by 22% in human evaluation and reduces the time required for RL training by a factor of 7.5.
This article sets out to demonstrate a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.

The particle in a box model features a classical Hamiltonian $H=p^2$ with $2m=1$, confined within a finite coordinate space of $-b<q<b$, where $0<b<\infty$. This system's simplicity lends itself well to canonical quantization, which has been extensively explored, serving as an introductory tool for understanding quantum mechanics. However, a recent analysis indicates that past conclusions may be invalid due to quantization problems, and the process of affine quantization yields a proper quantization method that leads to more complex eigenfunctions and eigenvalues, requiring further investigation.

Recent benchmark studies have highlighted an unexpected stagnation in some machine learning subfields despite the reported advancements in literature. The observed lack of progress can be attributed to the unreliability of numerous model comparison studies, which often fail to account for various known sources of irreproducibility. Consequently, these studies frequently produce unverifiable results. Our aim is to compile and analyze the reported causes of unreliability in academic literature. We delve into existing literature to develop a comprehensive overview and taxonomy, while also discussing the identified sources of unreliability. Furthermore, we outline three potential avenues for future investigation.

Scientific discoveries are frequently rooted in understanding relationships, often achieved through approximations. Although deep learning has immense potential for identifying relationships within data, its application in scientific research has been limited due to the difficulty in deciphering the learned connections. A crucial information-theoretic framework known as the Information Bottleneck has been developed to grasp relationships between inputs and outputs by optimizing a balance between approximation fidelity and complexity. By dispersing these "bottlenecks" across various components of the input, researchers have opened new avenues for developing more interpretable deep learning methods in science. The Distributed Information Bottleneck allows the examination of complex systems by restricting and monitoring the information about individual components, resulting in meaningful approximations. This technique has been successfully applied in fields like applied mathematics and condensed matter physics, demonstrating its explanatory capabilities. By using a systematic approach to approximation, the Distributed Information Bottleneck enhances interpretability in deep learning, thereby facilitating an in-depth analysis of information flow within systems.

To evaluate the ability of NLP models to adapt to multiple unseen tasks with given instructions, we created Super-NaturalInstructions, a comprehensive database of 1,616 diverse NLP tasks along with expert-written instructions. Our database encompasses 76 distinct task types, including classification, extraction, and text rewriting. This extensive collection enables thorough evaluation of cross-task generalization under instructions, where models are trained on one set of tasks and tested on unseen ones. Additionally, we developed Tk-Instruct, a transformer model capable of following various in-context instructions. Our experiments demonstrated that Tk-Instruct significantly outperformed existing models like InstructGPT by 9% on our benchmark, despite being an order of magnitude smaller. We also analyzed how model generalization improves with parameters like the number of observed tasks, task instances, and model sizes. Our goal is to advance the development of more versatile NLP models through our dataset and model.

Current studies on spin-orbit coupled states in transition metal systems, specifically in iridate materials and $\alpha$-RuCl$_{3}$, have garnered significant interest. By adjusting the balance between spin-orbit interaction and crystal field splitting, researchers have successfully created a new state, denoted as $\mu=\frac{1}{2}$, which facilitates Ising interactions. This was achieved through a chemical transformation that converted Li$_{2}$RhO$_{3}$ into Ag$_{3}$LiRh$_{2}$O$_{6}$, leading to enhanced crystal field distortion and diminished spin-orbit interaction. An analytical expression for the new $\mu=\frac{1}{2}$ state was derived using perturbation theory for the Ag$_{3}$LiRh$_{2}$O$_{6}$ compound, which differs from the conventional $J_\text{eff}=\frac{1}{2}$ state in Li$_{2}$RhO$_{3}$. The resulting change in ground state is accompanied by a marked shift in magnetic properties from a 6 K spin-glass to a 94 K antiferromagnet, presenting an opportunity to explore a wide range of magnetic phases by fine-tuning material properties.

Developing fast, precise, and stable solutions to time-dependent partial differential equations poses significant challenges. This problem can be addressed through the use of graph neural networks, specifically by learning from message-passing models to create efficient PDE solvers. Firstly, we establish a method for representing PDE data in a domain-independent manner inspired by traditional PDE solvers. Secondly, we demonstrate that graphs can effectively represent PDE data on complex meshes and that message-passing graph neural networks can accurately capture governing equations. Consequently, these networks can learn efficient solver schemes for both linear and nonlinear PDEs. Moreover, we show that the trained solvers can be applied to various complex domains without the need for retraining. Lastly, we show that a recurrent graph neural network can be used to find a sequence of temporal solutions to a PDE.

Single photon emitters are typically characterized with a Hanbury Brown and Twiss intensity interferometer, consisting of a 50:50 beamsplitter and two synchronized photon counters. For single photon emitters, the correlation of photon arrival times between the detectors, represented by $g^{(2)}(\tau)$, exhibits a characteristic zero-value dip at $\tau=0$. Conventionally, a heuristic for identifying single photon emitters is by measuring a system's $g^{(2)}(0)$ to be less than 1/2. However, our research demonstrates that this identification can be compromised when the detectors have unequal sensitivity and when the background noise exceeds half of the true signal intensity of the single photon emitter.

A new method called the single-pixel imaging camera, utilizing complementary detection and optimized Bernoulli modulation, has been developed to minimize the effect of interference in single-pixel imaging. Simulation results show that this camera maintains its accuracy even with significant fluctuations in interference light intensity when the coded pattern is at 50% probability. We compare the reconstruction results of both single-pixel imaging and differential single-pixel imaging to highlight the advantages of the proposed technique. The CSPI camera is poised to accelerate practical applications of single-pixel imaging lidar.

A class of enriched unfitted finite element methods, also known as generalized finite element methods, is explored to solve complex interface problems. These problems, specifically 1D elliptic interface issues, have solutions with discontinuities, and may involve interface jump conditions like those that are implicit or Robin-type. The main obstacle to developing generalized finite element methods is to create enrichment functions that effectively capture solution discontinuities without leading to a rapid increase in condition number. Recently, a linear stable generalized finite element method was developed with one enrichment function; we extended this to an arbitrary degree by using two discontinuous one-sided enrichment functions. As a result, we have achieved optimal order convergence in the L^2 and broken H^1 norms, including at all nodes. To demonstrate the efficiency of the method, the generalized finite element method was tested on a multi-layer wall model of drug-eluting stents, which features zero-flux jump conditions and implicit concentration interface conditions.

The $n$-qubit stabilizer states are preserved by a subset of the Pauli group and transformed by unitary operations from the Clifford group. A set of physically-motivated operations, consisting of Hadamard, phase, and CNOT gates, generates a graph structure representing stabilizer transformations. These "reachability graphs" have been explicitly constructed for $n\le5$ and further divided into separate, complex components based on restricted sets of Clifford gates. We explore the entropic structure of stabilizer states, focusing on subgraphs generated by Hadamard and CNOT operations on two qubits. We show how the two-qubit subgraphs evolve into more complex subgraphs at three and four qubits, proposing that no additional subgraph types emerge beyond four qubits. However, the entropic complexity within the subgraphs increases with the number of qubits, resulting in some states at four qubits having entropy vectors that defy holographic entropy inequalities. This transition in the reachability graphs highlights the difference between holographic and non-holographic states within the stabilizer framework.

The inaugural MultiEarth 2022 competition is a groundbreaking initiative focused on forest deforestation monitoring and analysis in the Amazon rainforest, regardless of time and environmental conditions. The challenge aims to establish a unified standard for multimodal information processing and facilitate collaboration between experts in earth and environmental sciences, and those specializing in multimodal representation learning, to compare the effectiveness of various methods in estimating deforestation under standardized conditions. The challenge will comprise three distinct sub-competitions: matrix completion, deforestation prediction, and image transformation. This paper outlines the guidelines, datasets, and evaluation criteria for the sub-challenges. The challenge's website is accessible at https://sites.google.com/view/rainforest-challenge.

Recent research has highlighted the need to reconcile conflicting objectives during model development (such as precision versus impartiality or various metrics of impartiality). These trade-offs exemplify a more extensive category of multi-objective optimization problems, in which optimization techniques aim to find Pareto optimal trade-offs between competing targets. In this research, we first present a measurable indicator that enables the direct optimization of group fairness (specifically, balancing accuracy across groups) in model development. Then, we demonstrate two model-independent multi-objective optimization frameworks for learning Pareto optimal parameterizations over distinct subgroups of neural classification models. We evaluate our methods on the particular task of detecting hate speech, in which previous studies have revealed a lack of group fairness among speakers of different English dialects. Experimental results across convolutional, sequential, and transformer-based neural architectures show improved empirical precision-fairness trade-offs in comparison to prior work. Moreover, our measure allows the Pareto machinery to ensure that each architecture achieves the best possible trade-off between fairness and accuracy based on the dataset, subject to user-defined error tolerance thresholds.

Tailoring the electronic properties of epitaxial graphene can be accomplished through intercalation, a method that also allows for the creation of thin layers with unique properties that differ from their bulk counterparts due to quantum confinement effects. In this study, we demonstrate a method for uniformly integrating lead into quasi-freestanding graphene on silicon carbide, resulting in a charge-neutral state with a remarkably high density of positively charged carriers of approximately 5.5 x 10^9 per square centimeter. Our use of momentum microscopy reveals new energy bands originating from metallic lead at the interface, and electron diffraction experiments indicate a specific arrangement of lead and graphene that is not currently reflected in existing band structure data. These findings showcase the potential for two-dimensional layering and associated band formation in heavy-element materials, which may give rise to strong spin-orbit effects and potentially even superconductivity at the graphene/silicon carbide interface.

Conversational systems that use existing responses can learn to rank suitable answers by comparing the similarities between response vector representations. But, training models on single dialogue contexts can hinder their ability to recognize natural dialogue variations during real-time conversations. Our proposed system tackles this limitation by incorporating multiple context variations into the learning process. We use a technique called contrastive learning to help models learn more robust dialogue representations that remain unchanged even when encountering variations. We tested our approach on several benchmark dialogue datasets and found that it complements existing dialogue augmentation methods and improves significantly over traditional BERT-based ranking systems. Additionally, we introduced a new method called ConMix that introduces random variations in dialogue responses by swapping tokens from other context conversations within a batch. This approach outperforms previous methods and produces more resilient dialogue representations that can withstand common real-world variations.

A promising method for enabling robots to develop skilled manipulation skills is imitation learning, as it doesn't require a highly-designed reward system or substantial computation power. Nonetheless, existing imitation learning approaches have limitations, including the need for complex data collection infrastructure and difficulties in generalizing beyond the training data. To address these challenges, researchers have explored ways to collect additional data that represents various operating conditions. This study examines the effects of corrective and randomly-collected demonstration data on the performance of a robot learning a policy for a pick-and-place task using a five-fingered robot hand. Our research demonstrates that corrective demonstrations yield significantly better outcomes than randomly-collected demonstrations when the additional demonstrations make up a larger portion of the total training data. Conversely, when there are more original demonstrations than additional ones, there are no notable differences between corrective and randomly-collected demonstrations. These findings reveal the inherent trade-off between the time and resources required for gathering corrective demonstrations and their advantages over randomly-collected demonstrations. Furthermore, this research showcases the potential for using cost-effective sensors like LeapMotion to lower the expense of collecting demonstration data for tasks involving dexterous manipulation. The source code for this study is publicly available on GitHub.

This paper outlines a system, BLCU-ICALL, developed for the SemEval-2022 Task 1, specifically the Definition Modeling subtrack. BLCU-ICALL achieved notable rankings, ranking 1st in Italian, 2nd in Spanish and Russian, and 3rd in English and French. We introduce a transformer-based multitasking approach to address the challenge. This framework incorporates various embedding architectures via cross-attention, and a masking language model objective is used to analyze gloss structures. Furthermore, a straightforward yet impactful model aggregation strategy is proposed to enhance robustness. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of our proposed method. The corresponding code can be found at: https://github.com/blcuicall/SemEval2022-Task1-DM.

Open clusters serve as crucial, coeval structures that aid in comprehending star formation and stellar evolution, and provide insight into the Galaxy's physical characteristics. Recent advancements in precise large-scale stellar parallax and proper motion data have significantly reduced the challenge of isolating open clusters from the surrounding field. Nevertheless, certain limitations persist due to the reliance on optical wavelengths in large-scale studies. Our study aims to extend the open clusters' sequences towards fainter magnitudes, complementing existing Gaia data with near-infrared information from the VVV survey. By employing a homogeneous analysis on 37 open clusters, utilizing a combination of two sophisticated methods, we successfully isolated the clusters from the field using near-infrared data. This process led to an increase of approximately 47% in new member candidates, on average, across our sample, with a high membership probability of at least 0.9. This study forms the second installment in a series seeking to provide a uniform, near-infrared view of open cluster sequences.

This survey provides an overview of the advancements made in the past decade towards understanding how to approximately solve constraint satisfaction problems using the streaming and sketching models of computation. Following a summary of the key results, we delve into the detailed proofs and offer insights into the tight dichotomy that emerges when applying sketching algorithms in the subpolynomial space paradigm.

The Earth's and other planets' rotational responses to external gravitational forces heavily rely on their internal makeup. Specifically, the presence of a specific oscillatory mode, called Free Core Nutation, is known to amplify forced rotational movements at specific frequencies. This mode bears resemblance to the Spin-Over Mode, describing the self-sustaining rotation of a fluid core. By analyzing a model featuring a two-layer planetary structure with a rigid mantle and fluid core, we found that the Spin-Over Mode frequency occurs when the planet's internal and external torques are balanced. Furthermore, we observed that energy loss at the Core-Mantle Boundary damps the Free Core Nutation, causing its resonance frequency to shift. This shift is approximately one day for Earth and can be attributed to the Spin-Over Mode's influence, resulting in a minimum transfer function magnitude and lower Quality factor than expected. Finally, we explore potential implications of this mechanism on Mars, the Moon, and Earth's long-term evolution.

A cutting-edge method in materials and life sciences, infrared hyperspectral imaging, has struggled to be effective in sub-diffraction nanoimaging. The technique relies on sequential data acquisition which greatly slows down the process. We developed a novel approach by applying the concept of low-rank matrix reconstruction to a sub-diffraction scheme in AFM-IR imaging to make hyperspectral nanoimaging more efficient. To test the effectiveness of our approach, we utilized Leishmania species as our biological sample of interest and used a 1300-1900 cm$^{-1}$ spectral range with a step width of 220 nm. We used HCA for extracting chemically distinct locations from the data. With 5% of the original data, we were able to reconstruct the full data set using low-rank matrix recovery. The results showed a significant agreement between the full and reconstructed data sets. Our approach can shorten the data acquisition time from over 14 hours to less than 1 hour, significantly increasing the practical application of hyperspectral nanoimaging in fields of nano- and bio-materials.

We have investigated the thermal photon emission rate of the quark-gluon plasma at a temperature of 250 MeV, based on lattice QCD simulations that utilize Wilson fermions. We compared the results from lattice QCD with theoretical models, such as perturbative QCD and supersymmetric Yang-Mills, finding that they agree within 10%. To further refine our analysis, we applied the Backus-Gilbert method to extract model-independent spectral functions. Using these results, we fitted the photon emission rate over different frequency ranges, with good agreement with mock data from both perturbative QCD and supersymmetric Yang-Mills. Our findings are particularly constrained at photon momenta around 0.8 GeV, where we estimate the differential photon emission rate per unit volume to be approximately 2.2 times 10 to the negative 3 GeV.

Since the discovery of magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, the study of flat bands in Dirac materials has gained significant attention as a potential platform for observing strong correlation effects in electronic systems. Our research demonstrates that the specific symmetry group that protects the Dirac cone in such materials dictates the feasibility of flattening a Dirac band through the adjustment of a small number of parameters. We establish a criterion to calculate the required number of parameters to achieve a vanishing Dirac velocity based on the symmetry group. We then apply this criterion to examine band flattening in twisted bilayer graphene and surface states of three-dimensional topological insulators. Following this investigation, we pinpoint the symmetries under which the vanishing of the Dirac velocity results in the emergence of perfectly-flat bands. This analysis enables the creation of new model Hamiltonians that exhibit perfectly-flat bands at specific points in the parameter space, including a toy model of two coupled three-dimensional TI surfaces and a quasi-crystalline extension of the chiral model of TBG.

We investigate the path-wise control of nonlinear stochastic systems defined by sets of stochastic differential equations. In this context, we introduce a concept called stochastic relative degree and a transformation that simplifies the system's dynamics to a stochastic standard form, facilitating the design of state-feedback control that linearizes and eliminates noise. However, this control strategy is unfeasible due to its reliance on inaccessible Brownian motion. Building on this idealized approach, we propose a hybrid control framework that achieves effective path-wise control by periodically adjusting the system's state to counteract the noise effect, utilizing actual measurements. We prove that this practical control scheme approaches ideal performance as the compensation interval shortens. We also explore asymptotic output tracking in both theoretical and real-world contexts and substantiate our findings through a numerical example.

A previously active Oort cloud comet C/2017 K2 (PANSTARRS) was observed for the first time in the inner solar system as it passed through at a distance of over 20 astronomical units from the Sun. The comet was observed using the Hubble Space Telescope on March 19-20, 2021, and further analyzed using data from the Palomar Hale Telescope on May 18, 2021. The observations showed clear variations in the color and polarization of the comet's dust at different distances from the nucleus. This data suggests that the comet's inner coma is primarily composed of micron-sized water ice grains that are undergoing sublimation, whereas the tail is made up of more stable millimeter-sized grains. A similar analysis of data from comet C/2012 S1 (ISON) revealed that previous findings on its polarimetric halo were likely due to observational errors.

Quantum computing is expected to significantly accelerate computationally demanding tasks, like solving complex optimization problems involving numerous variables. In the field of high-energy particle colliders, quantum-assisted algorithms have the potential to expedite the grouping of particles into jets. This study compares the effectiveness of quantum annealing for clustering particles based on optimizing the "thrust" in electron-positron collision events. The findings show that quantum annealing performs similarly to both exact classical methods and classical heuristics, but this performance is achieved only after carefully adjusting the annealing parameters. Without such tuning, comparable results can be achieved through the use of a quantum-classical hybrid approach.

We introduce cross-view transformers, an efficient model leveraging attention for
map-view semantic segmentation across multiple camera views. Our model
automatically learns a mapping between individual camera perspectives and a unified
map-view representation using a camera-sensitive attention mechanism. 
Each camera utilizes positional embeddings derived from its specific calibration settings.
These embeddings enable a transformer to infer the mapping across different viewpoints
without explicitly modeling the geometry involved. 
The architecture comprises a convolutional image encoder for each camera view and
cross-view transformer layers that generate map-view semantic segmentation.
Our proposed model is straightforward, highly parallelizable, and capable of real-time
processing. We achieve state-of-the-art performance on the nuScenes dataset, with
substantial inference speedup of 4x. The model's implementation is publicly available
at https://github.com/bradyz/cross_view_transformers.

The intricate dance of intracellular proteins plays a pivotal role in governing fundamental cellular processes such as cell division and movement, both of which involve the dynamic reconfiguration of cell shape. As cell shape evolves, it can, in turn, influence the behavior of pattern-forming proteins, thereby establishing a complex interplay between cell shape and chemical dynamics. Although numerous computational studies have delved into the rich dynamics resulting from this relationship, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. To better comprehend these mechanisms, we have developed a conceptual model for cell polarity on a dynamic, one-dimensional surface, drawing upon concepts from differential geometry. By deriving the equations governing mass-conserving reaction-diffusion systems on evolving surfaces, we have discovered that dynamic changes in cell membrane shape can induce pattern-forming instabilities in localized regions, which we refer to as regional instabilities. Furthermore, deformations of the local membrane geometry can also suppress pattern formation and spatially shift existing patterns. By applying the local equilibria theory of mass-conserving reaction-diffusion systems, we have identified a straightforward criterion for determining when geometry-induced pattern-forming instabilities occur, which is linked to the phase-space structure of the reaction-diffusion system. This intricate feedback loop between membrane shape deformations and reaction-diffusion dynamics gives rise to an astonishing array of patterns, including oscillations, traveling waves, and standing waves, which are not observed in systems with fixed membrane shapes. Our research demonstrates that the local membrane geometry serves as a critical dynamical control parameter for pattern formation in mass-conserving reaction-diffusion systems.

Euphemisms remain understudied in natural language processing, despite being a crucial aspect of both polite and figurative language usage. Analyzing them poses challenges due to language evolution, as well as varying human perceptions of what constitutes a euphemism. To address this issue, a starting point involves compiling and examining examples of euphemisms. Our work introduces a corpus containing terms with potentially euphemistic meanings, along with corresponding text samples from the GloWbE corpus, as well as a subset of texts that illustrate the non-euphemistic use of these terms. Furthermore, our research encompasses the results of various analyses conducted on the corpus.
