To assess the proposed approach, a cost benchmark is established for comparison purposes. Case studies were conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of the Intraday Block Pricing scheme, which yielded notable reductions in peak energy usage and economic benefits for the utility and consumers alike. Additionally, the simulation results revealed that the proposed solution method accurately approximated the optimal solutions.

Geschke established that a 3-saturated clopen graph exists on the Cantor space, but clopen graphs on this space cannot have 4-saturated subgraphs, although an $F_\sigma$ graph does achieve $\omega_1$-saturation. The space of closed graphs is restricted further, as no $\omega$-saturated closed graph exists on the Cantor space. We address this by proving the existence of a closed graph saturated with $n$ on $2^\omega$ for any given number $n$. A key probabilistic lemma forms the basis for the proof, and the resulting construction is derived from an inverse limit of finite graphs.

For a given permutation group $G$ acting on a set $V$, a subset of $G$ is defined as an intersecting set if any two elements within this subset map a certain $v \in V$ to the same image. The intersection density of a transitive permutation group $G$ represents the greatest ratio of the size of an intersecting subset to the size of its point stabilizer. A permutation group $G$ is said to have the Erdős-Ko-Rado property if the largest subset with this property within $G$ is its point stabilizer. This paper specifically examines transitive permutation groups with prime-order point stabilizers, primarily focusing on those with point stabilizers of order $2$ and $3$, and it is demonstrated that these permutations do not exhibit the Erdős-Ko-Rado property. The study further includes the creation of infinite families of transitive permutation groups with a point stabilizer of order $3$ and specific intersection density values. Moreover, the research establishes the existence of infinite families of such groups, where one family has a point stabilizer of order $3$ and an intersection density of $4/3$, and the other has a point stabilizer of order $3$ and an arbitrarily large intersection density.

To determine equilibrium radiation losses and decay times in coupled storage ring configurations, we analyze synchrotron radiation by applying its fundamental integrals to the lattice's normal vibration modes, accounting for orbital deformations. This process enables the computation of off-axis radiation effects, facilitating the derivation of efficient formulas for rapid calculation, which are subsequently incorporated into the OPA lattice design system.

We investigated the peculiar narrow line Seyfert 1 galaxy CSS J102913+404220 following its decade-long outburst in the optical spectrum. Observations revealed mid-infrared flares that peaked nearly two months later, with an exceptionally high luminosity that far surpasses supernovae explosions. This indicates that the optical outburst may have resulted from a stellar tidal disruption event, which also led to late-time X-ray brightening. We noted significant fluctuations in the X-ray flux, but not in the optical, UV, or mid-infrared bands. Similar variability has been seen in highly accreting Active Galactic Nuclei and could be attributed to changes in absorption. Notably, the UV/optical continuum remained stable, whereas the H-alpha broad emission line experienced a significant increase about a decade after the outburst, an unusual behavior. This anomaly might be caused by gas clouds and Broad Line Region excitation due to interaction with stellar debris and outflowing material. Our findings highlight the late-time evolution of tidal disruption events' influence on the accretion properties of Active Galactic Nuclei.

Recent research suggests that humans and artificial intelligence models, like OpenAI's CLIP, exhibit biases when recognizing images that have been embedded with words, known as picture-word interference. This phenomenon occurs due to the interaction between language and visual processing. A recent study aimed to understand whether this bias leads to similar interference in AI models, by introducing a new method to assess their biases. To do this, the researchers developed a benchmark test that involves evaluating how well an AI model classifies images with words superimposed on them, across various categories. When applied to the CLIP model, the results showed that the model is affected by the presence of words on images, but the effect does not seem to be related to the semantic meaning of the words and images. Instead, the study found that the words strongly dominate the image classification process in the CLIP model, even though the word and image representations are not shared.

To combat the spread of infectious diseases such as COVID-19, critical resources including personal protective equipment (PPE) are necessary to contain the outbreak and safeguard individuals who interact with infected patients. As cases surge, local production facilities struggle to keep up with escalating demand, while factory closures and transportation disruptions exacerbate shortages. Initially, the pandemic response in many regions prioritized domestic needs, yet our analysis reveals that implementing a cooperative sharing mechanism could significantly enhance global pandemic resilience. Through a theoretical model, we demonstrate how intercommunity resource sharing can prevent local shortages and lower the number of infections. However, the effectiveness of such a system relies on adequate time between outbreaks, necessitating the simultaneous implementation of global sharing mechanisms alongside strategies to impede disease transmission between communities. Our work serves as a starting point for designing a robust and adaptable supply chain framework that can effectively mitigate future pandemics, rather than being constrained by current resource inequalities.

To tackle the significant challenges associated with the cold-start issue in CTR prediction, we introduce a comprehensive Variational Embedding Learning Framework (VELF). VELF effectively mitigates data-sparsity induced over-fitting in two ways: by acquiring uncertain embeddings and incorporating adaptive priors, which leverage rich side information from cold-start users and ads. These two techniques are organically combined within a variational inference framework, resulting in an end-to-end training process. Extensive empirical assessments on standard datasets clearly demonstrate the merits of VELF, and further experiments show that our adjustable and regularized priors offer improved generalization capabilities compared to traditional fixed priors.

For future and ongoing neutrino oscillation experiments employing large Liquid Argon Time Projection Chambers (LAr-TPCs), accurately distinguishing neutrino interactions from overwhelming cosmic-ray noise is a major obstacle. Conventional methods typically require computationally intensive algorithms followed by manual selection techniques. However, this work presents an innovative approach leveraging a 3D Submanifold Sparse Convolutional Network that uses basic data from the light produced by particle interactions within LAr-TPCs. This novel method is applied to simulated data from the ICARUS detector at Fermilab and yields a notable 76.3% decrease in cosmic background noise while maintaining interaction detection efficiency above 98.9%. Furthermore, to counterbalance potential biases in simulated input data, the work introduces the application of Domain Adversarial Neural Networks, which involves generating modified simulated samples to mimic real-world scenarios and using a portion for adversarial training. In-depth mock-data studies demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique in significantly enhancing neutrino interaction detection efficiency, especially when compared to results without adversarial training.

Researchers have recently shown significant interest in constructing LDPC codes from permutation matrices. A key challenge is to create such codes with minimal short cycles in their associated Tanner graph, or equivalently, a large girth. This paper provides a framework to construct these codes by connecting cycle criteria with number-theoretic concepts related to Sidon sets. This framework allows for the generation of specific examples of LDPC codes with desired girth properties, as well as the extension to irregular LDPC codes.

We categorize isolated singularities at infinity for polynomials of degree 3 in three variables, defined as the sum of three homogeneous polynomials of degrees 1, 2, and 3, respectively. Building upon this classification, we determine the change in the Milnor number of a singularity at infinity when transitioning from a specific fiber to a general one. Furthermore, our research aims to utilize these findings to examine the global fibrations of degree 3 polynomials in three-dimensional complex space, and to explore the topological properties of fibers within each equivalence class.

In a variation of the standard Bayesian mechanism, players initially assess the outcomes and limitations, which is applicable to a significant type of modern online advertising. In this context, an advertiser is primarily concerned with their expected returns and potential type changes over time. The main focus lies in resolving the incentive compatibility issue within this Bayesian framework. Under relatively minimal requirements for the mechanism's environment, we have fully defined incentive compatibility using the taxation principle, and interestingly, we found that only a subset of auto-bidding mechanisms, which are extensively used in online advertising, meet these compatibility requirements.

Araci et al. previously introduced a p-adic extension of the Haar distribution, which they used to construct the p-adic Volkenborn integral. This paper extends that work by applying the Mahler expansion to derive a Radon-Nikodym theorem for the p-adic distribution on the p-adic integers.

A network of decision-making agents, guided by a previously developed quantum decision theory, evaluate options based on their utility, appeal, and the available data, which are combined to determine the likelihood of choosing each alternative. The interactions between these factors lead to a complex decision-making process, involving the exchange of information. This information exchange can occur in two forms: direct information transfer between agents and collectively generated knowledge within the society. The shared knowledge field among all agents tends to mitigate fluctuations in the probabilities over time, sometimes even eliminating them entirely. For agents with limited short-term memory, the probabilities tend towards their limiting values through significant oscillations, resulting in perpetual indecision. However, introducing the shared knowledge field can reduce the oscillations' amplitude and, in some cases, completely halt them, enabling the probabilities to settle at stable limits. A phenomenon described in this context is the dynamic disjunction effect.

M. Bhargava and P. Harron demonstrated that for $n=3,4,5$, the arrangements of
rings of integers in $S_n$-number fields of degree $n$ become uniformly
dispersed in the arrangement space, when the fields are arranged in ascending order of discriminant. We replaced the concept of arrangement with that of grid, allowing the retention of more field-specific details. As the space of grids is constructed over the arrangement space, we extend Bhargava-Harron's findings by showing that the grid arrangements of the rings of integers in $S_n$-number fields become uniformly dispersed within the grid space.

The Search-Oriented Conversational AI conference is an established platform for presenting recent advancements in conversational search technology. SCAI'21 was held as an independent online event that included a shared task focused on conversational question answering. Observing the teams' reliance on answer generation models, we pinpointed assessing answer accuracy in this context as the primary challenge and current knowledge gap. To complement automated assessment, two crowdsourcing experiments were conducted to gather annotations on answer plausibility and faithfulness. Following this shared task, the original conversational QA dataset used for evaluation was supplemented with additional correct answers generated by the participating systems.

We have implemented the adaptively compressed exchange (ACE) operator within the LAPW framework, ensuring that ACE's low-rank representation of the Fock exchange maintains total energy precision. In our non-relativistic calculations using the hybrid PBE0 functional, we applied ACE in all-electron total energy calculations, confirming its property holds true. Our results for light atoms and molecules closely match the precise outcomes from multi-resolution-analysis calculations, deviating by only a few $\mu$Ha. The incorporation of high-energy local orbitals, alongside ACE, was instrumental in achieving such high precision in Fock exchange calculations. Furthermore, our implementation allows for the calculation of PBE0 gaps in solids and facilitates comparison with other all-electron results.

A galaxy called NGC 1566 exhibits a unique behavior, displaying periodic X-ray outbursts that last for several years, with the most recent one observed in 2018 resulting in a significant increase of ~24 in X-ray flux compared to its historical minimum. By analyzing data from XMM-Newton and NuSTAR observations, researchers confirmed the discovery of a broad feature in the 5-7 keV band that could be interpreted as a relativistic iron emission line, which was found to increase along with the overall X-ray continuum. This phenomenon supports the idea that X-rays originate from a corona above the accretion disk and are reflected by the disk, producing the iron line. Moreover, a narrow iron emission line showed significant response to changes in the X-ray continuum within four months, which could be related to the location of the line-emitting region within the accretion disk. Comparing this to a similar galaxy, NGC 2992, the iron line variation in NGC 1566 appears more pronounced, potentially attributed to greater amounts of gas or iron responsible for the line production in NGC 1566. The intensity of the iron line and soft X-ray emission were also found to correlate with the accretion rate, possibly resulting from changes in the accretion disk state associated with the changing-look phenomenon.

In this study, a social learning model is examined, where agents randomly select a neighbour to obtain information from at each time point. We demonstrate that even with reduced communication, agents eventually converge to the truth, and, notably, achieve an asymptotic convergence rate comparable to standard algorithms that rely on more extensive information exchange. Furthermore, large deviation estimates of the log-belief ratios are derived for a specific scenario in which an agent updates its belief with that of the chosen neighbour.

More than two decades ago, researchers introduced the Dependency Core Calculus (DCC) as a fundamental approach for analyzing dependency within typed programming languages, which has since yielded significant benefits in the design of programming languages, including improved enforcement of security constraints and dead code elimination. We now propose an extension to this concept called Dependent Dependency Calculus (DDC) to cater to dependently-typed languages. By employing this calculus, we can track and manage both compile-time and run-time irrelevance efficiently, thus enhancing type-checking speed and program execution efficiency.

Our research into nonlocal dispersion compensation for broadband photon pairs in fiber optic communication, as per the G.652D standard, involved precise measurements of their temporal correlation over long distances. We successfully compensated for this dispersion with minimal loss by adjusting the propagation path, maintaining timing correlations near our detection device's resolution (approximately 41.0 ps). This approach proved viable even with larger fiber increments (1 km), which aligns with real-world implementation. Notably, we achieved consistent photon timing correlations down to 51 ps over two 10 km segments of deployed metropolitan fiber.

Online food service websites heavily rely on food reviews and recommendations.
However, the process of reviewing and recommending food can be complex due to
the variety of contexts and interpretations. This research utilizes multiple
deep learning techniques to tackle the challenges associated with sentiment
analysis, automated review classification, and retrieval of food reviews.
To develop the NTU Food Hunter system at Nanyang Technological University,
we incorporate deep learning approaches to assist users in food selection.
Firstly, we integrate BERT and LSTM models into the system for sentiment
analysis of food reviews. Next, a POS algorithm is developed to identify and
extract adjective-noun pairs from the content for review tag generation.
Additionally, a RankNet model is trained to enhance the re-ranking of search
results within our Solr-based food reviews search system. Experimental results
demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed deep learning approaches for real-world problems.

We investigate the multifaceted sensitivity of non-traditional spin states,
specifically those with spin-squeezing and Dicke characteristics distributed
across multiple addressable locations. By developing analytical formulas for
the spin-squeezing matrix of a range of states experimentally attainable with
today's atomic technology, we uncover the quantum benefits in multi-parameter
sensing, as well as the optimal methods for achieving maximum sensitivity. In
addition, we explore the mode entanglement of these states through the
derivation of a witness for genuine k-partite mode entanglement from the
spin-squeezing matrix. Our research underscores the superiority of mode
entanglement for distributed sensing applications and presents optimal protocols
for estimating multiple parameters using non-classical spin ensembles.

We examine the melting and undercooling processes in gold particles with a diameter of approximately 100 nanometers. These particles are contained in a highly vacuumed space within a quadrupole ion trap. The gold particles are heated using laser light and their thermal state is analyzed through two methods. The first method involves measuring the particle's mass loss rate during heating to infer its temperature. The second method utilizes optical measurements to distinguish between the light reflected from the solid and liquid phases of the particle. We investigate how the heating behavior of the particle changes when its size is varied, with a focus on repeatedly heating the particle to induce melting. Additionally, we induce undercooling by applying multi-stage laser pulses and measure the extent to which it persists below the melting point, comparing the results with theoretical predictions.

The paper 'On the five-fold transitive function of 24 quantities' by 'Emile Mathieu' was translated into English to facilitate our project focusing on expressing $M_{23}$ in terms of additive functions within the finite field containing $2^{11}$ elements.

Our research aims to enhance node alignment between networks by exploiting the network structure and node attributes. A major drawback of current node alignment methods is that they often discover multiple node pairs simultaneously, failing to utilize intermediate correspondence discoveries for improved subsequent matching. To address this limitation, we introduce Grad-Align, a novel method that systematically uncovers node pairs by fully leveraging initial correspondences exhibiting strong consistency. Specifically, Grad-Align first produces network node embeddings through graph neural networks and a reconstruction loss function that incorporates both local and global neighborhood structures. Subsequently, node matching proceeds incrementally, with nodes being aligned using dual similarity metrics, including multi-layer embedding and Tversky similarity, suitable for networks of varying scales. Moreover, we integrate an edge augmentation module into Grad-Align to reinforce the alignment's structural consistency. Experimental results on real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate Grad-Align's superior performance compared to existing node alignment methods.

In populations, disparities in wealth or resource distribution are notable occurrences that warrant investigation.  It is essential to examine the causes of these disparities and explore methods to mitigate them. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we developed a model of interactions between agents within a network aimed at reducing economic inequality. By interpreting the outcome of basic interactions within the network, we translate winning into reducing wealth disparities. Our analysis delves into various interpretations of this approach and their effects on agent behavior in terms of wealth distribution, using the capital-dependent Parrondo's paradox as an example. This study's findings shed light on the underlying mechanisms driving social inequality.

Temporal dynamics in users' activity paths have been effectively captured by recurrent recommender systems. Nonetheless, recurrent neural networks are known to struggle in identifying long-term patterns. This limitation often leads RNN-based recommender systems to give undue weight to users' short-term preferences. Known as the recency bias, this issue can have a detrimental impact on both the user experience and system health. To address the recency bias in recurrent recommender systems, we propose a novel technique called recency dropout, which is a straightforward yet powerful data augmentation method. We showcase the efficacy of recency dropout through various experiments, including simulation studies, offline evaluations, and real-world tests on a large-scale industrial recommendation platform.

The classic problem of Minimum Flow Decomposition (MFD) has long been studied in Computer Science, with variants also being used to model complex tasks in Bioinformatics, specifically in RNA assembly. However, MFD is an NP-hard problem, meaning most practical solutions employ heuristics or simpler versions that may not yield optimal results. In order to tackle this issue, integer linear programming (ILP) has been used in some RNA assembly tools. Unfortunately, these formulations are limited by the need to account for an extremely large number of potential solution paths, making them impractical. The current exact solver for MFD is also inefficient for large instances and cannot be easily adapted for more practical versions of the problem. In this study, we present a novel and efficient ILP formulation for MFD that can solve any instance in under 13 seconds, even for large flow graphs. Furthermore, our approach can be easily adapted for more practical variants of MFD, such as incorporating longer or paired-end reads, or minimizing flow errors. We believe that our results have the potential to eliminate the trade-off between complexity and tractability in multi-assembly models, paving the way for future practical RNA assembly tools.

A cosmic distance ladder with minimal discrepancies can be developed by utilizing measurements from a single location within an inhomogeneous universe. The calibration of supernovae distances in the Hubble flow is based on precise distance measurements to nearby objects. We demonstrate that this framework can be applied to a universe with minor irregularities by modeling lumpiness as small perturbations on a flat Friedmann-Lemaître Robertson-Walker spacetime. We found that local spacetime distortions near an observer contribute significantly (around 11%) to variations in the area distance from the background Friedmann-Lemaître Robertson-Walker model. The distortion originates from the electric part of the Weyl tensor, which is linked to tidal forces acting on the local spacetime. We provide a detailed analysis of how this distortion affects the calibration of supernovae absolute magnitudes in the Hubble flow. Our findings suggest that it is possible to resolve the discrepancies in supernovae and Hubble constant measurements without invoking early or late dark energy.

This research focuses on a hypothetical universe dominated by phantom energy, with the equation of state parameter being $w<-1$. It examines the far-future of such a universe, exploring the possibility of reaching a Big Rip singularity. Working within the general relativity framework, the author suggests that this singularity could be prevented by gravitational Schwinger pair-production, even without other mechanisms creating particles. The model describes the far-future universe as having a constant high Hubble rate, energy density, and low horizon entropy, conditions also present at the universe's beginning. The analysis proposes that the Big Rip singularity could be avoided and the universe might instead enter a new inflationary phase, leading to the creation of multiple universes.

In inertial navigation systems, gyroscopes for rotation sensing are a crucial component, and there is growing interest in developing more precise gyroscopes using quantum principles. Current quantum gyroscope schemes have limitations due to decoherence, but our proposed quantum-optical-gyroscope scheme utilizes two entangled light fields as a quantum probe, effectively circumventing these constraints. Our analysis shows that even in noisy environments, ideal sensitivity and the super-Heisenberg limit can be achieved when each light field forms a bound state with its environment, making it possible to achieve high-precision rotation sensing in real-world conditions.

A novel Boltzmann-Gibbs model is introduced, incorporating local interactions within its energy functional through a spatial coupling function inspired by smoothed particle hydrodynamics. This function is based on second-degree polynomial approximations derived from the Laplace operator and can be explicitly expressed for a specific smoothing kernel. The model seamlessly transitions from discrete data vectors to continuum fields, and its relationship to Gaussian Markov random fields and Matern fields is demonstrated.

This research revisits the concept of itinerant ferromagnetism within two-dimensional and three-dimensional electron systems characterized by varying spin-orbit separation and robust electron-electron interaction. By identifying the resonant scattering mechanisms occurring near the Fermi surface, it's found that these mechanisms cause the ferromagnetic quantum critical point to become unstable at low temperatures. Contrary to previous theoretical analyses, our study indicates that these mechanisms cannot be completely eliminated even when arbitrary spin-orbit separation is present. Our fully self-consistent and non-perturbative analysis of electron-electron interaction reveals that these mechanisms consistently destabilize the ferromagnetic quantum critical point and result in a first-order phase transition. These mechanisms can be detected through the non-analytic relationship between the spin susceptibility and magnetic field, observed both far and close to the phase transition.

In a system receiving status updates from multiple sources, each source generates packets according to a Poisson process with generally distributed service times. We've created a packet management policy for this multi-source system and calculated the moment generating functions for the age of information and peak age of information for each source, taking into account a policy that prioritizes newer updates over older ones. Additionally, we've derived similar functions for policies that are less aware of the source of each update. These calculations have enabled us to determine average age of information and peak age of information for a two-source model under different policies, and the results show that the best policy varies depending on the characteristics of the distribution of service times, with more robust distributions favoring a preemptive policy and less robust distributions favoring a non-preemptive policy. Furthermore, our research underscores the significance of higher moments of the age of information.

Gaussian processes are crucial tools in machine learning and statistics for modeling continuous processes. They enable the construction of interpolating surfaces from a finite set of known process values for predictive purposes. However, not all information is confined to a finite set of points, such as boundary value problems that involve uncountable data on domain boundaries. This paper addresses this challenge by developing a novel Gaussian process model that leverages reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, effectively bridging the gap between finite and uncountable data through conditional expectation and orthogonal projection equivalence. The model is explored within a statistical framework, incorporating both numerical considerations and a proof of concept.

The application of deep learning-based liver segmentation is gaining importance in clinical settings due to the increasing prevalence of liver cancer. Although numerous networks have shown promising results in medical image segmentation, accurately identifying hepatic lesions remains a challenge. To address this limitation, researchers proposed a hybrid network called SWTR-Unet, combining convolutional, transformer-based architectures and Unet-style decoders. This network was tested on real-world MRI data and the LiTS challenge dataset. Multiple state-of-the-art models were also implemented for direct comparison. Further analysis, including correlation studies and ablation tests, was conducted to investigate factors influencing the segmentation accuracy of SWTR-Unet. The proposed method achieved high Dice similarity scores of 98% for liver and 81% for lesion segmentation in MRI and 97% and 79% respectively in CT datasets, surpassing the performance of state-of-the-art models. The segmentation accuracy of SWTR-Unet was comparable to expert manual segmentations. Consequently, this approach could reduce time and resource consumption in clinical settings.

Recent studies have highlighted the vulnerability of deep neural networks (DNNs) to adversarial attacks, with 3D adversarial attacks on point clouds gaining increasing attention. However, previous methods for generating adversarial point clouds have shown poor transferability and are easily defended against. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a new point cloud attack, dubbed AOF, which focuses on manipulating the low-frequency component of point clouds. By combining losses from both the point cloud and its low-frequency component, AOF produces adversarial samples with enhanced transferability and resilience to state-of-the-art defense methods. Furthermore, AOF-generated adversarial point clouds exhibit more deformation than outlier-like characteristics compared to clean point clouds.

The effects of nuclear structure on particle multiplicity and anisotropic flow in Ru+Ru and Zr+Zr collisions at various energies (7.7, 27, 62.4, and 200 GeV) are analyzed using a string melting version of the AMPT model, comparing with recent STAR experiment results. It is observed that quadrupole deformation has a stronger influence on anisotropic flow in central collisions, octupole deformation in near-central collisions, and neutron skin effects in mid-central collisions, all of which become more pronounced at lower energies.

We revisit the theory of Importance Weighted Variational Inference (IWVI), a potential solution for learning latent variable models. This strategy uses novel variational bounds, known as Monte Carlo objectives, derived by replacing intractable integrals with Monte Carlo estimates obtained through importance sampling. Building on the work of Burda, Grosse, and Salakhutdinov (2016), who showed that increasing the number of importance samples tightens the gap between the bound and the likelihood, we provide a series of non-asymptotic results that establish a connection between the properties of Monte Carlo estimates and the tightness of Monte Carlo objectives. We challenge a common assumption that smaller Monte Carlo variance leads to better bounds, confirming the empirical findings of several recent studies that negative correlation reduces the variational gap. Additionally, we extend the original monotonicity theorem to include non-uniform weights, and discuss several practical implications of our findings, drawing from the theory of stochastic orders.

We investigate the dynamics of simple congestion games with two resources where an infinite number of agents follow a modified version of the Experience-Weighted Attraction algorithm. These dynamics are characterized by three key parameters: a choice intensity parameter capturing population rationality, a discount factor that represents a form of memory loss where past outcomes have diminishing influence over time, and a parameter that represents the asymmetry in the cost functions of the two resources. Within this framework, we identify a wide range of complex behavior transitions, including shifts from global convergence to equilibrium to limit cycles and chaos as the parameters change. We show that for any discount factor, sufficiently large choice intensity will lead to system destabilization. However, as memory loss increases, the chaotic regime gives way to a predictable system with a periodic orbit of period 2. Our analysis is supplemented by simulations and bifurcation diagrams that illustrate the intricate complexity of population dynamics in these simple games, including attracting periodic orbits of varying lengths.

A type of neural network called capsule networks has achieved notable success in computer vision tasks, but baseline versions struggle with more complex datasets due to their high resource demands. To address this issue, a new network architecture called the Momentum Capsule Network (MoCapsNet) has been proposed. Inspired by reversible networks like Momentum ResNets, MoCapsNets utilize reversible residual building blocks, which significantly reduce memory needs during the backpropagation process. This paper outlines a framework for incorporating invertible residual building blocks into capsule networks. It demonstrates that MoCapsNets surpass the accuracy of baseline capsule networks on several datasets while using substantially less memory, and the source code is available for further study on https://github.com/moejoe95/MoCapsNet.

To establish a framework for discussing continuity, we first need to establish a definition of what constitutes an open set within a space.  A topology is necessary for this purpose and is defined by a set of axioms that dictate the properties of open sets. In this work, we will examine the impact on continuity when one of these foundational axioms is modified.

Finding the shortest route through connected networks necessitates identifying the lowest overall cost for traversing the graph's connections. Traditional algorithms can efficiently solve this problem, assuming costs for each connection are predefined. However, these methods often struggle when costs need to be dynamically adjusted to accommodate specific task requirements. Our research reveals that neural networks can be designed to represent path-finding problems by converting cost values into synaptic weights, allowing costs to be adaptively updated using the network's learning capabilities. When starting with an initial activity value, the network will produce solutions identical to those generated by the Bellman Ford algorithm, while boasting comparable algorithmic complexity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that network learning mechanisms can modify the weights, thereby adjusting the resulting paths to meet specific task needs. The network successfully navigated through obstacle-ridden environments and followed predetermined path sequences, indicating the potential for this novel algorithm to expand the scope of path-finding applications.

The existence of axion particles remains uncertain, yet the axion field can be effectively utilized in developing local chiral U(1) gauge theory models exhibiting both classical and quantum invariance properties. Introducing analogous nonabelian axion fields has led to potential applications in constructing nonabelian chiral gauge theories, taking into account their inherent symmetries. Similar to previous instances, the introduction of these axion fields results in broken gauge symmetry, causing the gauge boson to acquire mass by incorporating the axions, thereby rendering them non-physical in this context.

We investigate four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=1$ gauge theories that exhibit S-confinement, being dual to a Wess-Zumino model, and specifically focus on those theories with a simple gauge group that have already been classified. We verify the validity of all S-confining dualities listed under the condition that the matter fields transform according to rank-$1$ and/or rank-$2$ representations. To achieve this, we rely solely on the established S-confining dualities for $SU(N)$ with $N+1$ flavors and for $Usp(2N)$ with $2N+4$ fundamental fields. Our methodology involves a systematic sequence of deconfinement and reconfinement processes, carefully monitoring the explicit superpotential at each stage.

In thermal equilibrium within multi-dimensional Euclidean space, we examine and prove the positivity of entanglement R\'enyi entropies for the free Fermi gas in local and bipartite systems. Our investigation covers various temperatures, and we establish the large-scale behavior of these entropies at high temperatures and large scaling parameters for both fixed chemical potential and particle density. These findings complete a key component required to fully confirm previously established low and high temperature results for this model, initially presented for a specific R\'enyi index.

The discrete Fourier transform is a crucial aspect of photonic quantum information, but scaling it up to higher dimensions relies heavily on the physical encoding method, with few practical approaches available for emerging technologies such as frequency bin systems. In this paper, we demonstrate that a specific quantum frequency processor can perform high-dimensional frequency bin discrete Fourier transforms by simply incorporating additional radio-frequency signals for each incremental increase in dimension. Our numerical simulations and experimental results confirm that the method achieves high fidelity and success rates up to ten dimensions. Furthermore, we successfully implemented the technique in a three-dimensional experiment, using multiple discrete Fourier transforms to measure entanglement and perform complete tomography on multi-photon frequency-bin states. Our findings open up new possibilities for high-dimensional quantum communication and networking protocols based on frequency bin systems.

This paper builds upon our prior research exploring spherical representations within the framework of operator algebras. Initially, we propose analogous concepts for dimension groups in the current context by drawing from operator systems and related theories. Subsequently, our study is applied to the inductive limits of compact quantum groups, leading to an equivalent notion of spherical unitary representations in infinite-dimensional Gelfand pairs, akin to Olshanski's work, adapted within the quantum group setting. Consequently, this establishes a justification for Ryosuke Sato's approach to asymptotic representation theory in quantum groups.

The approximate solution of the Klein-Gordon equation in the context of a real scalar field with mass $\mu$ within the geometric framework of a Kerr black hole has been extensively utilized to investigate the stability of black holes as well as the search for axion-like particles, originally obtained by Detweiler \cite{Detweiler:1980uk}. In this work, we validate a previously overlooked factor of $1/2$ in this solution, initially recognized in Ref.~\cite{Pani:2012bp}. The corrected result exhibits unusual properties that raise concerns about the power-counting strategy employed. We resolve this issue by incorporating the next-to-leading order (NLO) contribution, demonstrating that the NLO solution significantly improves the accuracy of the LO solution for all relevant values of $r_g\mu$. Specifically, it is shown that the NLO solution reduces the percentage error by a factor of 2 and achieves an error percentage of $\lesssim 10\%$ for $r_g\mu \lesssim 0.35$. The NLO solution also possesses a compact form and can be easily applied.

Natural language inference has become a crucial aspect of natural language understanding, necessitating the ability to determine the relationship between pairs of sentences, known as the premise and hypothesis. Recent studies have employed contrastive learning by leveraging the relationships between sentence pairs in NLI datasets to generate meaningful sentence representations. Although these methods focus primarily on comparisons between sentence-level representations, we propose a new approach called Pair-level Supervised Contrastive Learning (PairSCL). PairSCL utilizes a cross-attention module to learn joint representations of sentence pairs and incorporates a contrastive learning objective that distinguishes and separates different classes of sentence pairs. Our approach outperforms existing methods by 2.1% on average in NLI datasets and surpasses the state-of-the-art in text classification on seven transfer tasks.

The "isobar run" or RHIC experiment was established to analyze several collisional variables for 96Zr and 96Ru, in an attempt to discern charge-dependent effects. However, data from the STAR investigation revealed unexpected disparities between the two isotopes, resulting in effects surpassing those attributed to charge. Studies have been conducted to quantify these differences and their connection to various observables. A general understanding is that these disparities are linked to nuclear properties, particularly low-energy states. However, the precise correlation between high-energy and low-energy nuclear physics remains unclear. This paper proposes a connection between these fields via thermal density matrices for "preheated" nuclei, utilizing an effective temperature to define relevant excited states. Furthermore, a semiclassical "flucton" method is suggested at finite temperatures for calculating thermal density matrices.

A new probabilistic model has been developed to identify noisy pattern repetitions in binary data with low information density. This model builds upon the 'Noisy-OR model' previously used in disease and topic modelling. The capabilities of this model are showcased through the extraction of structure from retinal neuron recordings, and its potential applications include uncovering hidden patterns in noisy binary data. In the context of neural spike data, the model aims to explain individual neuron spikes as the result of coordinated 'cell assemblies' that fire together due to shared connections or other influences. The model estimates sparse activity in a set of binary latent variables representing different cell assemblies, where the activation of a cell assembly reduces the likelihood of its constituent neurons being inactive. Using an expectation-maximization approach, the conditional probability distributions of the latent variables are learned from the data by iteratively inferring the hidden states and adjusting the model parameters. The model's effectiveness is validated through the analysis of synthetic neural spike trains generated to mimic real-world retinal responses to white noise and natural stimuli. Additionally, the model is applied to real retinal ganglion cell data collected in response to a movie and the resulting structure is discussed.

We investigate a three-dimensional ternary system, which arises from the sharp-interface limit of a density functional theory of triblock copolymers proposed by Nakazawa and Ohta. This theory incorporates both an interface energy and a long-range interaction term. Although the binary case in two dimensions, as well as in three, and the ternary case in two dimensions are relatively well-understood, there is limited knowledge about the ternary case in three dimensions. Specifically, the existence of minimizers composed of a finite number of components is uncertain. In this paper, we demonstrate that the number of components within a minimizer is constrained by a quantity dependent solely on the total masses and the interaction coefficients. A major obstacle is the inability to decouple the long-range interaction from the perimeter term due to the complexity of the three-dimensional structure. This makes it difficult to determine the actual shape of minimizers, even for small masses, because we lack a quantitative isoperimetric inequality with two mass constraints in three dimensions. Consequently, the construction of suitable competitors becomes significantly more intricate.

A novel communication framework has been introduced, focusing on transmitting image semantics relevant to AI tasks, disregarding image quality. However, certain applications like autonomous driving demand simultaneous consideration of image quality and AI performance. To address this issue, the authors propose a communication scheme that integrates semantic reconstruction, achieving optimal rate-distortion balance. This involves a new semantic distortion measure based on mutual information between reconstructed images and task labels. By deriving an analytical solution and applying variational approximation, the authors obtain an extended rate-distortion formulation suitable for multiple AI tasks. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of this approach over existing systems in terms of image quality, AI performance, and multi-task generalization capabilities.

The degree of a Chebyshev's method applied to a cubic polynomial can be 4, 6, or 7, and studying these cases provides insight into their dynamics. For cubic polynomials that are unicritical or non-generic, it has been demonstrated that the Julia set resulting from Chebyshev's method is connected. A specific family of rational maps is derived from Chebyshev's method applied to a non-unicritical and generic cubic polynomial. This family of maps is characterized by the multiplier of one of its extraneous fixed points. The members of this family, denoted as $C_\lambda$, have a connected Julia set when the multiplier of their extraneous fixed point $\lambda$ falls within the interval [-1,1].

Epilepsy is a prevalent neurological disorder impacting people across all age groups worldwide. When traditional treatments fail, Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) has become a viable alternative. To optimize DBS procedure planning, it is crucial to develop an algorithm that accurately pinpoints the target area - specifically the Anterior Nucleus of Thalamus (ANT), a complex site to navigate. In this study, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation by comparing multiple localization techniques for ANT-DBS, encompassing both conventional registration and deep-learning-based methods, including heatmap matching and DSNT. The experimental findings reveal that deep-learning methods, particularly those trained with pseudo labels, can match inter-rater and intra-rater accuracy while significantly outperforming traditional approaches in terms of speed.

In this work, we explore the behavior of two-dimensional truncated Airy waves and solitons in a system consisting of two fundamental-frequency and second-harmonic fields, connected by quadratic interactions. This setup mimics optical media that produce second harmonics as well as mixtures of atoms and molecules in Bose-Einstein condensates. Besides stable solitons, our analysis reveals exact, stable solutions representing truncated Airy waves in a single fundamental-frequency component. We also find that it is possible to introduce vorticity into these 2D Airy modes. By means of computational simulations, we investigate interactions between 2D truncated Airy waves originating from different fundamental-frequency components, which bend in opposite directions via the second-harmonic field. Upon interaction, the waves merge into two narrow solitons, in contrast to the 1D case where they split into numerous solitons. Moreover, when two truncated Airy waves with identical vorticities collide, they create a new pair of solitons, whereas opposite vorticities result in small-amplitude "debris" in the output. When solitons interact with a stationary truncated Airy wave, slow-moving solitons bounce back, while faster ones get absorbed, and their collisions remain largely elastic. Furthermore, collisions between solitons lead to a single-mode merger or an elastic passage, depending on the relative velocities of the interacting solitons.

Amorphous solids under stress often undergo permanent changes due to mechanical forces applied.
Research has found that these deformations, characterized by quadrupolar patterns, can suppress the elasticity of amorphous systems, particularly those composed of granules.
At high concentrations of quadrupoles, the gradients of their field behave like emerging dipoles, leading to notable changes in their mechanical behavior, such as distortions in the displacement field.
This paper investigates how these deformations affect classical glass-formers, consisting of point particles connected by binary forces.
Both inverse power law and Lennard-Jones interactions demonstrate that the elasticity of these systems can be significantly suppressed, in accordance with recent theories.
Furthermore, a new parameterization is proposed to quantify the degree of deviation from classical elasticity theory, which has been shown to be directly related to the amount of energy dissipated due to plastic deformations.

A particular model of linear read-once branching programs is defined by a branching program where queries are linear combinations over the field of two elements, and each path within this program uses linearly independent queries. This model is then restricted in two ways to create weakly and strongly read-once models, both of which generalize traditional read-once branching programs and parity decision trees. Our key findings are the following:

  - Average-Case Hardness. We establish a pseudo-random set of functions known as directional affine extractors and demonstrate that these functions are difficult on average to solve for the strongly read-once model. An explicit construction of a function with desirable properties is also presented, which significantly improves upon previous results, specifically those given by Cohen and Shinkar (ITCS'16) for parity decision trees. Directional affine extractors are a more powerful class of functions than traditional affine extractors, making this discovery particularly significant. As such, our introduction of this new class of functions may be of standalone interest.

  - Proof Complexity. We also investigate the proof system $\text{Res}[\oplus]$, an extension of resolution that incorporates linear queries, which naturally gives rise to linear branching programs that solve the associated search problems. Conversely, we show that weakly read-once linear BPs can be converted into $\text{Res}[\oplus]$ refutations with a minimal increase in complexity.

We introduce a two-stage framework for creating approximation algorithms using Lyapunov functions. In the initial stage, a continuous-time approximation algorithm with a guaranteed approximation ratio is developed from the Lyapunov function. The second stage transforms this continuous algorithm into a discrete-time one with an almost identical approximation ratio and a provable time complexity. Our framework's key advantage is that it allows for the Lyapunov function's parameters to be specified later in the process, maximizing the algorithm's approximation ratio. The Lyapunov function approach has several benefits, including: (i) streamlining existing algorithms, (ii) providing a methodology for designing and analyzing new ones, and (iii) offering fresh insights to enhance existing algorithms. This framework is demonstrated using submodular maximization problems as examples.

A collection of sets is considered intersecting if at least two sets within the collection share a nonempty intersection. A collection of sets is said to possess the Helly property if all intersecting subsets have a nonempty intersection. A graph is referred to as /Helly/ when the collection of its maximal complete subgraphs satisfies the Helly property. Our proof demonstrates that for a given \(k\)-regular graph with \(n\) vertices, where \(n\) exceeds \(3k + \sqrt{2k^{2}-k}\), the complement \(\bar{G}\) does not exhibit the Helly property. Furthermore, we investigate whether the Hellyness property and convergence under the clique graph operator for the complement of \(k\)-regular graphs are equivalent, with a focus on small \(k\) values.

Revisiting the issue of a vanishing Noether current associated with local scale symmetry, specifically the Weyl symmetry, we demonstrate through the second Noether theorem that this current vanishes in all Weyl invariant theories within four-dimensional Riemannian geometry. The reason for this vanishing is attributed to the Weyl transformation's non-dynamical nature, characterized by the absence of a derivative term in the transformation parameter, in contrast to conventional gauge transformations. This finding is then applied to a quantum theory of general Weyl invariant gravity, enabling the derivation of currents associated with chiral symmetry, rooted in the $IOSp(10|10)$ supersymmetry.

For autonomous driving, detecting 3D objects in real-time is crucial and point cloud based methods have gained traction due to their precise depth readings. The nuScenes dataset, a significant expansion of the KITTI dataset, suffers from a severe imbalance of classes, but a proposed augmentation and sampling strategy aims to alleviate this issue. Nevertheless, its localization precision is impaired by the loss of spatial information during downsampling, prompting the suggestion of an auxiliary network to enhance its performance. This auxiliary network, optimised through point-level supervisions for foreground segmentation and centre estimation, can be seamlessly detached during inference, thus not affecting computational efficiency.

Our Aegis Combat System is an example of command and control technology, with its key components being missile guidance and tracking systems. To explore these concepts further, a simplified model will be developed that mimics the Aegis Combat System. This simplified model consists of a small, remote-controlled car that leads a smaller autonomous car, with the two cars representing the system's major components: the controller and two vehicles. By utilizing this model, the team can visually illustrate how real-world command and control systems operate, specifically in terms of command, communication, and sensor data integration. Figure 1 displays an image of the Aegis Combat System.

Research on decision-making theories, such as Fuzzy-Trace Theory, reveals that individuals often rely on the main point of a text when making decisions. To facilitate the assessment of this concept, we've developed GisPy, an open-source Python tool designed to calculate the Gist Inference Score in text. GisPy's performance has been validated through its evaluation on datasets from news and scientific writing, which showed that it successfully identifies documents with low versus high gist content. GisPy can be accessed at https://github.com/phosseini/GisPy.

Weakly supervised text classification often relies on deep neural networks trained using pseudo-labels. However, these pseudo-labels are frequently inaccurate due to their subjective nature, making the selection of high-quality ones a crucial factor in determining the final classification accuracy. While selecting samples based on their predicted probabilities might seem like a logical approach, our findings indicate that this method can be unreliable and inconsistent, primarily due to models producing overconfident predictions for incorrectly labeled data. Notably, recent research has shown that deep neural networks tend to learn and memorize clean labels before those with inaccuracies. Our proposed solution, LOPS, draws inspiration from this observation and considers the learning order of samples to select the most reliable pseudo-labels. We believe that the learning order reflects the likelihood of label inaccuracies and suggest selecting samples that were learned earlier. As demonstrated in extensive experiments across four real-world datasets, LOPS offers a potent performance-enhancing addition to various existing weakly-supervised text classification methods.

There are several reasons why assessing an explanation's faithfulness is desirable,
including establishing trust, understanding the explanation, and identifying model
errors. In this study focusing on the NLI task, we propose a new method called
Faithfulness-through-Counterfactuals, which involves generating a hypothetical
counterfactual explanation based on logical rules, then verifying if the model's
new prediction aligns with those logical rules. Our approach differs from existing
methods in not needing additional explanations to train a separate verification
model. We initially test the effectiveness of automatic counterfactual generation
using a few-shot learning method, and then demonstrate our proposed measure can
distinguish between human and model agreement or disagreement on new hypothetical
input. Additionally, we perform a sensitivity analysis to validate that our metric
is responsive to unfaithful explanations.

The transfer of angular momentum from guided photons to a two-level atom, facilitated by an optical nanofiber, is investigated. We establish that the generation of the axial orbital torque exerted on the atom is influenced by both the internal-state selection rules for electric quadrupole transitions and the principle of angular momentum conservation, taking into account the photon angular momentum as described in the Minkowski formulation. Our results reveal that this torque is contingent upon the photon angular momentum, the change in the atomic internal state's angular momentum, and the quadrupole transition Rabi frequency. By numerically calculating the torques for specific quadrupole transitions in $^{87}$Rb atoms, we find that the torque for the HE$_{21}$ mode exceeds that of the fundamental HE$_{11}$ mode, except in the instance where $M'-M=2$.

Our research marks the first investigation of lattice dynamics concerning the intermixing of the isoscalar pseudoscalar meson $\eta$ and the pseudoscalar glueball $G$ within the framework of $N_f=2$ QCD, specifically at the pion mass of approximately 350 MeV. The calculated mass of $\eta$ is $714.1(5.4)$ MeV, allowing us to apply the Witten-Veneziano relation to deduce a corresponding mass of around 935 MeV for its $SU(3)$ equivalent. Employing a large ensemble of gauge configurations, the $\eta-G$ mixing energy and angle are determined to be $|x|=107(14)$ MeV and $|\theta|=3.47(46)^\circ$ using the distillation method from calculated $\eta-G$ correlators. We have also found that the $\eta$ mass can be accurately derived from $\eta-\eta_c$ correlators with $\eta_c$ representing the pseudoscalar charmonium. Our findings indicate a minimal level of $\eta-G$ mixing and reveal that the topology-induced interaction is primarily responsible for the $\eta$ mass, driven by the QCD $U_A(1)$ anomaly.

To assess the efficacy of goal-oriented dialogue systems, it is crucial to consider how users perceive their assistance in achieving specific goals. Despite this importance, little research has investigated the perceived helpfulness and its implications on fairness of these systems. This paper addresses this knowledge gap by developing computational measures to evaluate helpfulness. Initially, we established a definition of a helpful response as being relevant, coherent, useful, and informative. Subsequently, we collected human feedback to gauge the helpfulness of responses based on our criteria, and then created a classification model to automatically determine helpfulness. Furthermore, we suggest using a dialogue system's level of helpfulness towards varying user queries as a means of measuring its fairness. Experimental evaluations of cutting-edge dialogue systems under three distinct information-seeking scenarios reveal that current systems tend to provide more effective assistance for queries concerning concepts from more economically developed countries than those from less developed countries, revealing potential fairness issues inherent to existing systems.

Over the past few years, researchers have developed advanced representations that utilize point clouds, enabling them to capture complex 3D data. However, existing techniques often falter when tasked with generating structured point sets. Drawing inspiration from spherical multi-view scanners, we introduce a novel sampling approach known as Spotlights. It encodes 3D shapes as a compact 1D array of depth values by simulating cameras arranged evenly around a sphere, with each camera casting rays that intersect with an object's surface, thereby creating a structured point cloud as a function of depth. Our approach is supported by a thorough geometric analysis, which demonstrates its efficacy in the context of point cloud completion. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world data reveal that our method outperforms other techniques in terms of accuracy, consistency, and computational efficiency. Additionally, we show that our method excels in the downstream point cloud registration task compared to state-of-the-art completion methods.

Recent studies have highlighted the potential privacy risks associated with 
large language models stemming from the memorization of their training data, 
particularly during the pre-training phase. However, there is a notable lack of 
research on the risks involved in the fine-tuning phase, where the primary 
concern is the varying memorization levels among different fine-tuning 
strategies. Given the increasing reliance on the "pre-train and fine-tune" model, 
it is crucial to investigate the memorization risks of distinct fine-tuning 
techniques, such as full model, model head, and adapter methods. Our study 
utilizes membership inference and extraction attacks to demonstrate the stark 
differences in the susceptibility to attacks among fine-tuning approaches.

Recent research on parameter-efficient transfer learning through lightweight fine-tuning methods, which only update a small set of parameters while keeping pre-trained models fixed, has shown promising results but lacks investigation into its impact on the pre-training stage. We investigate this knowledge gap by demonstrating that considering the chosen fine-tuning method during pre-training enhances the performance of parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques. By adapting MAML, a meta-learning approach, to our specific use case, we optimize pre-trained models for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, leading to improved performance of up to 1.7 points on cross-lingual NER tasks. Our study also shows that the modifications we introduced in MAML were crucial to achieving these gains.

The Paul Scherrer Institut's High Intensity Proton Accelerator cyclotron at PSI generates a 590 MeV continuous-wave proton beam with a maximum power of 1.42 MW. Following extraction, the beam is guided through a 120-meter channel to two target stations, TgM and TgE, for surface muon production. Subsequently, it reaches the spallation target SINQ, where its remaining power produces neutrons. To enhance the efficiency of the High Intensity Muon Beamline, the initial target will be replaced with a thicker one, but a significant challenge lies in minimizing proton beam losses along the beamline. To achieve this, researchers have developed a new approach, which involves correlating temperature measurements, beam profile assessments, and current readings with Monte Carlo simulations of combined power deposition and primary beam loss.

In 1984, Gauduchon studied a specific function of $L^2$-norm related to torsion on a compact Hermitian manifold. He derived the Euler-Lagrange equation for this function and found that in two-dimensional space, any metrics meeting specific conditions have a zero torsion. Building on his work, we have generalized this finding to higher dimensions, demonstrating that in all dimensions, such metrics are inherently balanced. Furthermore, our analysis of $L^2$-norm of Chern torsion reveals the existence of critical points that do not conform to K\"ahler metrics, as evidenced by specific examples.

We investigated how eccentricity affects our understanding of gravitational waves produced by binary neutron stars, focusing on how well we can estimate key properties of these systems. We looked at how small amounts of eccentricity, undetected in LIGO's advanced sensitivity, can distort our understanding of a binary neutron star's mass and other properties, such as its 'chirp mass','symmetric mass ratio', and 'tidal deformability'. By comparing two methods of analysis - a complex Bayesian approach and a more straightforward statistical method - we developed guidelines for when the simpler method can be trusted. We applied this statistical method to a diverse range of binary neutron stars with varying masses and eccentricities, calculating the accuracy of our measurements and the systematic errors that can arise. Our results show that the degree of eccentricity, rather than the masses of the stars, has the biggest impact on these errors, and we illustrate these findings with specific examples, including a scenario where failing to account for eccentricity could lead to incorrect conclusions about the neutron star's internal structure.

This paper proposes a novel approach for visually-grounded dialog called Generative Self-Training (GST), which leverages unlabeled Web images in a semi-supervised learning framework. GST starts by retrieving images from the same domain, then generates simulated dialogues based on these images using multimodal conditional text generation. It trains a dialog agent on both the artificially created dialogues and original VisDial data, significantly expanding the available training data (from 1.2 million to 12.9 million QA pairs). To ensure robust training, GST incorporates a perplexity-based data selection method and multimodal consistency regularization. Experiments conducted on VisDial v1.0 and v0.9 datasets demonstrate that GST achieves state-of-the-art results, with notable improvements observed in the low-data scenario, where performance gains of up to 9.35 absolute points in NDCG are achieved.

To combat noise in remote data qubits, spectator qubits are utilized. These highly sensitive qubits are frequently measured, and their findings are infrequently used to correct the noisy data qubits. In particular, we've developed a Bayesian method involving complex transformations for mitigating dephasing from random fluctuations in hardware systems. This approach yields a superior adaptive measurement and control strategy, which effectively suppresses decoherence. Furthermore, we've found that the sensitivity of the spectator qubits is directly proportional to the reduction in decoherence rate.

Text generation systems frequently generate unfaithful text, which is a significant concern in practical applications. Data-to-Text systems, specifically, require high factuality in their output to be trustworthy. Our solution is R2D2, a training framework that tackles this issue by teaching the model to produce accurate text while simultaneously evaluating its faithfulness. To accomplish this, we include additional tasks such as detecting replaced entities and learning what is unlikely. We also provide two methods to create unfaithful text examples. Furthermore, we recognize that D2T systems often struggle with identifying relevant entities, which is a key cause of unfaithfulness, so we introduce new metrics based on named entity recognition. Our experiments demonstrate that R2D2 can successfully prevent text generation errors and set a new standard of performance in FeTaQA, LogicNLG, and ToTTo with substantial improvements.

The objective of this thesis is to investigate and evaluate potential vulnerabilities in Iota network 2.0 by analyzing attack pathways and drawing from existing Distributed Ledger Technologies threats. This study examines the relevance of known attack vectors to the Iota 2.0 protocol and highlights a particular exploit that aims to compromise the ledger-writing capability of legitimate participants within a simulated environment comprising nodes running a full node software iteration.

The development of image captioning systems for multiple languages has been hindered by a scarcity of high-quality evaluation resources. We introduce the Crossmodal-3600 dataset, which comprises 3600 images annotated with diverse captions in 36 languages, reflecting various global regions where these languages are spoken. To minimize translation bias, captions were standardized in style across all languages. Our dataset is used as a benchmark to evaluate and select the most effective multilingual image captioning models, and we demonstrate better agreement with human assessments when utilizing the Crossmodal-3600 dataset as a reference standard for automatic metrics.

We present FLEURS, a novel benchmark for evaluating universal speech representations across languages through few-shot learning. Built upon the FLoRes-101 machine translation benchmark, FLEURS features an n-way parallel speech dataset in 102 languages with approximately 12 hours of speech supervision per language. This dataset can be utilized for a range of speech applications, such as Automatic Speech Recognition, Speech Language Identification, Translation, and Retrieval. We establish baseline models using multilingual pre-trained models like mSLAM and aim to leverage FLEURS to advance low-resource speech understanding and facilitate speech technology in diverse languages.

We derive the existence, uniqueness, and regularity inequalities for the following Cauchy problem in weighted Lp-spaces involving pseudo-differential operators: 

Given the equation \(\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}(t,x)=\psi(t,i\nabla)u(t,x)+f(t,x)\) for \((t,x)\in(0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^d\) with the initial condition \(u(0,x)=0\), we determine sufficient conditions on the symbol \(\psi(t,\xi)\) to ensure the equation's well-posedness in Muckenhoupt weighted Lp-spaces. Here, the symbol's smoothness with respect to \(\xi\) is characterized by a property of each weight and \(\psi(t,\xi)\) is merely measurable with respect to \(t\). 

We show that there exists a positive constant \(N\) such that for any solution \(u\), the following inequalities hold: \(\int_0^T \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} |(-\Delta)^{\gamma/2} u(t,x) |^p (t^2 + |x|^2)^{\alpha/2} dxdt \leq N\int_0^T \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} |f(t,x)|^p (t^2 + |x|^2)^{\alpha/2} dxdt\), and \(\int_0^T \left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} |(-\Delta)^{\gamma/2} u(t,x) |^p |x|^{\alpha_2} dx \right)^{q/p} t^{\alpha_1}dt \leq N\int_0^T \left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} |f(t,x) |^p |x|^{\alpha_2} dx \right)^{q/p} t^{\alpha_1}dt\), under specific constraints on the parameters \(p,q,\alpha,\alpha_1,\alpha_2\), and \(\gamma\).

The primary challenges in advancing event extraction stem from the limitations imposed by data scarcity and imbalance. In response, this study introduces the self-training with gradient guidance framework, which consists of a base event extraction model initially trained on pre-existing event annotations and then utilized to identify event mentions in large-scale unlabeled text data. A scoring model is employed to assess the likelihood of correct event predictions based on the event trigger, argument, and their respective paths within the Abstract Meaning Representation graph. The predicted event mentions and corresponding correctness scores are used to refine the base model by incorporating pseudo-labeled examples, where the gradient updates are influenced by the correctness scores. Experimental results across three benchmark datasets, including ACE05-E, ACE05-E+, and ERE-EN, reveal that the STGG framework achieves significant improvements, with F-score gains of up to 1.9, when compared to the standalone base models. Additionally, our analysis demonstrates the versatility of the STGG framework, which can be adapted to various base event extraction models, leveraging extensive unlabeled data and even when lacking high-quality AMR graph annotations.

The cartoon domain has witnessed a surge in popularity, but previous attempts to achieve portrait stylization have faced significant challenges. These challenges include the need for numerous training images and the inability to create abstract cartoon faces effectively. Recent methods have tried to address these issues, such as a layer swapping approach that only requires a limited number of images. However, these methods have their own limitations. This paper presents a new method called Cross-domain Style mixing that combines two distinct latent codes to achieve stylization. By doing so, it enables faces to be transformed into various cartoon characters at different levels of abstraction, utilizing a single generator and minimal training images.

Multilingual question-answering systems rely on retrieving relevant documents and identifying the correct answer within them.
We propose that multilingual QA systems are susceptible to information inconsistencies when handling documents written in different languages, as these documents often convey disparate information about a shared topic.
Our study aims to investigate the effects of language-specific information availability and cultural influences on multilingual open-domain question-answering models, specifically focusing on retrieval bias.
We analyze whether different retriever models retrieve varying passages given the same question in different languages on the TyDi QA and XOR-TyDi QA datasets, two benchmarks for multilingual QA.
We anticipate that the content disparities in documents across languages may be indicative of cultural differences and social biases.

A new resampling-based approach is developed to create a highly accurate test for subsets of hypotheses in high-dimensional linear regression models. This approach can be incorporated into any multiple testing method to generate confidence statements regarding relevant predictor variables. By combining repeated data splits with a variable selection technique, permutation test statistics for individual hypotheses are calculated; these statistics are then aggregated to define tests for subsets of variables. This procedure is highly adaptable, permitting various selection techniques and combining methods to be utilized. We present this method in both exact and approximate forms, the latter of which is optimized for reduced memory usage and faster computation times, making it more suitable for large-scale datasets. The effectiveness of the method is demonstrated through simulation studies and an analysis of actual gene expression data.

Current machine translation models still encounter difficulties with complex inputs, such as low-quality data and rare words or phrases. Various studies have attempted to improve model robustness by pinpointing specific types of noise and adapting models accordingly. However, a crucial yet under-researched area involves slight variations in expression (non-typos) that retain meaning in the target language. We identify this category, called Natural Asemantic Variation (NAV), and analyze its impact on machine translation robustness. We find that existing translation models underperform when faced with NAV data, but demonstrate ways to enhance performance by retraining them using human-generated variations. Furthermore, we discover that NAV robustness can be applied across languages and that artificially created perturbations can provide some benefits, but not all of those offered by authentic NAV data.

Mathematical methods like discrete integration, gradient descent, and state estimation, which are typically based on linear algebra, are primarily suited for use with vectors in Euclidean spaces as described in the literature. However, this article outlines how to adapt these techniques to accommodate state vectors in non-Euclidean spaces, such as those representing rotational and positional movements of rigid bodies. To achieve this, it offers a comprehensive examination of the SO(3) and SE(3) Lie groups - representing rigid body rotations and motions - focusing on the different ways these groups can be represented, the nature of their tangent spaces, and the impact of perturbations, as well as the necessary Jacobian definitions required for applying the aforementioned calculus techniques.

We investigate the eigenbundle (localization bundle) of certain Hilbert modules over bounded symmetric domains of rank $r$, leading to complex-analytic fibre spaces that are stratified with $r+1$ layers. These fibres can be characterised in terms of K\"ahler geometry as sections of line bundles over flag manifolds. Furthermore, the metric embedding can be computed using the derivatives of reproducing kernel functions. Key instances of this are provided by the determinantal ideals that arise from the vanishing conditions along the various layers of the stratification.

Large-scale, pre-trained language models are adept at producing coherent text but face challenges in being controlled when sampling outputs. In this study, we focus on constrained sampling of these language models: generating text that adheres to user-specified requirements while retaining fluency and maintaining the model's performance in subsequent applications. We present MuCoLa, a novel sampling procedure that combines the language model's log-likelihood with customizable (differentiable) constraints within a unified energy function. This method then generates samples through a non-autoregressive process. It starts by initializing the entire output sequence with random values and then iteratively applies Markov chain updates, guided by the gradients of the energy function using Langevin Dynamics. We assess the effectiveness of MuCoLa on text generation under soft and hard constraints as well as their combinations, achieving substantial gains over competing baselines in the areas of toxicity reduction, sentiment regulation, and keyword-guided text generation.

Similar to other areas of cybersecurity, machine learning techniques are gaining traction in detecting Android malware. Numerous proposals have been put forth using various algorithms and feature sets, yielding impressive detection rates. However, the lack of standard evaluation frameworks and replicability issues hinder comparison of these proposals.
