This paper conducts an in-depth analysis of 10 prominent research studies on Android malware detection using a unified evaluation framework. We identify five critical factors - duplicated samples, label accuracy, class imbalance, evasion techniques, and app evolution - that can significantly impact trained machine learning models and performance. Through thorough experimentation, our study reveals that existing machine learning-based detectors were evaluated unrealistically, justifying their reported successes. Consequently, it is crucial to create realistic experimental scenarios that account for these factors to develop more effective ML-based Android malware detection methods.

Modern natural language processing systems are built on top of large language models, which consistently deliver high accuracy and robustness across tasks and domains but have a high computational cost that can make inference slow and expensive. Researchers have explored techniques such as pruning, quantization, and distillation to reduce the cost of using these models. This paper investigates the transferability of models pruned using Gradual Unstructured Magnitude Pruning between domains and tasks, finding that models pruned during pretraining can be effective across novel tasks without extensive hyperparameter tuning or specialized approaches. Specifically, the researchers demonstrate that a general sparse model, Sparse*BERT, can be transformed into a specialized model, SparseBioBERT, by fine-tuning it on biomedical text, achieving similar quality to BioBERT with a significantly reduced number of parameters.

The cell's edge protrusions are crucial in detecting environmental signals, especially during cell movement and spreading. Recent findings indicate that these protrusions wrap around surrounding fibers. However, the coiling mechanism and underlying forces remain poorly understood. This study combines theoretical and experimental approaches to investigate how cellular protrusions coil around fibers of diverse shapes. Our theoretical model reveals that curved membrane proteins drive protrusion formation by harnessing actin polymerization forces and identifies key factors influencing coiling direction. According to the model, the cell's edge coils around round fibers, but this process is halted when fibers have an elliptical cross-section. Our results, verified through high-resolution 3D imaging, validate the model's predictions for fibers of various diameters.

Deep learning models trained on cardiac MRI data are often limited by the scarcity of labeled data and its inherent complexity. Recent research has shown that self-supervised contrastive learning can enhance performance in medical imaging tasks. Nevertheless, it remains unclear to what extent pre-trained models focus on the primary organ of interest as opposed to surrounding tissue. Our work explores the optimal method of incorporating anatomical knowledge into self-supervised learning. We investigate using a segmentation network to identify the heart in MRI images prior to pre-training with multiple diagnostic tasks using self-supervised learning. The results indicate that leveraging prior anatomical knowledge can substantially improve diagnostic performance in downstream tasks. Furthermore, pre-training with in-domain data tends to boost downstream performance and yields human-like attention patterns, whereas training from scratch and using pre-trained ImageNet networks generally do not offer significant benefits.

This study analyzed the impact of repulsive nucleon-nucleon interactions driven by the Pauli exclusion principle on the half-lives of heavy, even-even nuclei with atomic numbers between 84 and 92. The Pauli exclusion principle was integrated into the investigation through two approaches: adjusting the interactions according to the Bohr-Sommerfeld condition and modifying a double-folding formalism with a kinetic energy term. The results showed that when incorporating a kinetic energy term into the formalism, estimated using the extended Thomas-Fermi method, the discrepancy between calculated and observed half-lives decreased. Specifically, it was found that including this kinetic energy term in the double-folding formalism more accurately predicted the observed alpha decay half-lives.

The exotic nuclear properties in neutron-rich Ca, Ni, Zr, and Sn isotopes are investigated using the continuum Skyrme Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov theory formulated with the Green's function method. The model successfully reproduces available data on two-neutron and one-neutron separation energies, predicting shorter drip lines based on one-neutron separation energies. Neutron pairing energies in odd-numbered isotopes are significantly smaller than those of neighboring even-numbered isotopes due to missing pairing contributions. Single-particle structures, root-mean-square radii, and density distributions reveal the presence of halo structures in neutron-rich Ca, Ni, and Sn isotopes. A sharp increase in radii and diffuse density distributions are observed, attributed to low-lying angular momentum orbitals around the Fermi surface. These findings support the role of pairing correlations in the halo phenomena, consistent with the behavior of neutrons occupied above the Fermi surface.

The DeGroot-style opinion formation model assumes continuous interaction among social network members, making it unsuitable for handling temporary interactions with outsiders. This limitation applies to real-world entities such as companies attempting to influence a large number of individuals through time-limited campaigns. To address this, we developed a modified version of the DeGroot model that enables external agents to interact with permanent network members for a predetermined duration. By analysing and simulating the variant, we gained valuable insights into maximising an external agent's impact on opinion formation.

As networked control systems grow in size and complexity, ensuring the robustness of their interconnected components has become a pressing concern. Recent research has highlighted the need to reevaluate traditional system and control theory concepts through the lens of graph theory. This paper provides an in-depth exploration of graph-based methods for assessing the resilience of networked control systems. It delves into various decentralized algorithms employed in these systems and assesses their vulnerability to malicious actions by examining the underlying network's structural characteristics. Graph-theoretic techniques are presented to measure the impact of attacks, and certain system-theoretic concepts of robustness are reinterpreted from a graph-theoretic perspective to mitigate the effects of such threats. Additionally, the paper discusses several security-related challenges in networked control systems that utilize graph theory as an analytical tool. It concludes by outlining potential avenues for further research in this field.

This presentation utilizes contemporary visualization methods to dissect the microscopic architecture of the non-trivial QCD ground-state vacuum fields that constitute the basis of matter. Specifically, the study centers on the centre vortices discovered within the lattice QCD ground-state fields. The primary objective of our ongoing investigation is to elucidate how dynamical fermions in the QCD vacuum modify the centre-vortex structure, thereby yielding profound implications for the role of centre vortices in QCD's confinement and dynamical chiral symmetry breaking mechanisms.

When ions are densely packed, the steric repulsion between them becomes significant and needs to be incorporated into the conventional Poisson-Boltzmann equation. We derived a modified form of the Poisson-Nernst-Planck equations that includes steric effects. By taking certain assumptions, these equations can be transformed into a Poisson-Boltzmann equation with steric effects. The parameter Lambda determines the strength of steric repulsion, with higher values indicating stronger interactions between ions and solvent molecules. We investigated the limit of this modified equation as Lambda approaches infinity and found that it converges to a specific type of modified Poisson-Boltzmann equation. This suggests that our original equation can be viewed as a generalized form of the modified Poisson-Boltzmann equations.

Recent advancements in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) have led to the utilization of deep neural networks, which pose challenges in understanding and interpreting the results by human experts. On the other hand, research into interpretable reinforcement learning (RL) has shown potential in deriving decision tree-based policies from neural networks, but this has been limited to single-agent scenarios. To address this gap, we introduce the first set of algorithms capable of extracting interpretable decision-tree policies from neural networks trained for MARL. Our primary algorithm, IVIPER, modifies the existing single-agent method, VIPER, to accommodate multi-agent environments, thereby learning high-quality decision-tree policies for each agent. Furthermore, we propose the novel MAVIPER, a centralized decision-tree training algorithm that better captures coordination between agents by predicting their behavior and focusing on critical states. Both IVIPER and MAVIPER algorithms outperform their baselines, and MAVIPER-trained agents exhibit superior coordination and performance in comparison to IVIPER-trained agents on various multi-agent particle-world environments.

The inner workings of neural language models are notoriously challenging to understand.  Recently, significant advancements have been made in creating automatic explanations for these models, but there has been less focus on utilizing these explanations to enhance their performance.  To address this, researchers have been using explanation regularization to improve language models by aligning the generated explanations with human ones.  However, existing research primarily assesses the impact of explanation regularization within the scope of its training data, without thoroughly examining its effects on unseen data.  Furthermore, there is a lack of understanding regarding how different factors such as the choice of explanation criteria and the quantity and type of training instances influence the performance of language models using explanation regularization.  To address this, we propose ER-TEST, an evaluation protocol that assesses the out-of-distribution generalization of explanation regularization along three dimensions: novel datasets, contrast set tests, and functional tests.  Utilizing this protocol, we investigate three key questions: (A) Which explanation criteria are most effective in specific out-of-distribution settings? (B) How does the quantity and type of training instances with human explanations impact the performance of language models using explanation regularization? (C) Can explanation regularization improve performance even with limited and distantly-supervised human explanations?  ER-TEST allows for a comprehensive analysis of these questions across a wide variety of tasks and datasets, and our results demonstrate that explanation regularization has little effect on in-distribution performance but can lead to substantial gains in out-of-distribution performance across multiple metrics, also showing that the optimal explanation criterion is task-dependent, while explanation regularization can still improve performance even with limited and distantly-supervised human explanations.

A key issue in reinforcement learning is articulating objectives that are both understandable and verifiable. One well-established method is defining tasks through reward machines - simple machines that encapsulate the problem to be solved. We propose introducing skill machines, a format that can be directly learned from reward machines, encapsulating the solution to these tasks. Our framework enables an agent to initially develop a set of fundamental skills without rewards and then combine them with a learned skill machine to generate composite actions that conform to any logical rules, such as those in linear temporal logics. This grants the agent the capacity to map complex task specifications to near-optimal actions with no further learning. Our results show that our method effectively handles intricate, long-duration tasks, producing nearly optimal results without additional training in both simple and high-dimensional game environments. Moreover, our approach can be enhanced by offline reinforcement learning techniques when ideal behaviors are desired.

Our investigation focuses on the concentration phenomenon for discrete-time random dynamical systems with an unlimited state space. To derive exponential concentration inequalities for these systems, we develop a heuristic approach rooted in a purely functional analytical framework. Furthermore, our findings reveal that the existence of an exponential-type Lyapunov function not only confers stability but also yields exponential concentration inequalities when sampling from the stationary distribution, facilitated by a transport-entropy inequality (T-E). The significance of our results is substantial, particularly in reinforcement learning (RL) and controls, enabling the derivation of exponential concentration inequalities even for unbounded observables, without relying on reversibility or exact knowledge of the random dynamical system - assumptions that are central to concentration inequalities in statistical mechanics and Markov diffusion processes.

Those who delve into the world of circuitry are likely to be familiar with the three primary circuit components - the capacitor, resistor, and inductor. These fundamental elements are defined by their relationships with the four circuit variables: current, voltage, charge, and flux. However, Professor Leon Chua's 1971 proposal, rooted in the concept of symmetry, suggested the existence of a fourth fundamental element that connects flux and charge, which he called the memristor. This theoretical concept gained practical significance in 2008 when researchers at HP Labs created a physical model of the memristor. This paper focuses on the memristor's theoretical framework and potential applications, including its variable resistance, adaptability, lack of leakage current, and compatibility with CMOS technology. Due to its diverse characteristics, the memristor has led to the development of various models, which are reviewed in this paper. As a versatile device, memristors can be utilized in memory, logic, and neuromorphic systems, and their computer simulations can aid in analyzing circuit behavior to facilitate the development of memristor-based applications. This paper examines the VerilogA modeling of memristors under sinusoidal inputs, employing various window functions to validate their circuit analysis.

Federated Learning's user privacy concerns have been exacerbated by Vision Transformers' vulnerability to gradient-based inversion attacks. We discovered that the low-dimensional spatial information embedded in Vision Transformer position embeddings accelerates model training but also compromises data privacy. Enhancing the model's position-insensitivity is seen as a way to mitigate these privacy risks, yet simply removing the embedded information could worsen performance and increase the risk of data breaches. To resolve this conflict, we developed a Masked Jigsaw Puzzle method that breaks the chain of data leakage in Vision Transformers. Our approach can be seamlessly integrated into existing Vision Transformer models and outperforms them in both large-scale dataset performance and gradient attack resistance, as demonstrated by extensive experiments.

Current entity linking research typically relies on a comprehensive knowledge base, 
allowing all mentions to be linked. However, real-world applications often face 
incomplete knowledge bases and emerging concepts. To address this challenge, a new 
benchmark called EDIN has been created, where entities lacking descriptions and 
labeled mentions must be integrated into existing linking systems. By comparing EDIN 
with zero-shot entity linking, this paper reveals the increased difficulties it presents.
The proposed EDIN pipeline enhances existing dense-retrieval based entity linking by 
developing an end-to-end approach for detecting, clustering, and indexing unknown 
entities in context. Experimental results demonstrate that using a unified embedding 
per entity for multiple mentions outperforms indexing individual mentions separately.

Significant advancements in natural language processing tasks have been made using neural attention models, yet the high memory usage of the self-attention module for long texts hampers its application in summarizing lengthy texts. Rather than optimizing attention mechanisms for efficiency, we explore the possibility of comparable performance from models operating within limited contextual scope. Our model treats individual pages as localized units of analysis during encoding and decoding, segmenting the input text by locality principles. Experiments across different text granularities – from sentences to full documents – revealed superior performance of our model over strong baselines incorporating efficient attention modules, shedding light on the effectiveness of our locality-based modeling approach.

Recent Large Language Models (LMs) have reached outstanding results on numerous Natural Language Processing (NLP) evaluations. As more benchmarks emerge, developing increasingly larger and intricate LMs is becoming less practical due to substantial costs, time constraints, and negative environmental effects associated with them.  An alternative approach could be beneficial: can we transform existing data to align with the model's strengths, making a difficult question more easily answerable? We examine whether humans can break down a challenging question into a series of simpler ones that models can solve more effectively. Our analysis of multiple datasets with diverse reasoning tasks reveals that human-assisted question decomposition can notably enhance model performance by up to 29%, offering a feasible solution for incorporating human involvement in NLP research. The Human-in-the-loop Question Decomposition (HQD) strategy shows promise as a viable alternative to developing larger LMs.

Surveys play a crucial role in informing policy decisions, societal understanding, and decision-making. However, obtaining subpopulation level estimates from these surveys can be a costly and time-consuming endeavor. A novel approach called Multilevel Regression and Poststratification (MRP) enables the derivation of reliable subpopulation estimates from surveys with significantly less required data. To date, various visual representations have been employed to convey and assess the accuracy of MRP estimates. Notwithstanding, limited research has been conducted on optimal methods for visualizing MRP outcomes. Consequently, this study conducts a systematic literature review to examine the current MRP visualization practices and applies MRP to a real-world example, such as the 2016 US presidential election, to demonstrate the implications of prevailing visualization methods and propose alternatives for enhancement. Our analysis reveals that uncertainty is often neglected in visualization practices despite its significance in survey inference. Furthermore, our findings indicate that choropleth maps are predominantly used for displaying MRP estimates, which can lead to an oversimplification of results and obscure vital information. By utilizing various visual representations that incorporate uncertainty, we demonstrate the value of incorporating model variability into visualization and propose an innovative visualization strategy that considers the trade-off between bias and variance when evaluating MRP models.

As technology advances and multi-core processors are increasingly used in hazardous settings like space, faults caused by radiation are a significant issue affecting both performance and design. This research proposes an architectural method to dynamically enhance resilience against soft errors at the processor core level by introducing a novel redundancy grouping scheme called On-Demand Redundancy Grouping (ODRG). This innovative approach allows a multi-core cluster to switch between fault-tolerant operation and high-performance operation, with minimal run-time overhead. The ODRG unit incurs a relatively low area cost of less than 1% for the entire cluster, and is more efficient than existing commercial implementations in recovering from faults. Additionally, when redundancy is not needed, the ODRG approach enables the use of redundant cores for parallel computation, leading to a substantial increase of up to 2.96 times in performance for certain applications.

Measuring the connection or similarity between words or text is vital in text-based applications like knowledge acquisition, recommendation systems, and language processing. Ontologies have been developed to organize knowledge and have become essential for information systems. Calculating semantic similarity from ontologies has been refined and can be complemented by other similarity methods. In this study, we introduce a method for calculating semantic similarity based on ontologies in a recommendation system framework.

A novel technique for generating sets based on input token sequences learns a mapping to effectively handle set-related NLP tasks such as entity typing and dialogue emotion tagging. Current popular methods like Seq2Seq models treat sets as sequences, failing to fully exploit key properties including order invariance and cardinality. To address this limitation, we developed a sampling algorithm that generates informative orders from the vast label order space. By integrating set size into the model and utilizing autoregressive factorization, our method enhances any Seq2Seq model with set-related signals. As a result, augmenting training data without additional annotations leads to a 20% average relative improvement across four benchmark datasets using BART, T5, and GPT-3 models.

Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models have seen remarkable results in
generation tasks, but their low inference efficiency due to numerous denoising
steps limits their applicability. To address this, we introduce Early-Stopped DDPM,
a strategy that accelerates the model by stopping the diffusion process earlier
than usual and starting the reverse denoising process from a non-Gaussian
distribution. By leveraging a pre-trained generative model, such as GAN or VAE,
samples can be efficiently generated from the target distribution, significantly
reducing the number of required denoising steps. This approach not only achieves
improved sample quality but also surpasses the performance of both vanilla DDPM
and the pre-trained generative model in experiments across various datasets.
Furthermore, our method exhibits desirable properties like orthogonal acceleration
capability and simultaneous global and local control in image generation.

In hyperspectral image classification, traditional Deep Neural Networks have shown success, yet many prior works overlook the inherent characteristics of hyperspectral images, such as the physical processes generating noise, resulting in poor feature extraction and classification performance. To address this limitation, this study presents a novel deep learning approach incorporating a noise-inclined module and a denoising framework for hyperspectral image classification. Initially, the spectral signature of hyperspectral images is modeled using a physical noise model to account for the high variability within each class and overlapping features between classes. Next, a noise-inclined module is designed to capture the physical noise within objects and a denoising framework is implemented to remove this noise. Ultimately, a CNN is developed to leverage the noise-inclined module and denoising framework, yielding discriminative features and superior classification performance. Experimental results on two real-world datasets validate the efficacy of this method, with implementation details available on the repository at https://github.com/shendu-sw/noise-physical-framework.

To mitigate noise in data-storage qubits kept in isolation, an additional noise-probe qubit, known as a spectator qubit, can be employed, with corrections applied only when needed. Inspired by solid-state qubits, we investigated dephasing noise caused by a two-state fluctuator using a random telegraph process and a noise-probe qubit. We developed a theoretical model based on projective measurements of the spectator qubit and evaluated different measurement and control strategies. We started by analyzing the Greedy algorithm, which always prioritizes data qubit coherence in the immediate future, and found that this algorithm performs well. We simplified its adaptive strategy into a few-parameter model and developed a one-parameter family of algorithms using Bayesian maps. As the sensitivity of the noise-probe qubit increases, this family of algorithms reduces the data qubit decoherence rate. By setting the parameter to its optimal value, we created the Map-based Optimized Adaptive Algorithm for Asymptotic Regime (MOAAAR), which outperforms the Greedy algorithm, especially in high-noise regimes.

The phrase "nobody is safe until everybody is safe" emphasizes that global cooperation is necessary to combat pandemics like COVID-19, which are inherently global issues. In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, researchers have developed a model to simulate the spread of a virus in interconnected communities and examine different vaccination strategies. These models assume that vaccination effectiveness decreases over time and categorize communities as unvaccinated ("Bronze"), moderately vaccinated ("Silver"), or highly vaccinated ("Gold"). Studies have shown that when "Bronze" communities interact with "Silver" or "Gold" communities, the unvaccinated communities are the primary drivers of increased infections in the vaccinated communities. When different communities are interconnected in a network, two factors have a significant impact on virus spread: the coupling strength between communities and network density. In particular, when considering spread in Barabasi-Albert networks, moderately and well-vaccinated communities ("Silver" and "Gold") tend to have lower infection rates than unvaccinated communities ("Bronze"). However, even a small number of unvaccinated communities can still cause a significant increase in infections among the vaccinated communities. When studying the spread of a virus in dense Erdos-Renyi, sparse Watts-Strogatz, and Barabasi-Albert networks, it has been observed that dense networks can quickly reach a disease-free state, while sparse networks may not be able to eliminate the virus. Furthermore, a critical factor in preventing the spread of the virus is the uniformity of vaccination across the entire network.

A theoretical investigation was conducted on the $D\bar{D}K$ three-body system by employing the fixed center approximation to Faddeev equations and considering interactions between the $D$ and $K$, $D$ and $\bar{D}$ mesons within the chiral unitary framework. The study involved the scattering of a $K$ meson off a $D\bar{D}$ system potentially forming a scalar meson, such as $X(3720)$. The strong interaction between $DK$ facilitated the generation of a dynamically created $D^*_{s0}(2317)$ meson, which led to the emergence of a resonance structure in the three-body $K$-$(D\bar{D})_{X(3720)}$ scattering amplitude, supporting the possibility of a $D\bar{D}K$ bound state. The findings align with earlier theoretical studies, suggesting the existence of a new hidden charm $K$ meson, specifically $K_{c\bar{c}}(4180)$ with the quantum numbers $I(J^P) = \frac{1}{2}(0^-)$ and a predicted mass of approximately 4180 MeV. These results are anticipated to inspire experimental verification through direct measurements.

We investigate a dynamic resource allocation scenario, where divisible resources arrive over time and must be distributed among fixed agents. Each agent's utility is drawn from a known distribution and decisions are made immediately, without the option to reverse them. The goal of most dynamic allocation methods is to maximize the total utility, potentially resulting in some agents being over-served while others go unsatisfied. This paper, however, pursues an alternative approach focused on egalitarian welfare, striving to achieve a balance between the efficiency and fairness of resource distribution. We first analyze a policy based on a fluid approximation, which achieves a regret of order $\Theta(\sqrt{T})$ relative to the optimal egalitarian allocation when all utilities are known beforehand. Next, we propose a new policy called $\mathsf{BIRT}$ that re-solves the fluid problem no more than $O(\log\log T)$ times. This policy is proven to have $O(1)$ regret against the optimal egalitarian allocation, regardless of the time horizon length $T$ and the initial welfare. Numerical experiments are also provided to demonstrate the notable performance improvement of the $\mathsf{BIRT}$ policy compared to other benchmark policies.

As autonomous systems become increasingly sophisticated, their operation in unstructured environments raises critical safety concerns. This research addresses these issues by developing a safety layer for mechanical systems capable of detecting and mitigating unstable dynamics resulting from external disruptions. This safety layer is designed to operate in parallel with existing nominal controllers, such as pose or force tracking, and intervene when power flow could lead to instability. The underlying approach involves calculating the system's Largest Lyapunov Exponent (LLE) – a metric that quantifies the rate of divergence or convergence in the system's dynamics. By proactively monitoring this metric, potentially hazardous system behaviors can be swiftly identified. The calculated LLE is then utilized in conjunction with Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) to enforce power constraints on jerk-controlled systems. The proposed safety architecture has been experimentally verified on an Omnidirectional Micro Aerial Vehicle (OMAV) in various scenarios, including both unobstructed flight and interactive tasks.

We investigate a variation of the classic cake-cutting problem where agents are positioned on a graph. This variation considers a scenario where each agent compares their allocated portion only to that of their neighbors. Our goal is to develop an efficient algorithm for finding a locally envy-free distribution, where each agent values their share at least as much as any neighboring share, given a specific graph structure.

The current best algorithm for cake divisions by Aziz and Mackenzie has a significant query complexity. Our key contribution lies in identifying a particular type of graph, referred to as tree graphs with a maximum depth of two (Depth2Tree), which allows for an efficient query protocol under the Robertson-Webb query model. We designed a discrete protocol that can find a locally envy-free distribution among 'n' agents on a Depth2Tree graph, using no more than O(n^3 * log(n)) cuts on the cake. Furthermore, for a specific type of Depth2Tree graph, referred to as 2-Star, we demonstrated that O(n^2) queries are sufficient. Additionally, we established a lower bound of Ω(n^2) evaluation queries for a 1-Star graph, assuming the root agent partitions the cake into 'n' connected pieces.

Current cybersecurity threat and risk analysis approaches primarily automate certain aspects of the process, with critical decisions often relying on expert judgment. In reality, teams of specialists use workshops to manually assess system designs, but this can be influenced by personal biases and unequal representation of diverse perspectives, including gender. The impact of non-technical threat perceptions has been studied, but there is a lack of empirical research examining the effect of diversity on the risk analysis of technical products. This study aims to develop a research plan to identify the most significant diversity factors involved in risk analysis.

This study tackles the issue of mobility in massive MIMO systems, which significantly hinders the effectiveness of 5G mobile networks in real-world applications. We introduce a groundbreaking channel prediction method using the multi-dimensional matrix pencil (MDMP) approach, which leverages the channel's angular-frequency and angular-time domain characteristics to accurately estimate the path parameters. The MDMP technique also includes a novel path pairing scheme that pairs delay and Doppler based on the super-resolution property of angle estimation. Our method effectively handles realistic constraints imposed by user movements, which has been overlooked in previous studies. Theoretically, we demonstrate that with increasing numbers of base station antennas, the prediction error diminishes to zero, even when only two arbitrary channel samples are available. Furthermore, we derive a lower-bound for the number of base station antennas required for satisfactory performance. Simulation results based on the 3GPP industrial channel model show that our proposed MDMP method closely approaches the performance achieved in stationary scenarios, even at user velocities of 120 km/h and latency levels of 16 ms.

Personalizing human-agent interaction can be achieved by modeling virtual agents with distinct behavior styles, which can be synthesized using an efficient machine learning approach that combines prosodic features, text, and visual cues from various speakers, including those unseen during training. This zero-shot multimodal style transfer is made possible by leveraging multimodal data from the PATS database and disentangling the content and style of speech, enabling the model to directly infer style embeddings even for speakers whose data are not part of the training phase. The proposed system consists of two key components: a speaker style encoder network that generates a fixed-dimensional speaker embedding from multimodal data and a sequence-to-sequence synthesis network that synthesizes gestures conditioned on the speaker style embedding and the input modalities of the source speaker. By achieving zero-shot style transfer and generating high-fidelity 3D animations, the model outperforms a baseline in both objective and subjective evaluations.

Given a finite group, G, and a non-trivial subgroup H of G, we can define a specific graph called the generalized non-coprime graph. This graph consists of all non-identity elements in G as vertices, and vertices a and b are connected by an edge if their orders share a common factor and at least one of them belongs to subgroup H. We will be investigating certain properties of these graphs, with a focus on those resulting from cyclic groups. We will also examine the types of graphs that can arise when we broaden our study to include finite nilpotent groups and compare the results to other types of groups, specifically those with elements of prime power order.

A compartmental model based on a nonlinear partial differential equation (PDE) for COVID-19 generates a continuous map of infection across space and time. Increasing the spatial precision, adding new model components, and categorizing based on significant health indicators greatly increases the number of variables to millions. To efficiently solve these highly detailed models, we utilize a parallel solver that integrates domain decomposition and algebraic multigrid preconditioners at multiple levels. As a numerical example, we apply a five-compartment susceptible-exposed-infected-recovered-deceased (SEIRD) model to a large geographic area (Southern Ontario) to demonstrate the solver's scalability and performance. This allows us to predict infections over a three-month period for a system of 92 million, requiring only 7 hours of computation with 1780 processes, saving months of time compared to traditional methods.

Dorigoni, Green, and Wen's exact formula for a correlator of four superconformal primary operators in $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory has been studied for its large $N$ behavior. We have successfully translated this formula into a sum over $(p,q)$-strings, where due to $SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$ duality, a single governing function emerges, analogous to the fundamental string contribution. Analyzing the large order behavior of this function led us to discover non-perturbative corrections at large $N$, interpreted as D3-brane instantons in type IIB string theory, which also arises from a Laplace-difference equation for the integrated correlator.

Investigating how the physical properties of massive star-forming clouds can be accurately determined through observations is a crucial area of study. We aim to assess the level of accuracy with which the properties of these clouds can be deduced from observations. Specifically, we're interested in exploring the potential of the Next Generation VLA (ngVLA) interferometer. To do this, we utilize data from a magnetohydrodynamic simulation of star-formation and focus on a filamentary structure that mirrors the properties of an infrared-dark cloud. We create synthetic ngVLA observations of spectral lines, analyzing column density, gas temperature, and kinematics. We then compare the results to ideal and actual 3D model data. With ngVLA, we can achieve a resolution of 0.01 pc at a distance of 4 kpc, even in its most compact configuration. This allows us to map cloud kinematics and structure down to sub-arcsec scales for abundant molecules. Our results indicate that for molecules like NH3, we can accurately produce a column density map of the entire cloud and recover kinetic temperatures with high precision, even without additional data. However, at higher frequencies, there is a notable loss of large-scale emission. Our line observations accurately trace cloud kinematics, but the line-of-sight confusion complicates the interpretation, particularly for large-scale kinematics. The ngVLA will enable us to gather accurate data on small-scale structure and the physical and chemical state of clouds in high-mass star-forming regions at kiloparsec distances. Nonetheless, single-dish data are still necessary for estimating total column density and large-scale kinematics.

To achieve highly reliable and efficient downlink communications with robust security, we formulate an optimization problem that balances multiple objectives in the finite blocklength regime. Aiming to maximize overall secrecy rates while minimizing maximum error probability and information leakage rates, we tackle a complex multi-objective problem involving non-convex and non-smooth functions. To address these difficulties, we break down the problem into two stages using an alternating optimization strategy. Firstly, we determine secure precoders by optimizing lower bounds of the secrecy rate and employing a power iteration-based approach to solve the problem. Secondly, given these precoders, we minimize maximum error probability and information leakage rate using a weighted-sum method and Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions. The proposed approach is validated through simulations.

Calculations for entanglement entropy are conducted between two separated, maximally extended spacetime regions of a static black hole, with the dividing line being the event horizon. To start, the Schwarzschild black hole is examined and further calculations are extended to other types, including the charged Reissner-Nordstrom and Schwarzschild-de Sitter black holes with multiple horizons. Also considered is the static, spherically-symmetric solution for a more general F(R) gravity model. For each black hole, the entanglement entropy is calculated using the replica trick method, requiring the explicit form of the replica spacetime metric. Results show that the entanglement entropy for static, spherically-symmetric black holes follows the Bekenstein-Hawking area law for entropy.

Deep learning networks have shown impressive capabilities in a wide range of tasks, including image analysis, speech recognition, and language processing, but they also have a significant weakness. Adversarial attacks, which subtly alter images to make them nearly imperceptible to humans, can cause deep learning models to make completely different predictions. This study examined the efficacy of projected gradient descent and adaptive mask segmentation attacks on the image segmentation DeepLabV3 model using two architectures: MobileNetV3 and ResNet50. It was discovered that projected gradient descent was consistently effective in manipulating the model's predictions, whereas the adaptive mask segmentation attack had limited success in a multi-class setting. Nevertheless, the existence of these attacks poses a threat to all deep learning networks used for image classification.

In this study, we introduce a highly scalable and effective system for real-time bidding supply landscape analysis, utilizing a high-throughput, low-latency setup. Our approach to exploration is guided by the predictive uncertainty inherent in click-through rate forecasting models, which we have proven to yield improved model performance and key business metrics through online experimentation.

A significant obstacle in computational biology is achieving a balance between the accuracy and extent of data, as well as the complexity of mathematical models used to interpret it. Techniques such as identifiability analysis and information criterion have been developed to bridge this gap, but often fall short in reconciling the limitations of available data with the level of detail required to address crucial biological questions. Simple models, such as the logistic and Gompertz growth models, can typically be identified using standard experimental data. To extract meaningful information from complex, unidentifiable models that capture essential biological mechanisms, we investigate the geometric relationship between these complex models and simpler, identifiable models. By studying the quantitative connections between non-identifiable parameters in the complex model and identifiable parameters in the simpler model, we establish an additional layer of interpretation between these parameters and standard metrics such as goodness-of-fit or likelihood. Our approach is demonstrated by applying it to a series of mathematical models for the growth of multicellular tumour spheroids. Given that data from tumour spheroid experiments are often limited and noisy, and the corresponding models are frequently overly complex, our method is able to predict non-identifiabilities, divide non-identifiable parameter spaces into identifiable parameter combinations that relate to specific data features, and provide further insight into the biology underlying these complex models.

Heavy element nucleosynthesis relies on accurate calculations of photon strength functions. These can be experimentally determined through nuclear response to photons. This study investigates $^{66}$Zn's photoresponse between 5.6 and 9.9 MeV, with a focus on the contribution of its "elastic" decay back to the ground state, and distinguishes between electric and magnetic dipole transitions within that channel. Nuclear resonance fluorescence experiments using a high-intensity photon beam at the High Intensity $\gamma$-ray Source allowed for detailed analysis. The results indicate full photoabsorption cross sections, separating electric and magnetic dipole strengths for ground-state decay and determining the average branching ratio back to the ground state. Compared to a previous study using bremsstrahlung, the results show lower cross sections, and the estimated branching ratio based on statistical-model calculations underestimates the actual value.

Object localization with weak supervision, where objects are identified with broad category labels, is a complex problem. Most deep learning approaches, which focus on highlighting key parts of objects, overlook the complete object itself. Additionally, transformer-based methods prioritize background information over the entire object. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a re-attention mechanism called the Token Refinement Transformer (TRT), which captures object-level meaning to guide localization. TRT features a novel module, Token Priority Scoring Module (TPSM), to filter out background noise and concentrate on the target object. By incorporating Class Activation Maps, which are aware of semantic meaning, our approach restricts attention to the target object. Extensive experiments on two benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of our method compared to existing approaches that rely on image categories. Our code can be accessed on GitHub at the specified URL.

Graph Neural Networks have shown impressive performance across numerous domains. However, their effectiveness can be undermined by noisy or adversarial input data, which presents a significant challenge to overcome. Current defense strategies for GNNs are not only resource-intensive but also lack scalability. This paper introduces a universal framework known as Weighted Laplacian GNN, which integrates Weighted Graph Laplacian learning with the GNN architecture. Leveraging the positive semi-definiteness property of Laplacian matrices and feature smoothness, the proposed method creates a unified optimization framework. This framework effectively discards noisy or adversarial edges, allowing the model to assign appropriate weights to connections in the graph. A key demonstration experiment utilizes the Graph Convolutional Neural Network (GCNN) architecture, yet the framework is adaptable to any existing GNN architecture. Experimental results on benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed method in achieving both high accuracy and improved computational efficiency. The code for the proposed method can be accessed through a publicly available repository.

Predicting the movement of surrounding vehicles in autonomous racing scenarios is essential for optimal performance and planning. However, utilizing deep neural networks, which can be opaque, in safety-critical applications like autonomous driving poses significant challenges. To address this, we propose a structured method for forecasting opposing racecars' movements using deep neural networks, which ensures predictable output trajectories. The model's performance was evaluated in conjunction with an LSTM-based architecture on data from realistic simulations. Our approach significantly improves prediction accuracy while meeting quality standards, thereby facilitating a reliable real-world application. We have successfully implemented this model in the Technical University of Munich's Indy Autonomous Challenge 2021 vehicle. The source code used in this research is available on GitHub as open-source software.

Research suggests galaxies are categorized into two distinct types, star-forming and passive, where the latter have a large central bulge. However, we found this classification to be an oversimplification by analyzing a large sample of galaxies from the MaNGA survey. The distribution of galaxy rotation rates does not follow a simple binary pattern. Instead, fast-rotating galaxies can be divided into multiple subcategories, with disk-like systems making up a larger share of both mass and quantity. Star-forming galaxies predominantly consist of disks, while passive galaxies exhibit a mix of different structures. In fact, a significant portion of passive galaxies are actually disk-like systems, indicating that quenching mechanisms can be complex. Our findings reveal a universe where disk-shaped galaxies are the dominant form, with many becoming less rotation-supported after quenching.

Tractable density models known as normalizing flows can approximate intricate target distributions such as the Boltzmann distribution in complex physical systems. However, current approaches for training these models are hindered by mode-seeking behavior, reliance on samples generated through expensive MCMC simulations, or stochastic losses with high variance. To address these issues, we combine normalizing flows with annealed importance sampling (AIS) and utilize the mass-covering $\alpha$-divergence with $\alpha=2$, minimizing the variance of the importance weights. Our method, the Flow AIS Bootstrap (FAB), employs AIS to generate samples where the flow poorly represents the target distribution, enabling the discovery of novel modes. FAB is applied to complex, multimodal targets and achieves accurate approximations where previous methods fail. Furthermore, we demonstrate the first instance of learning the Boltzmann distribution of the alanine dipeptide molecule solely from the unnormalized target density without utilizing samples from Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations. FAB outperforms maximum likelihood training on MD samples while reducing target evaluations by a factor of 100. After applying importance weights to the samples, we obtain nearly identical unbiased histograms of dihedral angles to the ground truth.

Capturing the complexities of user behavior patterns is vital in modern e-commerce, often aimed at enhancing click-through rate and conversion rate forecasting. Most existing methods fail to consider two essential factors: first, user behavior on an item is influenced not just by the item itself but also by their past interactions with other items; second, users often exhibit frequent clicking but sporadic purchasing. To address this, we introduce HEROES (Hierarchical rEcurrent Ranking On the Entire Space), a multi-scale user behavior network that incorporates contextual information. HEROES features a hierarchical architecture with lower and upper layers that model engagement and satisfaction behaviors, respectively, and automatically determines the optimal time scale for each layer. The model employs a novel recurrent unit based on the Hawkes process, enabling it to capture item features and user behavioral patterns. Additionally, HEROES can be combined with survival analysis to create unbiased ranking systems. Experiments on large-scale industrial datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach compared to existing methods.

The Lightning Network has experienced rapid expansion in recent years and has become the leading solution for scaling the Bitcoin blockchain. Its security relies on nodes' ability to settle balances within a set timeframe by confirming transactions on the blockchain, which can be vulnerable to attacks seeking to congest the Bitcoin blockchain and prevent the correct execution of the protocol. In this context, we examine the susceptibility of the Lightning Network to'mass exit' attacks by a small coalition of adversarial nodes. This involves a scenario where an adversary forces a large group of honest protocol participants to interact with the blockchain, focusing on two types of attacks. The first type, a 'zombie' attack, involves a set of nodes intentionally becoming unresponsive to hold channel funds for a longer period than the LN protocol dictates. The second type, a'mass double-spend' attack, involves a set of nodes attempting to steal funds by submitting multiple closing transactions that use outdated protocol states, causing honest nodes to quickly submit invalidating transactions. Our simulations demonstrate that, under realistic congestion conditions, both types of attacks can be executed by a very small coalition under mild statistical assumptions on channel balances. To support our experimental findings, we formulated the problem of identifying the worst-case coalition of adversarial nodes as a graph cut problem and justified our results with a theoretical explanation based on the scale-free topology of the LN.

Our research involves photometrically searching for newly discovered cataclysmic variable stars, focusing on potential AR~Scorpii-type binary systems. By analyzing GAIA sources possibly linked to unidentified X-ray sources, we examined the light curves from the Zwicky Transient Facility, the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, and the Lulin One-meter Telescope in Taiwan. Out of eight candidate CVs, six were previously unknown, while two had been identified as CVs earlier but not thoroughly investigated. Two eclipsing binary systems were associated with unidentified XMM-Newton or Swift sources, as well as one promising candidate for a polar system linked to an unidentified ASKA source. Two possible polar candidates are located in the so-called period gap of a CV, and the remaining six candidates have orbital periods shorter than that gap. Despite not identifying a promising AR~Scorpii-type binary candidate, our study suggests that previous surveys might have overlooked CV systems exhibiting X-ray emission but without frequent outbursts.

Research on stratified shear instabilities often relies on the assumption that the shear and buoyancy interfaces align perfectly. We investigate how asymmetry affects the development of these instabilities, using linear stability analysis and direct numerical simulations. Our findings show that asymmetric instabilities combine characteristics of Holmboe and Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities, allowing us to categorize them as either Holmboe-like or Kelvin-Helmholtz-like. The asymmetric instabilities produce uneven mixing, displaying features of both overturning and scouring flows, which tends to realign the shear and buoyancy interfaces. In nearly all non-symmetric Kelvin-Helmholtz simulations, we notice a decrease in the variability of gradient Richardson number ($Ri_g$), suggesting that asymmetry minimizes the dependence of mixing events on specific parameters. The observed connection between turbulent behavior and small-scale shear and stratification details has significant implications for interpreting oceanographic data.

Recent advancements in unpaired image denoising have been notable.  Despite impressive results, current approaches often heavily depend on the noise characteristics or assumptions that are not always feasible in real-world scenarios.  In contrast, framing the issue from a structural perspective could lead to more robust solutions.  In response to this, we develop a self-supervised denoising method that operates without paired data and is instead based on a process involving spatial degradation and refined regularization. This new approach demonstrates significant gains over previous methods and achieves consistent performance across diverse datasets.

A crucial transmembrane receptor protein, integrin, plays a significant role in cell membrane organization by modulating the actin network and securing cell membrane attachment to the extracellular matrix via force-driven biochemical interactions. This protein enables the concentration of specific lipids and lipid-bound molecules, which is vital for a particular type of cellular internalization process, at areas influenced by integrin activity. To examine this phenomenon, we introduce a simple, solvable model that accounts for the stochastic switching between integrin 'on' and 'off' states and the inherent dynamics of the cell membrane. By deriving a mathematical expression for cell membrane distortion, local membrane velocity, and resulting lipid aggregation, facilitated by a single integrin, we demonstrate that these processes exhibit non-linear behavior and highlight the impact of stochastic switching timescales and cell membrane characteristics.

Researchers have found numerical solutions to the Einstein constraint equations on a variety of compact three-dimensional manifolds with complex shapes. These solutions, one with a simple constant mean curvature and another with a more complex non-constant mean curvature, were computed on specific manifolds representing three of the distinct geometric classes identified by Thurston. Additionally, the constant mean curvature solutions also address the Yamabe problem, which seeks to transform a given geometry into one with a uniform curvature.

The concept of homophily is described as "similarity begets connections." Within network analysis, we quantify this idea by evaluating the extent to which the classes of vertices in a given network partition form subgraphs that are more densely connected than those formed by randomly assigned partitions. This concept is formalized using the random coloring model for network homophily, where the sizes of subgraphs induced by the partition classes are seen as outcomes from a random vector. The input network is considered homophilic at a significance level of α if the one-sided probability of observing an outcome at least as extreme is less than α. Since approximating this probability is computationally intractable, we use a multidimensional extension of Cantelli's inequality to derive an upper bound on α, referred to as the homophily index. This index relies on the knowledge of the covariance matrix of the random vector, which we compute under the random coloring model. Notably, the resulting matrix is determined solely by the partition type and network degrees, and exhibits graph invariants that simplify its calculation.

The Fabbri-Russo model is an advanced representation of a two-dimensional dilaton gravity theory with the ability to describe multiple specific gravity types. A particular variant, the Russo-Susskind-Thorlacius gravity model, is an instance of this representation. By analyzing the Fabbri-Russo model, we examine how Page curves and the phenomenon of entanglement islands develop in eternal and evaporating black holes. Interestingly, in every black hole, the emergence of entanglement islands causes the rise in entanglement entropy to slow down after the Page time, upholding the principle of unitarity. In eternal black holes, fine-grained entropy reaches a fixed value equal to double the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy, whereas in evaporating black holes, it ultimately reaches zero. The model's parameter greatly affects the Page curve during extremely early stages. However, at late times and in the large distance limit, this parameter's impact is significantly reduced. Consequently, the shape of Page curves is largely independent of the parameter at a leading order. Furthermore, we discuss the relationship between islands and firewalls, demonstrating that entanglement islands are a more suitable solution to the quantum entanglement-monogamy problem than firewalls. Finally, we outline the gravity/ensemble duality as a possible solution to the state puzzle arising from the island formula.

A temporal point process is typically employed to model event sequences with probabilistic models conditioned on historical influences.
However, past studies focusing on maximizing likelihood to evaluate the fit of temporal point process models have shown unsatisfactory predictive results with generated timestamps being far from actual observations.
Deep generative models have achieved significant success in image generation tasks by producing high-quality samples, yet there is a lack of comprehensive research exploring their potential in modeling event occurrence for temporal point processes.
This study addresses the gap by developing a unified framework called GNTPP for generative neural temporal point processes, examining their feasibility and effectiveness, and enhancing their predictive performance.
Moreover, a revised attentive model is introduced that considers events' type and time relation with an adaptive reweighting term for better measuring historical influences.
Extensive experiments were conducted to demonstrate the improved predictive capability of GNTPP with a line of generative probabilistic decoders and the benefits of the revised attention.
To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to integrate generative models into a unified framework and investigate their effectiveness in the context of temporal point processes.
The codebase for GNTPP is available on GitHub, aiming to facilitate future research in neural temporal point processes.

Vehicular networks could benefit from federated edge learning technology to decrease computation demands while maintaining users' data privacy. In the edge learning system, vehicles transmit data to edge servers, which then train the data locally without compromising privacy. However, the limited edge cache queue and the variable wireless channels between servers and vehicles create complexities in determining the ideal number of vehicles to engage in data upload. This, in turn, affects model accuracy due to the varying resource capacities of the involved vehicles. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a novel vehicle selection approach that considers the status of all connected vehicles to optimize learning accuracy while maintaining a stable edge cache queue. Simulation results show that this approach outperforms existing benchmark methods.
